chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
A bouncy synth line yowls in the background of the news report, accompanied by footage of a busy stage. The newscaster’s voice is a diminutive buzz next to the music; not by any fault of the sound mixing, no, but by the sheer audacity of stuffing woodwinds, guitar riffs, and early electronica into a single caffeine-addled pop song.

“…marks almost a decade since our last Astral Fantasia win. That’s right, Euphrosyne by Sun and Thunder is turning ten this year, which also means it’s been ten years since Amphoreus has podiumed-”

The song teeters between unpleasant and frustratingly catchy, staying in the middle just enough to be considered ‘refreshingly novel’. Truthfully, it’s not a complicated thing to play. If you listen past the riffs and the licks, there are only four chords used in the entirety of Euphrosyne. Nothing flashy either. No diminished chords or major sevenths or anything so ambitious. It was kept simple to match the lyrics: a banal 3 minute campaign urging crowds to get up and dance.

Perhaps if it had been sung by the usual suspects, it wouldn’t have gotten nominated to join an international competition, let alone crowned as its best song. Instead, the clip showed a teenager performing his soul out on stage, donning a grin so boyishly charming that you could have heard the hearts of every teenage girl in Asdana break. He should have been a spokesman for a sports drink or something like that; extolling the benefits of electrolytes as he ran up and down the stage, sweat flinging this way and that with each backflip he attempted.

The most impressive part is how the teenager managed to sing above the din of the band behind him. His voice was a paradoxically sweet tenor, clear and invigorating, like a glass of cold water. It cut through the noise and tethered each meandering instrument into a single cohesive melody. There were the occasional flubs of course, with him dancing all over the stage, but nothing so disgraceful as a full voice crack.

Another voice occasionally joined in, perhaps a contingency plan in case a bad somersault took their main singer out. The energetic frontman never stayed in one place for too long, but if he had to, he’d settle down next to the other teenage boy on stage, who stood rooted in his spot. It would be difficult for him to move in the same manner, being preoccupied by his guitar and all.

His voice wasn’t any much lower than the other, but it was raspier, as if he’d forgotten to drink the entire day. The teenage girls that would have scoffed at the first one for being too clean-cut would have swooned at the sight of the second. He glared at any camera that pointed at him, but his teenybopper sensibilities declawed any threat he could possibly embody.

It was all a precarious balancing act, one that’s beginning to show its age. As the two boys harmonized into the same microphone, the sound of stifled laughter cut them off.

“Aw for Kephale’s sake Cyrene, do you have to watch that?”

A full blown laugh bursts out of Cyrene’s mouth as her brother strides into the room and callously shuts off the television. He pulls a baleful face to let her know how disheartened he was, but since Cyrene isn’t a dog, the sight of a grown man pouting only exacerbates her guffaws.

“It’s not everyday you’re on the news,” Cyrene says once she weans off the laughter.

“Hey, knock on wood! I don’t want to be on the news. You know how celebrities get on the news? Career-ending scandals and lawsuits. Or like, death or something.”

Point taken. Still, you can’t blame Cyrene for trying to take her little brother down a peg. Even now, in the sanctity of their parents’ home, Phainon is dressed in colors that only match with chromatopsia. No matter what basic sense dictates, he insists he pulls off the purple pants, that it’s more Prince than Wonka. Up top isn’t any better. His pastel turquoise polo plunges into a deep V-neck that makes Cyrene wish for a lobotomy, and all the extra fabric gets wasted into giving Phainon a collar that makes him look like a cartoon supervillain. It’s like he doesn’t know whether or not he wants people to look at his neck, and it would have stayed a mystery if not for that orange-as-hell tattoo.

Hmm, then again, Phainon’s never been much of a dresser. Did Cyrene ruin his chances at a normal life when she had that Cheetah Girls phase and decided that her brother should match with her?

No. It was the fame that did that. Cyrene is only a victim of this cruel system, while Phainon… well.

Over the past years, Phainon has carved out a home in the top charts, only being absent from the top 50 when he’s on a break between albums. Turns out, the Astral Fantasia Music Festival had only been the start. After that, anything with his face or name on it sold like hotcakes, and his vocal cords went on to be insured for an amount that Cyrene cannot possibly fathom. Phainon is a sensation, and the masses will never get enough of him.

Of course, only in Amphoreus.

But nationwide stardom is still big shoes for a village boy to fill.

“I don’t like how you’re looking at me,” Phainon says, crossing his arms. Thank god. That should give Cyrene a minute of freedom from his nip slips.

“Just thinking,” Cyrene replies.

“About what?”

“‘Bout that old acquaintance of yours,” Cyrene says. “You know, about yay-high, strawberry blond, looks like this?”

Cyrene does her best blue steel impression, but it falls more like Marlon Brando in the first Godfather. Phainon rolls his eyes.

“Ha ha,” he deadpans. “No, really, what’s on your mind?”

“Okay, I was thinking that, maybe, we shouldn’t dress like a gigolo when we celebrate mom’s birthday,” Cyrene says.

Phainon frowns as he gives her a once-over. “But you’re not dressed like a gigolo?”

“Really now? Did you turn into a vampire?” Cyrene asks, squinting. “Are mirrors not working for you or something?”

“Your mom said I look nice!”

“Mom’s from the seventies! You should run if she says you look nice! You’re going to be in photos next to Aunt Evi in her mumu and you’re going to look like the ghost of her dead boy toy-”

Later, when she’s two bowls deep in stew, Cyrene remembers her brother’s wandering attention span, and how easy it usually is to re-direct him from the topic at hand.

___

The television turns off, and Krateros turns to the man reclining on the couch.

“What do you think?” Krateros asks, something expectant looming in his tone.

The other man simply scratches his head. “I think the new song needs some cowbell.”

Krateros sighs. “You know that’s not what I’m talking about, Mydei.”

Mydei hums, but offers nothing else. What is there to say about news correspondents discussing an old song? Must be a slow news day if that’s what they’re broadcasting.

“It’s been ten years since the Fantasia win,” Krateros prompts. “That’s ten years since you’ve been out of the spotlight.”

“I’m aware,” Mydei answers.

“Don’t you want to… try coming back? See if you still got it?”

“I’m not interested in petty cash grabs.” Mydei says, getting straight to the point. “And I was never interested in performing in front of a live audience.”

“Right. I understand.”

Krateros drops it, but he continues to avoid Mydei’s gaze. A melodrama plays on the older man’s face, his features twisting into grief and pity between forced intervals of stoicism. As funny as it was, it’s no laughing matter when it’s at Mydei’s expense.

Mydei sighs out loud. “I’m telling the truth.”

“I believe you.” Krateros keeps the act up for a brief second longer, only to crumble when Mydei adds a touch of force in his glare. He lets out a sigh of his own. “Isn’t it unfair? That boy gets to ride out the success you paved for him, while people forget you even contributed at all…?”

“I consider that ideal actually,” Mydei says. “I’ve seen what the attention gets him. It’s not like my songs aren’t popular either.”

“The songs are popular. The songs rise right up to number one and get all the air time they deserve, but never with your name. They’re always attached to some pop star or a minute-fourteen singer who can never hold a candle to the original demo.”

“You can always find my name on the ASCAP listing.”

Judging from the look Krateros gives him, Mydei was beginning to grate on his nerves. Fortunately for him, Krateros always has some patience set aside for bullheaded songwriters.

“I think you deserve more credit than you’re currently getting,” Krateros says. “You’ve got a bunch of drafts in your back pocket that you never pitch. Like that one, about the ankles-”

“I’ve never written anything about ankles.”

“You know which one I mean. You didn’t even want to play it in full in front of me.”

“Because it was incomplete.”

“But it was great! Unfinished or not, it was way better than the throwaways you’ve been giving away,” Krateros says. “Are you telling me, that there’s not even a tiny part of you that wants to be proud of your own work?”

Mydei could readily say that he always takes pride in his songs, but even when he’s playing the fool, he understands Krateros’s words all too well. Ah, no matter. Even with the implications of Mydei’s silence, Krateros wouldn’t act on it. What is there for him to do, other than to proselytize on online music forums?

Instead, Mydei hums. “A cowbell between the hook and the chorus could give the transition more oomph.”

And because Mydei’s agent has never been anything less than supportive, Krateros holds back his grumbles. “Do you want me to search for a physical cowbell or do you have one already?”

As he plots the additions to his percussions, Mydei allows himself to wonder. What would taking advantage of the anniversary look like? It is true that Mydei was a part of that victory, but he didn’t achieve it on his lonesome. Nor was he the one in high demand. To release an acknowledgement on his own would be like chucking a pebble onto a typhoon; insignificant, and more effort than it’s worth.

Still, he can’t help but imagine. If Mydei would ask, what would Phainon say about a reunion?

___

“You’re kidding.”

“Do I look like I’m joking?” Anaxa asks. Frankly, he looks like he just stepped in dog doo-doo, but that’s just his default expression.

“I thought Lygus said it was ‘tacky’,” Phainon presses, leaning forward on Anaxa’s desk. “That it would ‘muddle the brand’ if we did something with Sun and Thunder?”

“Then that should tell you that Lygus wasn’t the one who made this decision,” Anaxa says matter-of-factly. He gives Phainon a sneer that makes Phainon feel like a regressed species. “The higher-ups thought it would be - ugh - ‘‘‘fun’’’ to have you cavort with your old playmate on a morning show or two. They dubbed it an ‘era of reflection’, whatever that means.”

“But, like, we’re not even signed to the same label.”

Anaxa’s patronizing tone deepens. “I know you’re Grove’s show pony, but surely you know you can collaborate with anybody, right? There’s no clause in your contract stating you can only work with the other sycophants.”

Phainon does know that. He did that one feature an eon ago with that rapper from Belobog, and the song was enough of an ear worm to see rotation in some niche clubs. As far as Phainon was aware, the feature was a success, but nowhere near as successful as Grove Records hoped it would be. Everyone learned then that the international market wasn’t something so easily breached, and any plans of joining forces with other musical acts got shelved for the foreseeable future.

Perhaps they’ve finally ventured into the unforeseeable future then? Or maybe there really is money in being tacky and pandering. Go figure.

“I don’t think Mydei would agree,” Phainon says. God, it’s been ages since he’s said that name proper. The muscles that sound out the syllables must have atrophied, because it comes out in a stuttered choke.

This moment of weakness will bite him in the ass one day, as they always do when Anaxa is watching, but for now, his manager extends him a rare mercy. “We’ve already reached out to his handlers,” Anaxa says. “And they gave us the green light.”

“But what about Mydei?”

Anaxa leans back in his chair. “He said something interesting, which is why you’re standing here instead of getting shoved into a recording suite without prior notice.”

“…He told us no?”

A twisted smirk creeps onto Anaxa’s face. “He told us to ask Phainon.”

___

Four months sounds like an ample period of time, but they still need to decide on the scope of the project, on the studios and session players to book, of the venues and sponsors to prioritize. If it was a deadline that can be pushed, then perhaps it wouldn’t be so dire, but there’s only one day out of all the days in the space of forever that marks Euphrosyne’s tenth anniversary.

There is definitely no time for both central figures to play hot potato with the final say, pushing the responsibility onto the other through a chain of increasingly tedious e-mails. The local fruit basket industry has never seen such a meteoric rise in their commerce. Dictionaries and thesauruses have been run ragged in the quest for new, innovative ways to say ‘maybe’.

This game of chicken comes to a head one cloudy afternoon, in the underground parking lot of Mydei’s workplace. He spots a shock of ivory hair half hidden behind a concrete foundation and the expletive shoots out of his mouth before he could stop it: “Son of a bitch.”

“Actually, it’s Phainon,” the demon says, a million dollar smile magically materializing on his face. “What should I call you, stranger?”

Mydei doesn’t respond, opting instead to leg it to his car a little faster. He doesn’t openly run because that would be admitting defeat, which ironically proves to be his downfall. Unlike him, Phainon is amenable to going into a full sprint indoors, so Mydei inevitably finds himself playing point guard to Phainon’s defense.

“I’m busy,” Mydei says as he attempts to step around Phainon, who hops right into place in front of him.

“So am I, but I can’t get any work done until I get either a ‘yes’ or ‘no’,” Phainon explains.

Mydei looks around to find neither hide nor hair of Phainon’s security detail. This is bad. Mydei can’t be alone with Phainon like this. He feigns left to pass around him, but the bastard blocks him in time with an outstretched leg.

“My side called last,” Mydei argues.

“Oh yeah, because ‘close affirmation’ is such a conclusive reply,” Phainon drawls.

“And ‘it’s schedule determinant’ isn’t?”

“It’s a reason.” Phainon shoves Mydei back when he tries to brute force his way through. “I told you, I’ve got things to do. I can’t go forward with any of them if I don’t get a confirmation.”

“Then confirm it, dumbass.”

“I’m being considerate to your schedule.”

“My schedule? You think I’m more booked than the guy selling out arenas?”

Mydei catches Phainon’s wrist when the pop star goes for another shove, and Phainon retaliates by grabbing Mydei’s arm. “You literally just said you’re busy,” Phainon points out.

“Because I have a job,” Mydei growls. “Same as you. Same as everyone you’re screwing over because you can’t make up your mind!”

“The fuck?” Phainon laughs in anger. “The pot calling me indecisive?”

Mydei pushes back against Phainon’s lunges. “Aren’t you? You could have ended it all with one word.”

“Oh you’d like that, wouldn’t you? So I get blamed if shit goes sideways?”

“Who gives a shit? The Okhema times? Sorry if the headlines don’t personally suck your dick this one time.”

“That’s fine with me. If you’re lucky, maybe you’ll get a shout out in the article. Aww, baby’s first mention in anything relevant ever!”

“Fuck you.”

“Stole the words right out o- mMPH!” A palm shoots out and covers Phainon’s mouth, fiercely gripping onto his jaw as if Mydei wanted to smush the bone underneath into jam. Phainon starts punching at Mydei’s arm for freedom, and when that doesn’t work, he reaches under and plucks a pinch of Mydei’s armpit hair.

“Shit!” Mydei immediately draws back.

“That’s what you get for wearing a muscle shirt to work,” Phainon says. “You don’t have good air circulation in here or what?”

There was no need for further heckling, because Mydei is back on Phainon in a flash, fists and elbows everywhere it could land. Phainon blocks as many hits as he can between his own occasional punches, making sure that wherever he strikes, it would sting like a bitch.

They were surprisingly even in strength, despite Mydei having worked his physique into idealistic proportions. Phainon, for all his jumping and gyrating on stage, had developed a practical set of muscles that functioned as good as they looked, and they were holding their own against Mydei’s brutal pounding.

Eventually it devolves once more into juvenile shoving and pushing, and when a particularly forceful thrust topples one onto the ground, the other follows suit with a straddle. The two of them continued to tussle on the floor, collecting scratches from rolling to and fro on the asphalt.

“Hello? Excuse me?”

The sound of a new voice forces Phainon and Mydei to look up. An elderly security guard stands there, tutting at the sight of of them. Understandable. There’s nothing dignified about Phainon sitting on top of Mydei, his hands holding tight to fistfuls of stained blond hair while the man underneath tries to kick his spine in.

“Is this really the best way to handle this?” The security guard asks. His voice is soft and wheezy, as if he’s perpetually out of breath.

The two men immediately jump up from the ground, frantically dusting off whatever debris they’ve accumulated. Phainon was the first to interject: “He started it!”

“So you should stoop to his level?” The guard chastises before turning to the other grown adult. “And Mydei. I know you never let emotions get the better of you. How could you do this?”

Mydei’s skin takes on a reddened flush. “I didn’t ask for a fight! If he’d just lea-”

“None of that now,” the guard cuts him off. “The ‘if’ isn’t important when it already happened.”

Mydei’s shoulders slump. “Sorry.”

“I’m not the one you should be saying that to. What if a car came over and couldn’t see you? You two could have gotten seriously hurt!”

“We won’t do this ever again, sir,” Phainon sheepishly promises. “It just got a little heated there for a moment, is all.”

The security guard shakes his head. “No matter how badly you disagree with each other, you should never let it get physical. Why, the wife and I have had plenty of arguments over the years, all more serious than whatever this tiff could be about. Not once have I ever thought of laying my hands on her.”

Phainon stammers. “I mean, she’s your wife-”

“Now more than ever, we need to practice kindness towards our fellow man,” the guard preaches. “Male, female, neither, both… Whether she’s your wife or your mortal enemy, everyone loses when we take up violence.”

“Agreed,” Mydei mumbles.

The guard crosses his arms. “If you really agree, the both of you would apologize to each other.”

That fails to earn a single twitch from either Phainon or Mydei.

“Go on,” the guard coaxes. “If a car were to drive into one of you and fatally injure him on the spot, the remaining one would regret not saying anything right now.”

At that ominous warning, the two grown men in front of him stiffly turn to face one another. With each second that passed without a single word being uttered, the old man’s disapproving stare grew heavier and heavier until Mydei broke.

“Sorry,” he spits out.

“Me too,” Phainon grumbles. “Sorry.”

That gets the security guard nodding. “If that doesn’t bury the hatchet, then there’s this café, two blocks down towards the city center. It’s got good soup and better sandwiches. You go there, and you order the mezze platter, the one with the big sharing portion. I’m talking stuffed grape leaves, grilled shrimp, and a huge blooming onion. You get that, and you come out of there the best of friends.”

The next few minutes pass in a haze, where the two of them were listening to directions in one moment and sharing an elevator in the next. They’re way out on the street by the time they come to, toddling along side-by-side in silence. Mydei glances to the man next to him, only to find him glancing back.

That’s when the confused laughter breaks out.

“What the hell?” Mydei asks through his befuddled snickers.

“I don’t know,” Phainon says, also sounding very confused and giggly. “I don’t know where we’re going.”

It seems they’re going to a café. Thankfully there weren’t too many people out on the pavement, and the few that were didn’t recognize the man cackling boisterously through layers of grime. The cafeteria itself was somewhat busier, but Mydei tactfully uses his size to shield Phainon from as many eyes as possible.

They settle down at a booth tucked near the back, placing them precariously close to the restrooms. As they wait for someone to serve them, Phainon fishes out a ratty beanie from his cargo pockets and plops it on his mussed hair, fulfilling the joint purpose of indiscretion and vanity. It takes a good while for a server to notice their table, but Phainon and Mydei make it up by ordering before the server could take out the menu.

Silence is generally an awkward thing, but neither men had minded it on their trip to the cafeteria. Maybe they were busy thinking of the right thing to say, or maybe they’re steeling their courage to propose the wrong thing.

Either way, they’re on the same page, and both seemed to agree that this silence is starting to get a little too long.

This time, Phainon is the one who starts. “So…”

“So,” Mydei echoes.

“…Are you planning something in the next few months?” Phainon asks. “Like do you have another recording to do, or…?”

“Nothing,” Mydei says. “What I do on a day-to-day basis is up to me. I might have a few mixes that need some refining, but nothing set in stone. You?”

“Brand deal,” Phainon answers, slumping on the table. “Can’t get into it, NDA stuff, but they probably won’t mind nudging it a bit if we did the…”

Do the what? No one knows what they were even pestering each other about. Grove had their ideas, naturally, but as the negotiations dragged on, they stressed that they were open to accepting suggestions from Mydei. It seemed that the important thing was to get Sun and Thunder in the same room again, and then they can take control under the guise of everyone’s tacit consent.

Mydei didn’t dare think that Grove was actually going relinquish some of their authority, especially if it’s to let him go wild on a project that had their biggest star attached. Grove might have been a welcoming no-name label back when Mydei was signed with them, but they’ve always been ambitious for more. With Phainon securing their growth year after year, Mydei suspects they’re a little more comfortable with slinging their power around.

If they’re really curious about what’s planned for them, then there’s an easy way for Phainon and Mydei to find out. It’s just that once they agree, there’s no backing out.

The sharing platter arrives, and as the server places it down, she makes eye contact with Phainon and lets out a small gasp. Phainon responds with a wink, short-circuiting the poor server as she makes her escape back to the kitchen.

Mydei watches her as Phainon digs in. “Any time, any place, huh?” Mydei comments.

“For these meatballs? Absolutely.”

That security guard was right. It would difficult to be angry when there’s a dozen delicious little morsels to distract you. The dish came with a bevy of dips and sauces, and finding out which tastes best with what mezze is half the fun. That’s probably why it was made to share, for friends and family to discuss new culinary findings. Phainon and Mydei decided they’re better off with their own game, in which one pretends they haven’t paired together the most disgusting combination on the plate while the other tries to gulp it down without flinching.

The platter is soon reduced into crumbs and sad swipes of sauce, and the conversation that they deemed far too difficult to broach is no longer as daunting. As the plates and glasses get cleared away, Mydei decides that it’s better to rip the bandage clean rather than continue going around in circles.

“It wouldn’t be the worst thing to work with you again,” Mydei admits as they wait for the bill.

“Hffomp?” Phainon says, accidentally stabbing himself in the gums with a toothpick when he hears Mydei speak. He tries again once he disposes the toothpick into a piece of tissue. “You’re agreeing?”

“…Sure.”

“Really? Really, really? You mean it?”

Mydei shrugs. “If you’re not too busy.”

“Hmm, let me double check with my calendar…”

Phainon takes out his phone and begins to scroll, watching the way Mydei’s brows furrow from the corner of his eye. When Mydei’s lips also starts curling downward, Phainon flings his phone to the side.

“Yeah, I’m free,” Phainon announces. With his elbow on the table, Phainon rests his chin on his palm and grins at Mydei. “What do you think we should do, big guy?”

Mydei’s looks over to the rest of the cafeteria, which is still very much bustling with customers. “I don’t think we should talk about that here.”

“Why not? Leaks hype people up don’t they?”

“Not this early it doesn’t,” Mydei says. “…Shouldn’t you have security guards telling you this or something?”

“I would have, usually, but I thought this was going to be a quick visit. Then you started punching me.”

“I didn’t start it.”

“To-may-to, to-mah-to.” Phainon waves Mydei’s excuses off. “The important thing is that we got things done, right?”

“Yes,” Mydei sighs. “Now the hard part begins.”

___

There’s only one perfectly working eyeball between the two of them, but somehow, they manage to stare a hole into Phainon.

If there was ever a time for Phainon to use his God given good looks, it was now. He subtly tilts his head low - an angle that every photographer is obsessed with him holding still - and sweetens his tone as he asks, “Is something the matter?”

Across the meeting room table, Aglaea pinches the bridge of her nose. “You want to re-record Euphrosyne?”

“Yep.”

“And write a new song?” Anaxa asks.

“As Sun and Thunder, yes.”

“You might have gotten your wires crossed,” Aglaea says. “We’re not looking for a full reunion. Just a small bit of recognition for the fans who stuck with you from the beginning.”

“Yeah, and what better way to do that than to release something from the vault?”

“You specifically said it was going to be new,” Anaxa points out. “Also, if you did have an extra song lying around, I would have known about it ages ago.”

“It’s not with me,” Phainon explains. “And it would be new to the fans.”

Aglaea is shaking her heads before Phainon even finishes. “Sorry, but I don’t think anyone would agree to this. Please tell Mydeimos that we can’t meet his demands.”

“Whoa, hey now. I didn’t say it was only Mydei who wanted this.”

“Why would you want this?” Aglaea levels him with another scrutinizing stare. “Is Anaxagoras not bidding on enough songs for you?”

“I got him an army of producers on speed-dial, keep my name out of your mouth,” Anaxa remarks.

“Would it be so bad to have one more?” Phainon suggests.

“We planned for one song,” Aglaea points out. “The idea was to go big with marketing, getting it into advertising, soundtracks, remixes- Whatever fits with whatever you end up with. Another song means splitting our efforts.”

“They can already do that with Euphrosyne now. Wouldn’t it be easier to have a second one to widen the net?”

“It doesn’t have to be a remake of Euphrosyne if you’re so opposed.”

“But Euphrosyne is the Sun and Thunder song.”

“That’s why I’d prefer it to be the song you work on,” Aglaea says, a touch sterner. “A new song would be lovely, but our projected budget works best with one release.”

“So I’ll fund what’s missing,” Phainon proposes. “Tell the board that I’ll pay for it right out of my pocket, then you can let it slip to a journalist or a blogger that I’m personally financing a portion of the process. People will spin it as like, me investing in it so much because it’s a passion project, which would be a even bigger honor to the fans. It’s more exposure and we reduce the reviews calling us sell-outs.”

Aglaea’s mouth hangs very slightly agape. She glances at Anaxa, who looks affronted to meet her gaze.

“What are you looking at me for? You’re the one that taught him all that,” he says.

As Phainon’s publicist, it’s Aglaea’s job to make sure he looks good regardless of what he does. It is not Phainon’s job, because ‘looks good’ means figuratively and literally. Phainon’s taste for bright jerseys and rubber clogs would not mesh well with that requirement. His only saving grace is his above-average appearance, which turns every sartorial faux pas he makes into a fashion statement, much to Aglaea’s anguish. It is Aglaea’s deepest wish to never see him calling the shots from her position.

Nevertheless, Aglaea finds some joy in knowing that her words and actions have taught him to be a little more shrewd. “I will admit that you present a compelling strategy,” Aglaea says, adjusting her glasses. “However, it relies too much on optimistic risk assessment. There’s a real possibility that people might view you as a try-hard instead.”

“How? You’re really good at controlling the narrative,” Phainon says.

“Flatterer. Although I can’t promise I will always be so infallible."

“I think that still means it’s worth a try,” Phainon insists. “At this point, why not challenge ourselves?”

Aglaea and Anaxa exchange a look. Consensually this time. They appear doubtful, but the fact that they’re taking the time to think about it bodes well for Phainon.

“It’ll take some arguing with the bigwigs,” Anaxa warns Phainon before he gets too excited. “We might have some pull, but the executives don’t like taking risks like these.”

“How is it risky?” Phainon says. “We’re doing what they asked for and doubling it.”

“Let me ask you this.” Anaxa steeples his hands. “Do you think you’ll be able to make a good song? Better yet, do you think Gorgo’s brat can write a good song?”

Had Anaxa stopped at the first question, Phainon would have hesitated. It is to his luck that his manager continued, so Phainon can answer with the most affirmative nod he can muster. “Absolutely. Mydei can definitely write a good song.”

“Is he already writing one? Have you heard a snippet?” Anaxa questions.

“No, but he’s the one that wrote Euphro,” Phainon states. “He’s gotten ten years of experience since then, so I know he can pull it off.”

“In half a month, mind you,” Aglaea reminds him.

“He can do it. Just listen to the songs he’s put out, you’ll know he can do it.”

“God,” Anaxa sighs and rolls his good eye. “He’s gone full gaga for this guy.”

Phainon only smiles, because he doesn’t have to tell them everything.

___

Writing two songs in three weeks is impossible, but it was the hand he was dealt with, so Mydei grunts and bears it with grace.

For once, he’s glad for his collection of abandoned songs, because now there’s a way out of this hole. Sure, there’s years of incomplete music to sift through and he doesn’t remember all of them, but he’s certain that he’s got something stowed away for this exact occasion.

“Found anything yet?”

Mydei is folders deep in his computer when Phainon enters the room holding two mugs. Figgy takes this chance to weasel in, nearly bowling Phainon over to get to her spare dog bed. Without any more spontaneous mountain dogs to ambush him, Phainon decides to leave the door open to concentrate on transporting the mugs safely. He sets one down beside Mydei and squints at the screen, as if it could help him hear what Mydei’s Sennheisers are playing.

This is another complication with the project. Since Sun and Thunder means Phainon and Mydei, the superstar apparently needs to be present for the conception of their new song. It means that sometimes Mydei has a babysitting job to do, and that sometimes he’s got an extra laborer to exploit. Personally, it doesn’t feel great to have Phainon listening in on his half-baked melodies, but at least he’s got someone to deliver snacks for him.

“I haven’t found it yet,” Mydei says before taking a sip of his drink. It tastes of black tea, grenadine syrup, and clumped protein powder, which isn’t good, but it’s what Mydei deserves for taking advantage of this monkey’s paw.

“What about the one you played before I left? I thought it was okay,” Phainon chirps.

“It’s okay but it’s not amazing,” Mydei says.

“Couldn’t we… make it amazing? Like maybe it just needs some tweaking?”

Mydei shakes his head. “We can do better.”

Easy for him to say. Phainon has no idea what Mydei thinks the definition of ‘better’ is. First of all, Mydei isn’t even letting him listen to all of the tracks. Phainon only gets permission to listen to the demos that Mydei deems worthy, which could be anything really.

Then, every time he asks for Phainon’s opinion, Mydei vetos Phainon’s approval and says that there’s a ‘better’ option somewhere. It’s gotten to the point that Phainon wonders if this is Mydei’s way of telling him that his music taste sucks ass. Phainon wouldn’t put it past him, but Mydei’s not the kind of guy to play around in a professional setting.

Come to think of it, the setting is not that professional. They were working in Mydei’s two bedroom apartment, which appears to have been converted to a one-bedroom-one-music-studio apartment after Mydei signed the lease. The home studio is cozier than what Phainon is usually used to, but it’s as well-equipped as any production house worth its salt. There are keyboards and drum pads standing by in one corner, while the opposite corner has three guitars hanging on the wall. Phainon guesses they must be replicas of more famous guitars, because he recognizes one to be Serval Landau’s signature Misa Kitara.

Underneath the hanging guitars is a lineup of guitar cases, and next to it is a set of shelves filled with pedal boxes. A hefty upright bass sits by the amps and monitor speakers looking out of place, but not as out of place as the panpipes proudly lounging out with Figgy. Every instrument that Phainon can name is probably in this room, and those he can’t find is likely to be in the computer’s gigantic VST library.

Out of boredom, Phainon starts absentmindedly rummaging through the cabinets while he nurses his mug of red bull. No, it’s not snooping. There’s nothing to find in here other than loose equipment- or so Phainon thinks until he opens the second last drawer.

In it lies stacks of sheet music: far from pristine, but still reasonably put together. Phainon can’t sightread, regardless of how hard he tries, but he doesn’t need to read the notes to know that these are the scores for Mydei’s songs. The titles match with his known releases, though there’s not enough sheets to contain all of Mydei’s discography. Maybe he only makes these once in a blue moon, like if people ask for it, or if he’s struggling with a song and has to work it out like a math problem. The latter becomes more probable with how Mydei’s writing litter the margins with bullet points. His comments are blunt and unforgiving, no matter if it’s directed at a band or Mydei himself.

Near the end of the third stack, Phainon finds something curious. Between volumes full of neatly printed staves lies a single page of notebook paper, scrawled on with blotchy blue ink. The other sheet music were all as traditional as it gets, as if they were the first pass at an orchestral arrangement. This scrap paper - while technically counting as sheet music - barely even has a title. It only has three letters hanging clumsily above the notation, giving the impression that Mydei had given up on writing mid-stroke. Phainon doesn’t match the consonants to any of Mydei’s songs, so there’s a good chance this is a new one.

Mydei continues scrolling through his files, even as Phainon grabs one of his acoustic guitars and trades his mug for that piece of worn paper. Unlike the rest of its frumpy siblings, this song was written down in tabs, making it something that Phainon can actually play on the spot. As his fingers strum the first note, however, he notices a problem. He has no idea about its timing or strum pattern, having never heard the song before. He attempts a guess by looking at the gaps between each note, but his fingers don’t quite glide along the nylon strings. Through his experimental strums, Figgy stares at him judgmentally, but it’s a given considering her owner.

Phainon is in the middle of working out a chord when the guitar is snatched out of his arms. “Hey!”

His cry goes unheard as Mydei grabs the guitar and the tattered page. He carefully places the guitar back in its place before crumpling the sheet of paper into a ball and tossing it into the top drawer of his desk. The drawer gets locked too, and the key gets thrown into Mydei’s pants which is… not where Phainon would have said is the safest place.

If it were an appropriate time, maybe Phainon would have shown Mydei how secure his Lululemon joggers really were, but this doesn’t feel like an appropriate time. There’s a tense energy in the room as Mydei wordlessly seats himself back into his chair, one that Phainon hasn’t felt since the last time he got grounded. It doesn’t get any better when Mydei yanks his headphone cable out of its port with enough violent ardor to nudge his entire set-up forward.

Phainon gets the terrible vision of Mydei doing the same to his arms. Luckily for him, all Mydei does is twist his volume knob and say, “Listen to this.”

The order comes out gruff, from anger maybe. Phainon obeys without further ado, because as funny as they would be, he really doesn’t want to test out his theories. Even as he takes note of how Mydei’s neck has gone peony pink, Phainon keeps mum and does as Mydei tells him.

The headphones stay unplugged for the rest of the day.

___

“No, wait, play it back! That one sounded pretty good.”

“It sounds like dogshit.”

“No it doesn’t!”

“It doesn’t sound good either.”

“Maybe not good good, but I like how the bridge opens the second chorus. I don’t know if the glockenspiel is our sound, but-”

___ Human ears weren’t meant to be listening to rough, inscrutable cuts of music on a 24-hour loop, so by the second day of their increasingly grim search, Mydei reluctantly steps back. For now. Just until everything stops sounding like white noise.

“You said you were taking a break,” Phainon says, exasperated. “What about this is a break?”

Mydei pauses the recording. “I needed a break from going through those songs. So I’m getting a head start on Euphrosyne.”

“That’s not a break,” Phainon whines.

It seems the only thing he’s taking a break from is Phainon, because Mydei brushes him off to dive right back into song production.

Mydei is a smart man, maybe one of the smartest that Phainon knows, but he must have missed the memo about how working on a song requires a significant amount of listening. This is even worse than simply sorting through his unfinished catalogue, because now Mydei has to listen to individual tracks over and over again until he gets an idea on what to improve.

They might have agreed on remaking Euphrosyne, but it was under the context of doing it together, and Phainon doesn’t remember agreeing to Mydei working like a dog. With his wellness in mind, Phainon grabs the back of Mydei’s roller chair and pulls him away from his computer, earning him a shout from the cranky workaholic. Phainon does as Mydei has been doing and ignores his protests as he unplugs Mydei’s guitar from the computer. A loud pop rings from the speakers as the jack is flung halfway across the room, but Phainon powers on to undo Mydei’s guitar strap, skillfully evading Mydei’s open palm and freeing him of the guitar.

“What the hell do you think you’re doing?” Mydei growls, jumping out of the chair as Phainon attempts to push him out of the room.

“Showing you what a real break is,” Phainon says.

Mydei tries to march back to the computer, only for Phainon to crouch low and scoop him up into a fireman’s carry.

“What the fuck?!” Mydei exclaims. Once again, he is reminded of the hard work Phainon does to be one of the nation’s most sought out eye candy, because Phainon hauls him around the apartment as if Mydei was no heavier than a sack of tangerines.

Upon seeing her owner in peril, Figgy barks and hops around Phainon to stop him, but his legs are too long for her to be an obstacle. Perhaps realizing this, she lays down into a sad puddle of fur and whimpers.

“Aww. Sorry girl, but I have to borrow your master for a sec,” Phainon apologizes.

“The hell you don’t!” Mydei thumps a fist against Phainon’s back.

Phainon pats his flank in return. “Not in front of the baby, dear.”

“Let go of me!” Mydei demands, growing more fearful the closer they get to the front door. “No. Don’t. Don’t you dare. You will not step a single foot out of here. You God forsaken hyena, don’t-!”

It had been precisely 5 minutes since Phainon had entered Mydei’s house, and he’s already walking out of the door. After ensuring that the door is nice and locked, Phainon pulls his mask back up and takes a jaunty trip downstairs. Mydei mentally swears at the salesman that sold him that electronic lock. More secure, his ass.

Usually, when people see a man in a mask and a dark hoodie carting a person off, they would make the quick connection to something nefarious and attempt to help in any way they can. Alas, society is yet to divorce itself from orthodox thought, for no one bats an eye at the burly man hurling insults at his unmoved kidnapper. Mydei flails about enough to make himself dizzy, and he is still nowhere near breaking free of Phainon’s grasp.

“Fuck!” Mydei screams in frustration. The only person who reacts is a mother who hastily covers her son’s ears. She gives Mydei a crazy stink-eye, but why is her son even out of school on a weekday afternoon?

Despite Phainon’s iron grip, Mydei finds himself gradually sliding out of place. Maybe if it helped him get out of this situation, he wouldn’t mind, but all it does is move Mydei’s ass so it’s resting right on Phainon’s forearm. Mydei tries to jump up and adjust himself, which accomplishes nothing but polish his crotch against Phainon’s shoulder, so he’s not doing that again.

Mydei pitifully ragdolls over Phainon. “…Fine, I get it. Put me down.”

“Huh?” Phainon asks. “You say something?”

“You win,” Mydei says through gritted teeth. “Now put me down.”

“No can do. What if you run back home? It was a loooot of work getting you here as it is.”

Mydei can hear the effort it took from how Phainon responds to him in halting breaths. As evidently strong as Phainon is, even the fittest of lifters would be drained lugging around a weight for as long as he had. Especially if it’s anything near as heavy as Mydei.

“I won’t run,” Mydei swears.

He feels Phainon shake his head. “Can’t trust you to keep your word.”

“Haikas,” Mydei snarls. “You’re doing this to humiliate me.”

“It’s okay. No one’s going to remember this.”

“They’re my neighbors.”

Phainon drums a beat on Mydei’s thigh. “Hmm… alright. I’ll put you down on one condition.”

Mydei sighs in resignation. “Anything.”

And that’s how Mydei finds himself standing in line at a hot dog stand with Phainon’s arm wrapped around his waist, the pop star's hand seated firmly in Mydei’s front pocket. He suggested that Mydei should mirror him by stowing away his hand in Phainon’s own pocket, but Mydei refused to play conjoined twins with him. Phainon claimed he could always stick it into his back pocket instead, and got a disdainful look for his troubles.

At this time of day, the park mostly consisted of tourists and truant teenagers, all of whom were too busy with their own business to notice the two men playing tug of war with their private space. When it’s finally their turn to order, Mydei takes on the onus of ordering for the both of them.

“Two veggie dogs fully loaded, two chicken with ketchup and mustard, one medium cola, and a small bottle of water,” Mydei says.

He feels a tug on his shorts, directing his attention towards the perpetrator. The mask and hood covered everything except Phainon’s eyes - his most dangerous feature. Mydei has no idea how Phainon can dilate his pupils at will, but 3 seconds of looking at his damp gaze is more than Mydei can reasonably handle.

“And a small cup of vanilla ice cream,” Mydei begrudgingly adds.

Being a well-practiced stall with pre-cooked hot dogs, their order comes out fairly quick. Mydei would have preferred to eat on one of the tables, but Phainon steers him away from the logical choice and herds him towards a bench facing a landscaped portion of the park. Phainon withdraws his hand as they sit down, thankfully not commanding Mydei to feed him while his hand is out of commission.

The chicken franks tasted and felt like they were boiled to high-heaven, but it was something to do while Phainon takes his sweet time nibbling on his meal, somewhat hampered by his increasingly messy mask. Mydei wasn’t hungry at all when they arrived, though he might be by the time Phainon finishes a single hot dog.

“Any day now,” Mydei prompts.

“Why are you looking over here anyway?” Phainon says between sips of soda. The vendor had given them two straws, both of which Phainon used to suck up his flat coke. “The splendor of nature is right front of you, but you’re too busy negging me? Should I be flattered?”

Mydei clicks his tongue and averts his eyes. What splendor is there in a public park? What Mydei thinks of as nature is sharp, steep, and shadowed by wilderness. It is a sandy trail through a rocky outcrop, a swaying weed reaching out from a crumbling boulder, a nest of snakes in the hollow of an old olive tree. It is not… a piece of topiary shorn to resemble a cluster of grapes.

The dull thrum under his skull ebbs out into silence for the first time this week, leaving only a pulsing heat in the back of Mydei’s eyeballs. He rubs at his eyes to alleviate some of the pressure, unaware of the airplane full of vanilla ice cream descending towards in his mouth.

Mydei almost knocks Phainon’s head clear off his shoulders when the spoon goes in, but the sweet cream hits his tongue right after, and it mellows him out into a civilized person again. Phainon swiftly retracts his spoon from the danger zone, only to find Mydei too tired to engage with his antics.

“…I want to go home,” Mydei groans.

“Soon,” Phainon says as he digs into his ice cream.

“I never want to go with you anywhere ever again.”

“This wouldn’t have happened if you took real breaks. You got this weak in like two days.”

“Shut up.”

“When I was feeling you up, I could have sworn you lost muscle definition…”

Mydei covered his head to tune out Phainon’s voice, and Phainon rewards him with the most annoying laugh to have ever endeared itself to him.

___

“What about combining the verses on four with the breakdown on seven?”

“What key would it be in?”

“I dunno. I can go pretty high if you need me to?”

“Let’s avoid doing falsettos if we can.”

“Hey, I pulled off a killer falsetto on Scapegoats. Wanna hear?”

“No, sto- Haikas! Don’t scream in my ear!”

___

Finding a good song in Mydei’s bin of rejects was a crapshoot from the beginning, but Euphrosyne made up for it by being a sure thing. Phainon and Mydei decide to pivot for now, hoping they could reboot their senses with a new task. When Anaxa calls for updates, Phainon nonchalantly tells him that it’s going great, and when Anaxa offers to add more producers and songwriters into the mix, Phainon conveniently finds himself driving into a tunnel.

Currently, a sheet of printer paper stares back at Phainon, with the words ‘what works’ circled several times. A few bubbled words float around the central question, citing things like ‘pop sound’, ‘youthful image’, and ‘sick piccolo section’.

“I don’t think ‘cuteness’ was a factor in us winning the Fantasia,” Mydei says in regards to Phainon’s addition.

“If you don’t consider how much of the audience demographic are middle-aged moms,” Phainon says.

“Ew.” Mydei grimaces. “I hope that wasn’t it.”

“Not in a perverted way, jeez! Get your head of the gutter,” Phainon exclaims. “I’ve just had a lot of fans say I’m like a son to them.”

“We already covered ‘youthful image’.”

“Yeah but like. We’re also kinda good looking.”

“So it was a pervert thing,” Mydei says as he flicks the pen onto the paper. “And not anything about the music.”

This entire discussion only emphasizes how accidental Euphrosyne’s success was. The title itself sounds like patriotic peddling, which isn’t something that typically gets far in Astral Fantasia. It makes the actual content of the song sound insulting in comparison, especially since it wasn’t even written in an Amphorean dialect. There was no call to action or soulful romance to be found in its lyrics either, as if it was purposefully trying to defy the winning formula.

If you asked Mydei, it was probably because almost all other songs were ballads that year, though he’s really been trying to be nicer to his 16-year-old self.

The two of them ruminate in silence, with Mydei seated by Figgy’s bed and Phainon cross-legged on the floor across from them. As he mulls things over, Mydei runs his hands over Figgy’s hair, brushing out the milder tangles and giving her gentle pats. She responds by continuing to snooze on, a reminder that some dogs are easier to handle than others.

“…What if we strip it down?” Phainon says.

Mydei was prepared with a rebuttal, ready to tear into him for suggesting something so insipid as an acoustic rendition, when Phainon hurriedly explains, “We could have it start out with maybe a drum intro, and we add in the bass guitar after a bar, and then the piano, and then-”

“-Build it up,” Mydei finishes for him. He muses over the idea, trying to imagine the sound as he get up and walks over to the computer.

A duplicate of the song’s mix was already open on his DAW, and without even sitting down or listening to it, Mydei starts working on the track. In the span of a quick minute, an adjusted intro is produced, and all that’s left is to beckon Phainon over to be its first victim.

The song plays. It sounds exactly as Phainon thought it would, except Mydei made the decision to start with the vocals instead. His teenage voice opened the song, bare save for a subtle modulation to round it out. It makes him sound smaller, like it’s trying to convince the listener that this turn-of-the-millennia party jam has some pathos to it. The drums enters shortly after, then the bass, then the piano with the rest of the instruments following closely behind.

“Hm. Maybe that part where they all come in should be more abrupt?”

Mydei re-adjusts the multi-tracks and plays it back once more. The jump after the build-up is slightly satisfying to hear now, though Mydei’s twitchy hand tells Phainon that he’s thinking of more.

“I like it,” Phainon says, smiling.

“It’s not bad,” Mydei admits.

The change is nothing spectacular. Crazy Train did it better. It’s not groundbreaking stuff, nor is it the most fitting improvement. What it could be, however, is a conversation. A catalyst to break through the block.

“It’s a departure from the actual song,” Mydei says.

“I think it’s good to freshen it up. The song’s been around for a long time. Wouldn’t be surprised if some people are getting sick of it.”

“I just don’t want to alienate the fans.” Mydei’s nose scrunches up as he says it. “Does it even have fans?”

“You’re asking me as if we’re not remaking the song because of demand.”

“A demand from your label,” Mydei points out.

Phainon shrugs. “Haven’t seen them do something that never earned money. Speaking of money making ideas, what about those horns on the second verse?”

___

“What’s this?”

“Leftovers. You can have it while working.”

“Whoa, really? All this for me?”

“Don’t drop anything on the floor.”

“I won’t, I won’t… Wow, this is some soft bread for day old leftovers.”

“…Didn’t say it was from yesterday. Now be quiet and pay attention-“

Chapter End Notes

I couldn't resist extending certain parts, and now the pacing is crazy as hell. It's okay, that's just how the Amphoreus patches are going. I'm just gonna send it so I can stop thinking about this chapter yippee!

Thanks for reading, hope to see you soon!

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Side B
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

The preview for Phainon's animated short makes me wish I wrote them as a hair metal band instead ahhhhhh well that's for the version of me in the next cycle to write I guess

Experience has sharpened Mydei’s senses over the years, and nothing makes it more obvious than hearing him recreate his old work bit by bit. He’s learned some restraint since then, no longer relying on overlays-upon-overlays when a single polished track would suffice. The melodies that his younger self struggled to bring to life were whipped into shape on his first pass. He combed through Euphrosyne with the methodical regard a general would have towards his infantry’s defenses, quick to pick out its failings and even quicker to act upon them.

Some things never change though. Mydei’s soft spot for elaborate productions hasn’t disappeared, only moving on from grand, sweeping pads to gritty new wave distortion. He still immortalizes each new iteration of his projects into its own file, still paranoid about needing the synths from three versions ago. When his mind wanders while he has a guitar hanging from his neck, his hands still automatically ghost over a chromatic scale, even when the tuning has changed.

“The duh-duh-duh-duh,” Phainon sings and mimes the melody. “It needs to match the bum-bum-bum on the next line, but not as wet.”

“Like the room is getting bigger,” Mydei says through his focused haze.

“Yeah, yeah! Oh, and remember, the gain-”

“I got it, I got it.”

The clacking of Mydei’s keyboard and mixer could be mistaken for a part of the song. He moves as if his mind is paces ahead and his body is desperately trying to catch up. Phainon stands behind him buzzing with energy, his eyes zipping all over the computer screen in an attempt to follow Mydei’s alterations.

Mydei mashes the ctrl and S keys several times before replaying the verse from the top. The end result sounds like Euphrosyne in the modern world: tighter, cleaner, less brute force on the sound. There’s still a shadow of dissatisfaction on Mydei’s face when he looks up at Phainon, and it might be wishful thinking, but Phainon thinks the doubt melts away when he flashes Mydei a grin.

Mydei doesn’t reward with that same courtesy, so Phainon will have to settle for his prolonged eye contact, another excuse to admire the golden shine of Mydei’s hazel eyes.

“Good job,” Mydei says, breaking through the spell Phainon had been trying to cast on him.

Phainon laughs. “I thought you were going to say you did all the work.”

“I did,” Mydei says. “But good job on loitering and looking pretty.”

“Aw, can we go back to when you were praising me?”

“Take it or leave it,” Mydei tells him as he turns back to the computer. “Go, report this to your manager. I’m going to export the demo.”

Rather than do the sensible thing, Phainon decides to linger for a teensy bit longer, which unfortunately ends with him getting blindsided by the sound of the front door opening. Mydei might not be alarmed by the fact that he’s getting burgled, but Phainon is. Even as the stranger walks into the studio, Mydei remains unperturbed through Phainon’s mini panic attack.

“I swear, De, if you don’t put me on your will after my incredible act of selflessne-” The man freezes in place when he makes eye contact with Phainon. “Whoa, okay. He’s actually here.”

“Is there another way to read ‘don’t come, I’m working with Phainon’?” Mydei asks, completely deadpan.

“I wasn’t born yesterday, I’m not going to fall any random lie,” the man says, his eyes flitting every so often to Phainon, mirroring his astonishment. “I guess it’s not a lie, but I haven’t seen you by the gym lately. I thought you were just too embarrassed to admit you got sick.”

“I don’t get sick,” Mydei says. He checks on the export one last time before turning to the unnamed man and continuing the conversation in Kremnoan.

The alarm bells haven’t stopped ringing in Phainon’s head. If anything, they’ve gotten louder. In front of him is a long haired pretty boy decked out in athleisure, carrying a whole 6 pounds of protein powder with one hand. He acts as if he’s not conscious of Phainon’s presence, casually conversing with Mydei in perfect Kremnoan while Figgy, Mydei’s beloved dog, excitedly hops up his leg to be petted. Whatever the man is saying gets Mydei to abandon his laconic character altogether, turning him into some blushing maiden through some manner of witchcraft.

“Hi,” Phainon suddenly interrupts. “I’m Phainon.”

Both Mydei and his mystery man look taken aback to hear him. At least they have the decency to look embarrassed.

“I know,” the man says, holding out his free hand for Phainon to shake. “I’m a fan.”

Smiling, Phainon holds the stranger’s hand in both of his. “And by what name should I call my dear fan…?”

“Hephaestion,” Mydei answers as he stands up. “Don’t tell anyone about this.”

Phainon was about to scoff. Is he so untrustworthy that Mydei has to give him a disclaimer? Why would he relay any of this to anyone else anyway? It’s not his business to care about.

He’s too busy scrolling through his chat log with Hephaestion, amusing himself with old banter about oblique twists instead the commotion by the entryway. He ignores what he sees from the corner of his eye. What does it matter if Phainon walks pass him with nary a word? It’s not like Mydei acknowledged him either. This can only be a good thing. Maybe they’ll get on with recording earlier and Mydei can leave in time t-

The sharp sting of cold glass nips at Mydei’s neck, causing him to jump out of his seat to glare at a certain irradiative nuisance. It fails to deter Phainon’s innocent smile as he holds up a bottle of grape soda towards Mydei.

“How’s it going?” Phainon asks.

Mydei grabs the bottle from Phainon. It’s not even a twist-off. “It’s alright,” he grumbles. “You?”

“Better now that you’re here.”

Mydei scoffs, but he fails to inject enough snark in it and it comes out no different from a normal laugh.

Around them, the studio comes to life. With Phainon in the room, people jump to their positions, triple-checking even the most insignificant of factors. Mydei is unsure of how much of the effort is from Phainon’s star power, and how much of it is from Phainon’s affability. Even the most professional of Mydei’s colleagues wouldn’t trip over themselves to buff out Mydei’s mic stand. Mydei would have complimented Phainon on his management skills, had he not been so sure that it would offend Phainon instead.

With everyone and everything else occupied, the two of them are left standing around in silence. To say that Mydei has nothing to talk about would be incorrect. In the same way Phainon’s entrance had summoned a cavalcade of greetings, Mydei’s head is suddenly awash with dull nothings he wanted to share with the boy wonder. Things like how the piano reminds him of the finish on his ancient Kawasaki bike, or how Figgy had started waiting by the apartment door every afternoon, or how he wondered whether Phainon remembered what a proper breakfast was without Mydei to cook for him. It just feels unnatural to say these things outside his apartment, where they’re a little more than Phainon and Mydei.

Despite his aversion to keeping his mouth closed for longer than 5 minutes, Phainon looks content with keeping quiet today. The absence of his voice doesn’t make him any less expressive though, and Mydei, having been long fluent in Phainonry, reads him with ease. Right now, the side-to-side motion of his feet says that he’s excited, while the incline of his head gives away the smallest hint of nerves.

Mydei shoots him with a smirk, and Phainon’s swaying develops a tiny bounce.

“Alright,” the producer calls out. “Places, people!”

With one last glance at each other, Phainon and Mydei allow themselves be herded into the live room. Naturally, the first song they decided to record is Euphrosyne, because they can mess up the other song as much as they want, but God forbid Euphrosyne sounds even the tiniest bit off.

As the name implies, Sun and Thunder is a duo, not a band. They had a revolving door of touring members back when they were in action, but there was never really a permanent line-up. If any of them are in the studio, Mydei wouldn’t know. Not that it’s going to be a problem; the average demographic of this room would have been in high school when Euphrosyne debuted. The old band was well in their twenties by then.

That doesn’t mean Mydei doesn’t trust the musicians he’s recording with today. It’s a four-chord pop song that’s been around for a decade, and they’re professionals sought out by known record label. Even without practicing together beforehand, they should be able to cinch the song in an hour, tops. All they need is a warm-up to get them all on the same speed (a customary thing, Mydei doesn’t need to justify his suggestions) and when everyone feels like they’re solid, the producer steps up behind the mixer and signals for them to start.

As novel as it was, Phainon and Mydei’s initial rework of the intro didn’t stick around for long. It made the whole section drag, which is a cardinal sin for a song trying to make people groove. So they compromised, kicking off instead with a frantic burst of sound before crashing into immediate catatonic silence.

Then, it launches back into full blast, demanding the utmost energy the band can provide. During their rehearsals, Phainon would practice with them by reciting the lyrics with a sing-song lilt. Now his voice booms through the room, crisp and resonant even as the music competes with him. Without shouting or raising his volume, Phainon’s singing cements itself as the strongest instrument there.

The band follows relatively well for their first serious session. Everyone plays as if they would follow Phainon into battle, even when he sings that

embarrassing line comparing the dance floor to a chess board. Regardless of how hard Phainon and Mydei had tried, there’s only so much they can improve upon a base like that. Mydei, for example, had desperately wanted to minimize the piccolo’s overwhelming presence, only to be informed that it had gained a cult following over the years and that Mydei would be shanked on the street for even thinking about it.

At least the piccolo break gives Phainon a reason to step back. As he takes the opportunity to drink some water, Phainon’s gaze automatically locks on to Mydei. Above the trill of that dinky flute, their eyes meet, and Phainon takes advantage of the moment to reward him with a wiggle of his eyebrows. The corner of Mydei’s mouth twitches, but he manages to hold in his snort to show Phainon how to hold down a barre chord with a middle finger. It never fails to surprise Mydei how easy it is to make the singer laugh.

Phainon saves the recording by transitioning right back into song, but Mydei’s not sure if that’ll fly next time.

The song winds down, and as the final note rings out the producer is quick to jump in. “Beautiful. Absolutely fantastic. For the second take, let’s try the synth with less swell. Yes, like that! Very nice. I also noticed the bass lagging on the verses, can we get a handle on that, please-”

As the producer gives them a run down of his notes, Phainon skips all the way over to Mydei to place his water bottle down next to his unopened grape soda. Mydei frowns up at him. That’s a bad idea.

Phainon pouts. Some exercise won’t hurt me.

Alas, Mydei couldn’t shove the bottle back into his arms, can he? It would be rude to make a commotion when someone is in the middle of announcing something. Phainon hits him with a wink when he senses Mydei’s resistance wane, and Mydei wonders if it’s too late to give him a kick in the shin.

“-get that? Great, let’s give it another try from the top. On three-”

On the second day of recording, Mydei is welcomed into the studio by a bright flash. The cameraman responsible hastily squeaks out an apology, but Mydei’s default frown is too scary to appear anything but furious. Naturally, the poor cameraman escapes into the live room while his colleague explains their presence.

“We’re taking some behind-the-scenes footage for the press kit,” the man’s colleague says. “We’ll pop in every now and then, but I promise we won’t get in the way.”

True to their word, camera crew was a scant sight throughout the day, though there’s only so much the average person can do to ignore a camera pointing right at them. Being performers, the band is used to that kind of attention, but it’s an entirely different thing when a director comes up to you in between takes to ask for your thoughts. Even if Mydei gets out of it by dint of his comportment, it’s still a hassle to wait for his co-workers’ interrogations to end.

In spite of that, the day ends with the team making significant headway into Euphrosyne, close enough to call it done if it weren’t for the decision to record some extra stems. The camera crew kindly warns them that they’ll be back, and Mydei wonders if that’s a sign that he should put in some overtime and get a head start for tomorrow. Recording a single song shouldn’t have taken more than a couple of hours, and yet-

A flick to his forehead ceases that thought. Grimacing, he looks over at Phainon and wonders the best way to take him to court over this.

“You don’t have to look at me like that,” Phainon says, stepping back. “I just wanted to let you know that they’re locking the studio in twenty minutes, so unless you want do an all-nighter, you better skedaddle.”

“I’m going, I’m going,” Mydei grumbles.

Most of their co-workers have clocked out by now. The ones that are left are those with unfinished business in the building. There’s nothing in the studio that Phainon has to pack up with him, and even if he did, he’ll have to bring it back in the morning anyways.

“Do you still have some work to do?” Mydei suddenly says.

“Huh? Oh, yeah, I need to approve photos with Anaxa later,” Phainon answers.

Mydei hums in acknowledgment before swiftly heading for the door.

“Whoa, whoa, whoa,” Phainon says as he grabs Mydei by the arm. “Why’d you ask?”

“…You still owe me for the hot dog.”

“The what?”

The hot dog from how many weeks ago. Never mind the fact that Phainon has been ordering and paying for the entire team’s lunch these past few days. Mydei needs to be reimbursed for that sad, mushy excuse for protein.

“That lunch we had in the park,” Mydei says succinctly. “You need to pay me back and I don’t feel like cooking today, so…”

Phainon stares at him with the comprehension of a newly born goldfish, making Mydei regret ever saying anything at all. So he shrugs, cool as cucumber, and says, “You’re busy though, so nex-”

“No, no! I’m free,” Phainon insists.

“But your manager-”

“Okay, to be honest, I don’t think I’m even needed there,” Phainon admits. “I mean, I have no idea how to pick out the PR disasters from the normal stuff anyway. That’s why I have all those departments working for me, right?”

“Right…” Mydei concurs. “But you should still be there. It’s your face.”

“I trust them,” Phainon says. “Way more than I trust me. Besides, I don’t like being in debt. The interest stacks up.”

“I’m not charging you interest.”

“That’s what they all say,” Phainon sighs as he pushes Mydei out of the studio. He nods at the security guard standing by the reception and leads Mydei all the way out to where Phainon’s car is parked.

“I can’t leave my car here,” Mydei protests in the elevator.

“I’ll pick you up tomorrow,” Phainon says. He retracts the offer when he gets a frown in reply. “Don’t worry, I’ll get people to handle it.”

The ‘people' in this case ends up being Phainon’s chauffeur, who looks so used to this behavior that he doesn’t even try to dissuade his client. He simply takes the keys from Mydei and bids them adieu. Phainon dismisses his security personnel too, citing Mydei’s gym routine to convince them of his safety.

“And you call me spoiled,” Mydei comments as he straps himself down in the passenger seat.

“Aren’t you? I just let you borrow my driver because you didn’t want your Camry to feel left out,” Phainon says. “Now I have to get him a rideshare, or he’ll be stranded at yours. Where’s my thank you?”

Mydei shakes his head as he pulls out his phone. The click of Phainon’s seatbelt is followed shortly by a small ding, prompting him to take out his own phone and groan at the sight of it.

“It does not take that much to get a taxi from your place to his,” Phainon nags, swiping away from the notification informing him of a kind donation to his digital wallet.

“Then you better make this a good dinner,” Mydei says. Phainon gives him a petulant moue of woe before turning back to the wheel with a haughty

sniff.

Grove Records’ headquarters is nestled in the heart of Okhema’s media city, and being a somewhat prolific character in its music scene, Mydei is well-acquainted with all the ins-and-outs of the district. So imagine his surprise when he can’t recognize the route Phainon takes him down. The scratchy rembetiko album playing on the overpriced car stereo clashes with the modern shapes of the new world architecture outside the window, a step off from the stumpy studios and benign beiges of the music quarter. Skyscrapers sculpted from glass and metal litter the dustless streets, looming over the bustle of people all clad in the same shade of business casual.

Phainon parks inside a comparatively nondescript building, warning Mydei to keep his doors closed until he says so. Mydei complies after a little begging, watching in silence as Phainon hops out of the car and jogs straight towards its passenger side. As Phainon rounds the corner, Mydei opens the door himself and steps out.

Phainon huffs at him. “That was part of the experience, you know.”

“Should have been faster,” Mydei gloats.

Oh how Phainon pouts at that. It gives Mydei a difficult time resisting the avuncular urge to pinch his puffed up cheeks.

Remembering his role as a gracious guide, Phainon wastes no time in leading Mydei through the building. Mydei vaguely recognizes the name on the signs directing them in, but it’s not until he sees the restaurant in the distance that Mydei understands the danger he’s in.

Mydei pulls Phainon to the side before they could reach the entrance. “You can’t be serious,” Mydei hisses.

Phainon blinks at him. “You wanted a good dinner.”

“Steak and eggs at an IPC franchise would have been good dinner. This-” Mydei gestures subtly to the restaurant behind him. “-Is overkill.”

“Don’t be silly, it’s just your run-of-the-mill eatery,” Phainon says, complete with a fake posh brogue.

The run-of-the-mill eatery he had described had been the titleholder of Okhema’s best fine dining establishment for the past 3 years. Mydei of all people should have known that Phainon is not one to meet a challenge half-heartedly, and yet here he is, conveniently ignoring the chandeliers and expensive art plastered all over the corridors to follow Phainon to what he called a ‘nice place for good eats’.

“A private table please,” Phainon calls out to the maitre d’, who had been standing a touch too far for Phainon to address in a polite volume. They haven’t even entered the restaurant yet, and Mydei is already mortified.

Despite Mydei’s expectations, the lady standing by the front of house only smiles at them. “Welcome back, Sir,” she says as she elegantly beckons them in. “Please, right this way.”

Don’t be fooled by its empty vestibule: Aurum has been fully booked since its opening, lacking the capacity to even entertain walk-ins. The amount of times Mydei has failed to secure a reservation attests this, but apparently Mydei is free to saunter in anytime if it’s at the behest of a beloved pop star. He doesn’t know if that makes it less or more embarrassing when he’s walking pass the sea of occupied tables. Mydei feels it should be embarrassing, seeing how everyone else is dressed in smart formals while he barely has sleeves on.

The maitre d’ shows them to a quiet aisle of closed booths and kindly seats them at one with a nice view of Okhema’s skyline. She hands them two menus made from pressed paper before disappearing with a bow.

Being a humble aficionado of food, Mydei is aware of what he’d find on the menu in front of him. Aurum specializes in Xianzhou fusion cuisine, and the photos never fail to lead Mydei to another unsuccessful booking. The smell of the restaurant is beyond divine, with spices familiar and foreign wafting through the air like temptation manifest.

“Found anything yet?” Phainon asks as he peruses the menu.

“…A glass of water.”

“You know, the fermented cod here is pretty good. It’s fresh and tangy and it’s got a crazy kick at the end. Pretty good with rice or some pita honestly.”

“Hm.”

“I bet you’d love the bean curds though. I don't know how they get it so crunchy under all that sauce. They serve it with some yogurt in case it’s too hot for guests, but I could take it either way.”

“Ok.”

“And check out this chicken stew! They actually use the same broth for the soup dumplings, and it’s wild how changing the shape makes them taste so different. It goes so good with the fish and-”

Phainon continues his running commentary on each and every item on the menu, but Mydei holds strong. When the server comes to take their order, Mydei places a single request for bottled water and nothing else. He’s foolish to think that’s enough to make a statement when Phainon is free to order an entire buffet to their table.

“Deliverer.”

“I’m telling you, it’s Phainon,” Phainon tells him.

“It’s Deliverer,” Mydei grounds out. “Because you’ll have to take up delivering groceries to bounce back from this.”

Phainon laughs at the idea of his own bankruptcy. “It’s not that bad!”

“The hot dogs costed me five balance coins.”

“And you hated them,” Phainon says. “Good food costs more than five bucks. Live a little, why don’t you?”

It’s hard to live with the weight of a month’s salary disappearing in the span of a single meal. Mydei doesn’t think he can’t forget the price tag so easily,

but his resolve shakes the moment the first dish is placed down. Once the line of food has finishes making its way over to their table, the concept of numbers has completely vanished from Mydei’s head.

So yeah, he takes a bite of some fried wontons, after wringing the shit out of his fancy mineral water.

Phainon puts on an act about accidentally ordering too much and not knowing what to do with the excess, but Mydei folds too fast for the theatrics to be necessary. Once he popped that wonton into his mouth, it was game over. There was no winning here; everything tastes too wonderful to keep up the fight. The food is so good that Mydei allows Phainon to feed him his recommendations by hand, regardless of how cumbersome the table between them made it. When the pear crumble comes out, Mydei nearly cries.

Mydei manages to hold in his tears, though it was a close call when the bill came.

The smug bastard has the audacity to grin at him. “Was dinner okay?”

“Can it, haikas,” Mydei mumbles. He’d been joking about Phainon being in his debt, but Mydei didn’t think the night would end with him being in real debt to Phainon instead.

Phainon seems to know what’s running through his mind, because of course he does. “If you’re feeling that bad about it, why don’t you treat me to dinner next time, huh?”

Mydei gives him a sidelong glance before grunting, “I know what you’re doing.”

“And?”

A few crisp banknotes appear in Mydei’s hand, disappearing a second later into the check holder. “And you forgot to tip, Mr. Big Shot,” he says.

Neither of them remind the other that they have access to each other’s bank details, too busy finding out who could melt their complementary mint the fastest.
