All in all, Euphrosyne’s revision takes 2-ish days to record, a process that felt both too fast and too slow. Too slow because Mydei normally finishes up a new song in a couple of hours. Too fast because he hadn’t gotten sick of it by the end. Maybe it was the change of pace after how the writing had gone, or maybe there’s really something in the grassy fragrance they spritz all over the building.

Today’s recording is dedicated to finishing up any isolated tracks they might need. Mydei only had to be in to record vocals and some lead guitar, but the producer had offered to let him stay and watch the rest of the recordings. Apparently, being the co-writer of the song gets you some privileges - or extra labor, depending on the perspective. Mydei respectfully declines, despite his interest. It’s just best that he avoids stepping on any toes while working on this project.

He does step on Phainon though, which is a given with how the pop star sits sprawled out by the studio door.

“Oww,” says Mydei’s sulky rug. “I think you punctured my liver.”

A good samaritan would apologize and maybe fuss over Phainon a little to help him recover faster. Mydei breaks the mold by physically hauling Phainon to his feet with the delicacy of a rampaging bull.

“I didn’t know there was something wrong with the chairs in here,” Mydei says sardonically.

“I didn’t want to risk missing you,” Phainon reasons. When he realizes how that sentence could be misconstrued, he adds, “Honey.”

Mydei grimaces as he pushes that grinning face away from him. “Gross.”

“You hate me,” Phainon whimpers under his palm. “You want me to die.”

“If you’re going to die, do it after this,” Mydei says, turning away from Phainon. “Let’s go.”

Phainon happily obeys, falling in step with the man in front of him. With a stride like his, Phainon catches up all too easily, so Mydei continues to quietly speed up faster and faster until they’re both awkwardly trotting through the office building during working hours.

Phainon smacks his hand down on Mydei’s car hood. “I win!”

“Win what?” Mydei says, trying to downplay his panting. “Was there something we were doing?”

Phainon squints at him, but Mydei jumps into his car to avoid his whingeing. The engine revs soon after, and Phainon has to rush to get in before Mydei drives off without him.

During one of their breaks, Mydei had mentioned a certain girl with a case of the blues, and Phainon hypothesizes that she would be cured with an immediate dose of his TLC. This is proven the moment Mydei’s door is opened, and Phainon immediately topples over to the force of 90 pounds of dog.

“Who’s the good girl?” Phainon coos through Figgy’s frenzied kisses. “Is it you? Are you the good girl? Yes you are!”

“You two weren’t like this before,” Mydei says as he nudges both man and dog clear of the door.

“Sometimes you don’t know what you have until it’s gone.” Phainon sniffs. “And while you were busy giving me the cold shoulder, Figgy was there for me.”

“I can see that.”

It also helps that Phainon has a baggie of freeze dried beef in his pocket. Phainon rewards her with a couple of cubes, and Figgy pays him back with

another fusillade of slobbery kisses.

As Mydei disappears to get Figgy ready for her walk, Phainon starts working on his appearance. Wigs are too much of a pain to be working into a disguise, but as Sun and Thunder’s secret reunion draws closer, some vigilance would be much appreciated, especially with the glaring beacon that is Phainon's hair. Aglaea provides him with a decent piece that isn’t too hard for a schlub like him to figure out, and with his clothes being as plain as they can be, Phainon could almost pass for his own cousin.

The real test is how far Mydei jumps. Mydei takes a step and a half back when he lays his eyes on Phainon, which isn’t too bad.

“I’m surprised you didn’t put colored contacts on,” Mydei says as he leashes Figgy. “You didn’t even go for glasses.”

“Being kind of different is better than being totally different,” Phainon preaches.

“I don’t know, I see your face everywhere,” Mydei says.

Figgy shakes to settle the fur under her collar. With her all dolled up, Mydei stands up and hands Phainon a tube of cream.

“What’s this?” Phainon asks.

“For your ribs,” Mydei explains. “So that they don’t bruise.”

Mydei’s kick didn’t actually hurt, but he doesn’t have to know that. “Are you going to put it on me or…?”

“Handle it yourself,” Mydei mutters, walking away and leaving him to his own devices. Rude? He has no appreciation for such a natural opportunity to behold Phainon’s abs.

Phainon thinks about putting it on anyway, timing it so Mydei still catches him with his shirt up. Maybe if it wasn’t a waste of medicine. Perhaps he could pretend he’s putting the ointment on…?

In the end, Mydei returns not to the sight of Phainon oiling himself up, but to a man trying to teach his fully grown dog how to jitterbug. Phainon would have loved to show Mydei his progress with Figgy, but the ungrateful man doesn’t let him speak, wasting no time in shoving Phainon’s head through what feels like a tight ring of terry cloth.

“Hey, what the hell?” Phainon splutters as fabric slides over his mouth.

“Stop moving,” Mydei orders, holding him into place.

Phainon frowns, but allows him to continue his work. There’s a lot of tugging here and there as Mydei tries to work the headband over Phainon’s wig, his hands shockingly gentle as they brush synthetic hair out of Phainon’s face. To keep himself from being too aware of their distance, Phainon focuses on Mydei’s braid, his eyes tracing the embossing on the cuff dangling over the man’s sculpted clavicle.

Mydei steps back, finished with his fiddling. He slaps Phainon’s hand out of the air when he tries to feel up Mydei’s work, so Phainon toddles over to the bathroom to check on his appearance.

A red sweatband sits where the wig meets Phainon’s forehead. Pieces of his artificial fringe hide most of the vibrant band, blending it further into his ensemble. It’s not what Phainon would have worn, but that’s the point, right?

“The hairline was giving it away,” Mydei says. “Don’t worry, it’s been washed.”

Phainon had the option to choose a sweaty one? “We sorta match now,” he says instead.

Whether accidentally or not, the blond wig and the red sweatband nicely paralleled Mydei’s fair roots and coppery hair. Ever the cynic, Mydei scoffs at the comparison. “You are colorblind.”

Figgy barks to demand respect for those with difficulties perceiving color. Or perhaps to remind them of their greater purpose. As an apology for

neglecting her, Phainon and Mydei immediately drop everything to get her downstairs as quickly as possible, breaking out into a brisk jog as they hit the ground level.

The usual route takes around half an hour to walk, but since this is Figgy’s day, Mydei allows her to savor her time with a longer trail. Instead of rounding back to the apartment, the three of them make a detour towards the street market further down the road.

For a weekday afternoon, there’s more people at the market than Phainon and Mydei had anticipated. Even with some stalls being devoid of customers and others missing their vendors, there are enough people milling around to make Phainon conscious of his disguise.

“Stop messing with the wig,” Mydei quietly scolds him.

“But it feels kinda loose,” Phainon says.

“It’s not. You’re just making it obvious by pulling at it like that.”

Mydei gets yanked out of their conversation by an excited Figgy, who has found a new playmate in a bushel of freesias. Mydei steers her away from the flowers before she gets too worked up, offering an apology to the vendor when they pass by.

While there are no more fresh produce at the market today, there are kiosks selling all sorts of snacks; be it homemade cookies or deep-fried-somethings. Oily food doesn’t interest Mydei very much, but Phainon stares at them yearningly as if he’s peering through the mists of Shangri-La. A by-product of Phainon’s celebrity diet, maybe. Mydei indulges him by purchasing a few cholesterol bombs for him to do as he likes, although Phainon wastes half of it on Mydei, insisting that street food is made to share. As the dog happily exercises, the humans stuff their gob with everything that catches their eye.

“Season three had good moments, okay?” Phainon argues as he tosses an empty fry container in the trash. “Yeah, the show shouldn’t have lasted that long, but at least it went back to what people loved about season one.”

“Because they literally went back into prison,” Mydei says.

He would have said more, but Mydei pauses their debate about Prison Break when he spots a speck of sauce on Phainon’s cheek. He automatically moves to wipe it off with his thumb, interrupting Phainon’s rant about kingpins in fictional jails.

“Ugh,” Mydei grunts at his sticky fingers. “I need a napkin.”

Phainon pats at his pockets. “Crap, I think I left my wipes in my other pants.”

Mydei doubts Phainon’s pants ever had wipes or pockets, considering how form fitting they are. There’s no need for Phainon to fret though, since Mydei can always find a use for him.

“I’ll be back,” Mydei says as he hands Phainon Figgy’s leash. “Don’t go anywhere.”

Phainon salutes proudly. “Aye, aye, captain.”

After strolling about the market for roughly an hour, Figgy’s energy had finally been satisfied, allowing her to sit contently beside to Phainon without a fuss. Mydei had left them by the flower stand they encountered by the entrance, and since he doesn’t want impede their business by hovering menacingly, the least Phainon could do is to play the part of a curious customer.

A perfunctory look at the stall’s selection tells Phainon that they’re accomplished floriculturists. The flowers are all lush and vibrant, with varieties that aren’t exactly easy to grow in this region of the country. Little placards also accompany each pot with key information about their care and expected growth, though Phainon mostly skims through to read the fun facts at the end.

One flower in particular piques Phainon’s curiosity at first sight. A stout little pot sits half-shaded by the stall’s canopy, and in it lies a squat plumage of flowers. They’re still quite young, but Phainon can tell they’ll grow into

tall cascade of lush bells. That along with how their soft yellows fade into vermillion remind Phainon of a certain lock of braided hair.

“Are these bad for dogs?” Phainon asks, pointing at the flowers.

The vendor jerks in place, as if she hadn’t expected him to speak up at all. “Huh? Oh, naw, you’re all good. Snapdragons aren’t harmful to most household animals.”

Phainon makes the decision to buy the flowers shortly after that. The vendor kindly teaches him the essentials of taking care of his new plant before taking the pot away to be wrapped. As Phainon waits, a tap on his arm grabs his attention.

“Excuse me,” a charming voice hesitantly calls.

It’s embarrassing how two words are enough for Phainon’s stomach flip over, but he nevertheless greets the question with an amicable smile. “Yes?”

The girl in front of him gives him a shy look that Phainon has become quite familiar with by now. Especially when she pairs it with a coy twist that lightly swishes her sundress in the wind. “… Could I pet your dog?” She asks.

Ah, she’s curious about something else. Phainon’s instincts instantly back off. “Sure!” He answers cheerfully. Mydei wouldn’t mind, right?

The girl bends to stroke Figgy behind the ears. Mydei’s dog is pretty ambivalent to strangers, but she’s too much of a sucker for rubs to be hostile to the girl. At best, Figgy stares at her in confusion.

The girl doesn’t seem to notice. She smiles up at Phainon. “Is it a girl or a boy?”

“She’s a girl,” Phainon answers, snickering at how Figgy moves her head to guide the girl’s hand to the right spot. “Her name’s Figgy Stewdust, but we just call her Figgy.”

The girl gasps. “That’s so cute! That’s like the perfect name.”

“Thank you, I came up with it,” says a voice behind her.

The girl whips around to see Mydei, lifting her head in panic when she accidentally makes eye-to-pec contact. Behind her, Figgy breaks out of Phainon’s hold to run up to Mydei, reminding Phainon that he’s the side-piece and that Mydei will always come first.

The flowers also finish up at the same time, so Phainon trades in the dog for an armful of plant. Mydei looks up from appeasing Figgy with scratches to ask about his new acquisition. “What is that?”

“I wanted to try raising some flowers,” Phainon says.

“You? You have time to take care of a plant?”

“Yeah, well. I thought it would look nice by your balcony.”

Mydei shakes his head. “Haikas…”

“Um,” the girl cuts in. Her hands cover her mouth in some type of emotion that matches her wide eyes. “I’m so sorry! I didn’t know!”

Mydei’s brow furrows at that, but the girl keeps going. “This is so embarrassing. I would never- You two are so cute, and your baby is so adorable. I wish you all the best!”

The girl turns to leave, but not before stopping to baffle the two men and their dog one last time. “I’m an ally,” she declares, her palm pressed against her heart.

Then she runs off to what is presumably her group of friends, who appear to laugh in consolation as she recounts the incident to them. Phainon doesn’t say anything that Mydei’s incredulous look doesn’t already convey, but he does burst into laughter at his shellshocked expression, which only pisses Mydei off.

“I left you for a few minutes-”

“I didn’t do anything!” Phainon says in defense.

“Now I have a plant and allegations… Did you do something in a past life to be this troublesome?”

“First off, it’s my plant-” Phainon tries to argue, but Mydei stops him smoothly plucking the pot out of his grasp.

“Let’s try to keep it alive first, then we can talk about who’s got custody,” Mydei says, briskly walking away. Phainon stands there watching the flex of Mydei’s well-formed lats before the theft finally registers.

“Hey! My flowers-!”

___

Barring a tiny hiccup during set-up, the recording for Amber Dawn has been pretty smooth so far. At the very least, Mydei feels they’re progressing faster than they did with Euphrosyne. The songs could probably go live by next week if they keep going on at this rate.

Becoming acquainted with the rest of their improvised troupe could have also contributed to their increasing efficiency. After days of collaborating together, Mydei can now recognize the girl trotting up to Phainon as one of their technicians.

“It’s the cord, I think,” Phainon says, tapping at his mic’s connector.

Cynane sighs. “I’ll have to check our spares, but it’ll take a while.”

“Then maybe it’s not?” Phainon says. He must have noticed Mydei watching him, because he’s quick to call him over. “Come here for a sec, we need your help with something.”

Placing his guitar to the side, Mydei gets up and walks over to the troubled pair. “I don’t know how to fix that either,” he admits.

“I know. I was just wondering if we could sing into the same mic instead,” Phainon says. “Like old times.”

“Please don’t,” Cynane says. “I don’t want to piss off my boss by recording you two on one track.”

Mydei looks over at their producer, who is shaking his head at the mixer. “What if I give you guys my mic instead? We can record the back-up vocals later,” Mydei suggests.

Cynane shuts this down too. “It’ll get messy if we start mixing up the sources. And Mister Phainon said the problem is in the cable.”

“I said it could be in the cable,” Phainon clarifies.

The trumpet player pipes up, “We could use the spare drum mic.”

“The drum mic is completely different from a regular mic,” the other guitarist helpfully supplies.

“Yeah, but we can use the cable, no?”

“I just said I didn’t want to mix the sources!”

“Guys,” the other sound technician calls through the intercom. “We fixed the signal interference. It was just the connection on our end! Please don’t touch the drum mics.”

With that, Phainon cheerfully waves Cynane off. “Thanks anyway, Arty!” He says.

Okay, so maybe Mydei needs some more practice telling Artakama and her sister apart. He’s still not too far off. Mydei doesn’t typically fraternize at work, especially with people he’s just met, but a certain busybody had taken it upon himself to turn this professional workplace into a convivial get-together.

Mydei supposes it’s not too bad. Conversations with people who understand his work can be enlightening. Like Mydei, the band and some members of

the sound team work freelance, but they have obligations to prioritize certain labels. Mydei himself has an agreement with Phagousa Entertainment, but more often than not he’s producing something with the indies. From what he’s gathered over the last few days, Grove Records is clingier than he suspected, because everyone he’s talked to mostly mentioned artists signed to Grove and not much else.

As everyone in the control room finishes up solving what needs to be solved, the producer, Callinicus, cues them in for another take, “We’re almost there. We just need one more perfect run.”

With every compliment Amber Dawn gets, Phainon visibly brightens, to the point where it’s almost blinding to see him smile. Mydei, who stands a meter or so away from the singer, is nearly incapacitated when Phainon shoots the band an encouraging thumbs-up.

The recording sign flickers on, and Phainon’s playfulness recedes to something tolerable. The rhythm section opens the song alongside a soft sigh of a melody. That limp drum roll that Mydei once cursed has been reborn as a robust beat on a timpani - a nightmare to configure in tandem with the band, but worth every effort once Phainon opens his mouth.

If the drums are meant to be the bellow of a hillside battalion, then Phainon’s voice is the breeze blowing through the valley beneath. Without the specter of a past song to pursue, Phainon and Mydei are free to experiment with whatever, and the result is a reflection of how their tastes have developed since then, a microcosm of the passing years. It’s calmer sound, as if Sun and Thunder has embraced the adage of ‘less is more’. When he’s feeling more subjective, Mydei wonders if he just grew up to be boring.

The roar of the guitar assures Mydei that he’s still somewhat interesting, as do the oscillating synths. Krateros had once asked him if he finds his songs too safe to claim as his, to which Mydei had jokingly denied ever siring an orphan. The truth is, his artistic pursuits are only palatable when there is something to bridge the gap, and there’s only really one thing that Mydei has found that works.

“I kinda messed up the last verse on that one,” Phainon says as the take ends. “Sorry guys!”

The band jokingly boos him. “We should draw and quarter this guy,” the bassist says.

“Aw, don’t,” Phainon says, laughing. “One lozenge and I’ll bounce back, promise.”

“There’s too much sugar in those,” Mydei remarks. “It’ll dry up your throat faster.”

“If you say so,” Phainon concedes. “You’re sweet enough for me, anyway.”

“Haikas, are you asking to be punched?”

“Mom and dad are fighting again!” Someone tattles.

Callinicus buzzes in. “Don’t fight, please. We need to get this record done this month.”

“Can dad get me in the divorce?”

“What do you mean dad? They’re both dad.”

“Yeah, that’s the point.”

Mydei groans, but Phainon’s laughter pulls him back in. If that's not enough, Phainon ensures it by flashing him a plump heart formed with his hands, a sight that gets Mydei to misplay on their very next take.

Chapter End Notes

I keep thinking that the 'slow burn' tag is inaccurate but this was such a yapacious chapter only for nothing to happen. I pray for the word count of this fic

Thanks for reading, hope to see you soon!

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Side C
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

I got E0S2 Phainon in 110 pulls so I've been busy touring him around the end game modes haha... The 3.4 patch also made me so sad that I had to keep going back and forth making sure this chapter isn't too heavy oh Shaoji when I get you.......

The baking dish comes out of the oven swathed in plumes of steam, filling Mydei’s apartment with the smell of warm aromatics. The scent is a lot closer to what Mydei had envisioned, making him a little more optimistic about this attempt.

Mydei peels back the aluminum foil and gets a good whiff of those spices. Yeah, definitely closer. Everything else also seems to be intact. Mydei had accidentally fallen asleep waiting for the dish to finish baking, but it appears he made it in time. In fact, the additional 2 minutes might have made it slightly more tender.

The apartment is cast in darkness, save for what the oven light illuminates. Under its incandescent glow, Mydei places the baking dish onto the counter prods at it with a wooden spoon, feeling the give of each vegetable. Once he’s satisfied, he picks up a spoonful and tentatively gives it a taste.

He chews on it for a good long second, despite immediately knowing it’s all wrong. The taste is decent and he’d made the right choice with the charring, but the texture is still off. Some parts are too mealy, while others are too tough. It’s as if half the ingredients were only added midway through cooking.

With a beleaguered sigh, Mydei grabs the notebook on the counter and jots down another note on parboiling. He leaves the dish on the counter to cool as he cleans up, ready to be Mydei’s breakfast come morning.

___

“On three. One, two-”

Demos are like what a script is to a film. Without it, the film has no structure to work on, no sense of coherency or chronology. Even the most laissez-faire of films have a basic outline planned before going into principal photography. Like a script, a demo serves as the backbone of a song, the very thing a song is built-on.

And like a film, the end result of a song almost never sounds like that first draft. Who cares if the script called to be filmed under red LEDs? The cinematographer thinks it’s more dramatic in the dark, as well as ever so slightly cheaper on the electric bills.

That’s where the band finds themselves. Amber Dawn has been beaten into their muscle and instincts by the third day of recording, yet they harbor no complaints as they play on. For the sake of their paycheck, yes, but also because each new day breeds another variation of the song. Everyday, a new arrangement awaits them in the studio, with changes just fresh enough to be worth being curious about.

It’s clear that there’s a sound Phainon and Mydei are chasing after, one that they couldn’t capture in that rushed demo. They can’t describe what it is, but its form comes to them in heuristic increments of imperfect vocalizations.

The timpani slows as the song reaches its climax. Somewhere along the way, the outro had changed from an old school fade-out to a solemn reprise of the intro, and it has stayed that way since. As the mallet falls for a final time, Phainon repeats that first line once more, softening his voice to match the slow descent into silence. Everyone holds their breath to the decrescendo, letting its ending steep.

The click of a camera shutter fractures the silence. Someone snorts.

“It’s okay, we got it down,” Callinicus reassures everyone. The room collectively sighs.

Callinicus calls for a long break, and the live room empties out in what feels to be a matter of seconds. Phainon makes to depart with the rest, but the peace sign he flashes to the camera sends a bit of a mixed signal, leading the cameraman to take it as permission. The camera goes in for a closer shot, and as the production crew starts fishing for a reaction, Mydei wonders to what extent Phainon really tolerates the attention.

As if reading his thoughts, Phainon hooks an arm around Mydei’s neck before he could make himself scarce. There’s a million ways Mydei could have broken through Phainon’s loose grip, but there’s a total of zero that would have been acceptable on record. Which means that Mydei has to give the camera his best smile.

Phainon nearly jumps out of his skin when he sees Mydei’s face. “Are you okay?” He asks, concerned.

A pinch at his hip revives Phainon’s superstar grin. “Sorry,” Phainon says to the camera. “Mydei over here gets a tummy ache sometimes.”

“Yes,” Mydei says through his crumbling impression of a normal human smile. “Too much air-conditioning.”

“This guy’s the real heart and soul of the songs,” Phainon says, ignoring the insinuation that the air-conditioning is pumping straight-up miasma into Mydei’s stomach. “He’s the one that comes up with all the beats, the solos, the remixes-”

“I wouldn’t have come up with them if it wasn’t for Phainon,” Mydei says truthfully.

“I just say things to him and he takes it from there,” Phainon counters. “As you know, I never formally studied music-”

“-But good music doesn’t only derive from the learned.”

“That’s a good line. What is that, Shakespeare?”

Mydei shakes his head. “I think it’s more impressive that Phainon doesn’t know what he’s doing. Music is purely intuition to him, so he works harder to bring it to the real world. That’s what makes it special.”

Phainon lets out a perfect laugh. “Modesty, folks. That’s the real secret.”

The crew thanks them for their input before leaving them be. Phainon and Mydei stand there playing the part of bosom buddies before Mydei decides that the arm around his neck is getting heavy.

“Why can’t you be this nice to me all the time?” Phainon asks.

“I’m plenty nice to you,” Mydei argues.

“Yeah, but there’s nothing wrong with giving a guy a compliment every now and then,” Phainon says.

“I say all those things so people can get to know you better,” Mydei elaborates, crossing his arms. “I shouldn’t be saying anything you don’t already know.”

“See? That’s what I’m talking about.” Phainon thumps a fist against Mydei’s shoulder. “Now say ‘Phainon is the strongest and handsomest in the whole wide world’.”

“Haikas.”

“You’re missing a couple syllables. Or do you want me to start? Mydei is the strongest and hands-”

“How are we both the strongest and the most handsome at the same time?”

“We tied, but if you want to step down, be my guest.”

“Hah, maybe after you’ve beaten me in arm wrestling at least once-”

___

It’s been a while since Phainon’s been the target so many disdainful stares. The last time was probably during that album cycle where he tried to pull off a 60’s pastiche. Or that time when he was pictured standing next to a popular actress outside a nightclub. Phainon appreciates Aglaea for drilling extensive media training into his soft-shelled brain, but he wishes she’d also teach him the etiquette of getting to his seat in the middle of a fully-seated theater.

“Sorry. My bad. Excuse me. Sorry-”

Would it be fucked up if Phainon admits that it’s a little exhilarating to be glared at by a bunch of dusty curmudgeons? Don’t get him wrong, he feels bad stepping on their toes, but it’s nice that he doesn’t have to overthink it for once, and that an accident can just be an accident. Phainon still tries to avoid stomping on their feet though; a broken toe is no joke.

After trudging through a trench of legs, Phainon finally reaches the seat assigned on his ticket. Naturally, Mydei is already seated beside Phainon’s spot, and as Phainon settles down without a single glance or ‘hello’ from the blond, he wonders if he’d left Mydei waiting for far too long.

His fears are unfounded as Mydei leans in and beckons for an ear. Phainon obliges him, allowing Mydei to whisper, “I told you to come early.”

“Couldn’t get out of the shoot fast enough,” Phainon whispers back. “This guy’s really popular, huh?”

Other people might take that as a low blow from Phainon. A popular pop singer would have seen whole stadiums filled better than the half-empty theater before him. Mydei, too used to the inner workings of Phainon’s mind, retorts, “You could use the competition.”

“No need, I’ve already got my hands full with you,” Phainon says, shifting in his seat to get himself comfortable.

The action catches Mydei’s attention. He turns his head to give Phainon a proper once-over. “…Hm, you dressed up to match the occasion.”

Neither Phainon or his stylist had intended to match him to The Dawncloud Theater, although Phainon supposes the bowl cut and the round frames makes him look the part. He fits in better than Mydei does, despite the turtleneck and the blazer doing wonders for Mydei’s scholarly affectation. It does delight Phainon somewhat to see Mydei’s navy turtleneck match with the subtle indigo of his wig; like a teenage girl getting giddy at the sight of her prom date’s matching corsage.

When Mydei brought up his extra concert ticket, Phainon didn’t know what to expect. He’s attended a number of theater shows in his lifetime - even genuinely enjoying a few - but this might be the first time he’s watching one from the mezzanine floor. He didn’t think it would be any different from sitting in a theater box. It’s fascinating how seats that seem so close could turn out to have completely different views.

Calloused fingers reach under Phainon’s chin and pushes his mouth shut. “A bug is going to fly in,” Mydei warns.

“The orchestra looks so tiny from here,” Phainon says, almost reverent. “It’s hard to believe we’ll be able to hear anything this far back.”

Mydei’s chuckle comes out as a huff. “These seats are considered to be close to the stage, you know.”

“I know, I know,” Phainon says. “It’s more like- I knew the place was big, but didn’t think it was so… open."

“You should watch more shows here then.”

“You should invite me to more free shows.”

“Shameless.” Mydei shakes his head. “What kind of economy makes a concert ticket unaffordable for you?”

A smattering of courteous applause interrupts them as a tiny tuxedoed figure exits the wings. That must be Peucesta. Phainon was curious to see the friend Mydei spoke so favorably of, but it’s tough to get a good look from where they’re sitting. He can only make out the vague shape of a man

walking over to the front of the stage to give the audience and orchestra a bow. As the clapping subsides, he steps behind the grand piano and waits for the conductor to give her signal.

Mydei mentioned that the concert might help them with recording their song, but as Peucesta launches into a beautiful display of finger dexterity, Phainon couldn’t be any more confused. Did Mydei want him to add more piano to Amber Dawn? Is he saying Phainon should learn how to play one? Should they interpolate Tchaikovsky somewhere, or did they already misappropriate one of his themes by accident? Phainon tries to figure it out by maintaining a critical ear, but he’s more of a lover than a critic, and it doesn’t take long for him to get lost in the concerto. Despite not knowing much about this area of the music world, the song is too lovely for Phainon to treat so clinically, and it reverberates in the theatre with such veracity that it sweeps Phainon off his feet with ease. Even the company Mydei keeps is unnaturally skilled.

In spite of the orchestra’s enchanting performance, Phainon’s attention could only stand firm for so long. There are people out there who can handle prolonged periods of physical inactivity, who can sit hours on end without any kind of stimulation. Phainon had never counted in those numbers. He’s too much of a plebeian to be fulfilled by cerebral pursuits alone, and against his better nature, Phainon grows more and more restless the longer the concerto plays on.

Something suddenly takes hold of Phainon’s hand, stilling his jostling knee. As the clarinet serenades the tinkling piano, Phainon identifies the culprit. With his hazel eyes fixed firmly on the stage, Mydei draws lazy circles over Phainon’s thumb, a diversion from how the rest of his fingers shyly slot themselves in between Phainon’s.

It takes a moment for Phainon to recognize what the pressure on his thumb means. He quickly withdraws his trapped digit from Mydei’s hold, giving the blond an indignant look at his childish behavior. Mydei pretends to be too invested in the performance to pay him any mind, but as Phainon tries to pin his thumb in return, Mydei’s hand avoids him too readily to be uninterested.

The music escalates into an organized cacophony of keys and strings. Their placement isn’t conducive to thumb wrestling, but if Mydei can evade Phainon while keeping their palms together, then Phainon will chase his thumb without breaking their hold. It was obvious they were tied in thumb strength, although the real challenge here is to carry out their game without visibly fidgeting or making a sound. The disgruntled lady sitting on Mydei’s far side indicates that they’ve failed to some extent, but Phainon’s got bigger fish to fry. As the movement reaches its apex, so does Phainon’s assault, timing his chance perfectly to catch Mydei on a downbeat.

Phainon shoots a cocky grin at Mydei, who only rolls his eyes.

They very clearly agreed that Phainon had won, but their hands remain interlinked through the rest of the concerto, occasionally testing each other with surprise attacks. The last part of the concerto might be Phainon’s favorite. He’s a pop star, so he’s a sucker for a bright sound. It was quite cinematic too, with Peucesta’s hands ricocheting up and down the keys as the song rises in intensity. Phainon tries to eke out another win in the middle of it, and almost breaks his thumb in the process.

The concerto ends magnificently, leaving Phainon with slightly more admiration for classical music as they exit the theater. He’s still not sure he understands though - either Mydei’s homework or the music itself.

“What did you think of the show?” Mydei inevitably asks.

Mydei had taken Phainon to the hall that leads to the theater’s backstage, where they wait for Peucesta to emerge. Phainon had been pondering that question way before Mydei had asked, but he’s still not sure what Mydei wants him to say.

“It sounded like Celine Dion,” Phainon says.

“Okay…” Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Anything else?”

Phainon has to really wrack his head for something, because the observations he comes up with don’t translate well into words. He could move his hands around, use motion and mouth sounds to express how the

blabbitybibbity evoked dippitydah in the refrain, but that would only get him a spanking new straitjacket.

Maybe Phainon could start with how he felt. “It sounded like a funeral dirge.” Okay, maybe that’s too honest.

Still, it catches Mydei’s attention. “Really now?”

“I mean only at times,” Phainon starts. “And maybe it’s not something that would actually play at a funeral. It just sounds like something along those lines. Like someone was mourning and it sucked.”

“So it was sad?”

“Not really. It’s more like that feeling you get when something slips from your hands and you try to catch it.”

“Panicky.”

“No. Maybe. It’s like, you didn’t manage to grab it in time, and you’re annoyed that it made you feel bad,” Phainon elaborates. “I guess it’s kinda sad throughout, but I’d probably say that about most classical songs.”

“The second movement didn’t sound as sad.”

“The what? Oh, I think it was sad,” Phainon says. “It’s the thing the song is sad about, like looking back on the good times. I think it’s- I think it’s really, uh…”

“You think it’s what?” Mydei presses.

The flickering lightbulb in Phainon’s head stabilizes into a steady light. “I think… we need to change the hook,” Phainon proclaims.

“Huh?”

“The hook on Amber Dawn is too mopey,” Phainon says. “What if we dial it back, so it doesn’t get lost in the song?”

“Hm.” Mydei thinks it over. “I think I get what you mean.”

“Do you think Cal’s gonna be mad if we tell him we have to rewrite that whole part?”

Mydei shakes his head. “I don’t think we have to. What if instead of following the melody, you went-” He hums a line for Phainon, substituting the dip at the end with a higher note.

“Hey, that might be it,” Phainon says. How sinister of Mydei, to excite him for work when he’s on a day off from the studio. “Er, what about you?" He asks Mydei. "What did you think about the concert?”

Mydei shrugs. “I don’t know. I never paid much attention to the classics.”

“Too late to be humble now,” Phainon teases, lightly elbowing the other man, whose humorless expression remains unbudged. Phainon waits for a reaction, but the longer Mydei stares at him, the more Phainon thinks he’s missed something. “…Wait, you’re dead serious.”

“Yes? Why would you think I’m authority in traditional music?” Mydei asks, sounding genuinely confused.

“Because you told me I have to watch an orchestra perform?”

“It was a suggestion,” Mydei corrects.

“You literally said it would help.”

“Inspiration can strike from anywhere,” Mydei says. “And it did. Congratulations.”

Phainon replies with a punch to Mydei’s bicep, which earns Phainon nothing but a fistful of sore knuckles. “Why’d you even ask me to go with you?”

“I had free tickets.”

“So take Hephaestion or something.”

“He can go straight to Peucesta if he wants. As if Hephaestion hasn’t seen him play countless of times, with or without me.”

“Couldn’t you just have said all that from the start?” Phainon groans. “Here I was, thinking this was a business trip or something.”

Mydei crosses his arms. “You wouldn’t have come if I didn’t say so.”

“Hm? And why is it so important that I come along?”

Mydei’s wit fails him, and even as he recovers in mere seconds, Phainon already considers the upper hand to be his again. The blond grunts, “…I thought you could benefit from some culture. Don’t overthink it.”

With his arms crossed over his prodigious chest and his flushed face angled away, Mydei embodies the platonic ideal of every conflicted heroine in Cyrene’s trove of awful romantic comedies. Except here, instead of cringing and gagging, Phainon is unreasonably enthralled by the sight.

An indulgent thought creeps up on him. Could it be, that Mydei meant this outing to be a d-

“Peucesta,” Mydei suddenly calls out.

The man of the hour approaches the two, dusting a stray petal off his shoulder. Unlike how he had been on stage, the Peucesta in front of them walks leisurely at a gait that matches the vacant look on his face.

“Congratulations on another great show,” Mydei says.

Peucesta nods slowly, appearing neither shy nor arrogant.

“Any plans to do something else from Rachmaninoff’s catalogue?”

Peucesta shrugs.

“After your work with the youth orchestra then.”

Peucesta nods again. Phainon is in the midst of deciphering their conversation when Peucesta’s gaze slides over to him. As with his slouch and his unhurried movement, Peucesta’s droopy eyes communicate a haggard kind of tiredness, something of a running theme amongst virtuosos. Phainon supposes that’s the reason why Peucesta turns away before snapping back to Phainon with full awareness.

“This is my colleague, Kevin,” Mydei introduces Phainon with the thinnest cast of feigned innocence.

“Nice to meet you,” Phainon says, playing his part.“That was a great show.”

“Um.” Peucesta tries to speak, skeptically glancing at Mydei. “Colleague…?”

“Yeah, we work at the same studio sometimes.”

“I… see.”

“I told him a lot about you, so he wanted to see you in action. He really enjoyed it.”

“Oh…”

Phainon has never been too great at reading people like Peucesta, but he knows what starstruck looks like, all wide eyed and slack-jawed like the pianist currently is. Peucesta stares Phainon down like a hawk, perhaps matching his face to the one in his memory. And to think Phainon actually put in effort in hiding his identity this time.

Mydei continues to practice his sadistic bent. “Do you recognize who this is?” He asks.

Peucesta shakes his head profusely.

“Shame,” Mydei sighs. “Hephaestion already got an autograph.”

Peucesta looks up at Mydei in surprise.

“He was pretty happy about it, though I think he’s planning to sell it online…?”

The pianist lets out a horrified gasp, which he covers with a well-mannered hand. He steals a few more glances at Phainon, as if he’s desperately trying to confirm his suspicions.

Mydei pretends to look down at his watch. “It’s nice to see you again, Peucesta, but we have an early day tomorrow, so I think we better head out soon.”

“Wait-!”

Peucesta calls out, despite neither Phainon or Mydei moving an inch. They wait for the rest of his orders, but Peucesta only stands there, frozen. It takes an awkward while before Peucesta clears his throat and reverts back into a world-class pianist.

“My mother is a fan,” Peucesta patiently says. “If you may be so kind to humor a request…?”

“Sure,” Phainon answers.

Peucesta excuses himself as he trots back to where he came from. Mydei waits for him to disappear around the corner before snickering.

“I can believe he recognized you,” Mydei tells Phainon. “I guess Hephaestion was right. He is a fan.”

“Yeah,” Phainon says. “I guess.”

The limp reply causes Mydei’s smile to drop into a puzzled frown. “What’s the matter with you?” He asks.

“Nothing,” Phainon mopingly responds. He jumped the gun and ended up shooting himself in the foot, is all.

It’s not unreasonable for Phainon to sulk, right? Like yeah, Phainon gave Mydei the go-ahead and they never signed any NDAs or something, but

“They also said you stink and they’re tracking you by your giant stink lines.”

“Okay, give me that.”

Phainon tries to grab the phone away from Mydei, and in the span of a few familiar motions, the two find themselves grappling each other instead, phone lying neglected on the floor. Everyone else in the room jumps to break them apart, mistaking the glee in their faces for unbridled animosity.

Apparently, Phainon’s clothes were lent to him for the show’s taping. Aglaea does her best to make Mydei understand what that means.

“Next time,” Aglaea mutters as she fixes a wrinkled collar. “Wait until he’s naked.”

They both choke at the same time. It seems this fight ends with a tie.

Chapter End Notes

The initial onslaught of apprehension doesn’t seem to be letting up any time soon, but Phainon has too much trust in Aglaea too much to fret just yet. Negative feedback upsetting to see, yes, but there’s at least a few lone souls out there with good taste. It takes a small amount of searching to find them, and as… tawdry as the posts are, it’s proof that there’s an audience Mydei can appeal to.

Did Phainon make a new private account specifically to archive all the posts about his mysterious new guitarist? No comment. Is his phone storage suddenly weighed down from all new photos and videos taking up precious space? Purely research, Phainon insists.

“Does the creepy collage of his hands count as research too?”

Phainon isn’t proud of the sound he made when he felt a sudden whisper in his ear, but Cipher is. Her Cheshire grin serves to taunt him further, as if Phainon isn’t used to her brand of mischief by now. It’s a good reminder that Phainon shouldn’t be talking to himself in a corridor accessible to hundreds of employees.

“Hello, Cipher,” Phainon greets her placidly. “I didn’t know Aglaea was coming in today.”

“She’s not,” Cipher says, brushing off her thick coat. Phainon suspects she keeps her guard uniform in impeccable condition simply for the irony. “That’s not going to make me forget what I saw on your phone, by the way.”

“I didn’t think you’d want to talk about it.”

“You’re right about that,” Cipher groans. “Those photos need to be powerwashed out of my brain, blech.”

Phainon smiles. “I hope that taught you a lesson on peeping.”

“Why's that my fault now? You’re the one looking up creep shots of your coworker in the middle of a busy office,” Cipher says, jabbing Phainon in the chest with each accusation.

Phainon inconspicuously glances around the hall as he gestures for her to zip it. No one is probably listening in, though if they were, they would have a hell of a hit piece to knock Phainon down with.

“It’s for research,” Phainon insists, hoping that saying it even louder would make it ring true. “I can’t help it if that’s what people are posting about the guy.”

“An academic now, are you?”

“It’s true,” Phainon insists. “Aglaea was worried about him.”

“Hm. And here I thought she was happy with the little prince…”

“She is,” Phainon swears. “But you know Aglaea, always coming up with contingency plans. I mean, I wouldn’t be the one looking this up if the rest of her team wasn’t so busy.”

“Sheesh, leaving their main star with the grunt work,” Cipher says with a shake of her head. “This dump gets lousier by the day.”

She’s too adept at sarcasm for Phainon to detect any, but most people know not to take her words at face value. Phainon’s sure that Cipher would have continued teasing him anyway if the subject matter wasn’t so mutually appalling. He takes the opening to circle back to the beginning: “So why aren’t you with Aglaea anyway?”

“‘Cause you’re not as slick as you think,” Cipher says. She picks on a hangnail, sounding half-bored. “Your bodyguards have some awfully fat pockets for a pair of bozos missing in action.”

“There’s not a lot of action when I’m working on a song,” Phainon points out. His heart hammers in his chest, held back by a flimsy mantra that’s more delusion than truth. She’s bluffing. She doesn’t know. No one knows. How would she know? “And I didn’t want them to go broke because I keep sending them home.”

“See you say that, but I smell something fishy brewing in that clever little head of yours.” Cipher squints at Phainon as if she’s spotted something to crack the case wide open. Then it’s gone in a flash, too serious for Cipher to care about for more than a second. “You’re lucky I don’t give a damn. I had half a mind to give you hell while I’m temporarily assigned to you, ‘cept it’s bad karma to shit on a kid just ‘cause he’s a suckass.”

“Oh.” This is the first Phainon’s heard of this reassignment. “Who’s with Aglaea now then?”

“Barty, obviously. No one’s gonna mug her anytime soon, she says, so she’s making do with that bum and a taser gun.”

“I guess… that’s not too bad?”

“Speak for yourself,” Cipher huffs. “Aglaea goes to spa centers and fancy tailor shops that give out refreshments for free. You go to the sweatiest stadiums out in the ass end of Amphoreus.”

“I have to be honest, I don’t feel very protected right now.”

“Have some faith, wise guy.” Cipher elbows him. “I’ll do whatever it is they’re paying me for. I’m just saying, it might look like there’s too many middlemen to keep count, but that doesn’t mean you don’t have eyes on you.”

Oddly more threatening than enlightening. If Phainon didn’t know better, he would have assumed the arrest on her record had something to do with racketeering, and not petty thievery.

“You’ve been watching too many mafia films,” he says.

Cipher throws her hands up. “Hyacine was the one who chose Mean Streets last time, okay?”

“Really?” Phainon asks, pulling his phone out. “Not a slasher?”

“Not even a Kalevalan comedy,” Cipher reports.

Phainon opens his phone. He’s been neglecting the movie night group chat due to his busy schedule, and he estimates that he’s at least 3 movies behind the current assignment. He would have checked the exact number if his phone hadn’t automatically opened to Weaver and blasted a discriminating video out loud.

Phainon swiftly turns the screen off. He glances at Cipher, who appears to have gone through some kind of harrowing experience. Not a fan of armpits, Phainon reckons.

She grimaces at him. “Are we going to do this the whole time I’m with you, or…?”

“Absolutely not,” Phainon says, immediately hiding the phone away in his jean pockets. He thinks of it for a second longer. “Don’t tell anyone.”

“You’re really not helping your case here, hotshot.”

Phainon takes out a 50 from his wallet and places it in her waiting hand.

“You’re suspiciously quick with that,” Cipher remarks. She pulls her hand away before Phainon could rescind his generosity. “Wasn’t complaining. Just admiring.”

“You know how the smallest things become the worst rumors,” Phainon says.

“If you were really worried about that, you wouldn’t be jerking it in the open, would you?”

“I wasn’t jerking anything-“

The sound of a door swinging open interrupts their conversation. Literally, because the door is situated right in-between the two of them. Phainon steps back from its trajectory to see Anaxa scowling at them both from the doorway, doing a poor job of hiding them from the rest of the meeting room’s occupants.

“Is there some kind of half-wit convention happening in the corridor?” Anaxa sneers. “Did they make it illegal to have silence when people are trying to hold a discussion in peace?”

“You told me to wait out here,” Phainon argues. It’s the wrong thing to say, judging from the furrow of Anaxa’s brow, but it is factually right.

“If you’re so adamant to chat, you should go to the lounge or the cafeteria,” Anaxa sidesteps the accusation. “Or a fire escape or a bathroom. Go anywhere, as long as it doesn’t disturb the people trying to stay gainfully employed.”

He fixes his judgmental eye on Cipher, still displeased. “I told them to fix up Phainon’s security. Why is it that you’re the one who comes calling?”

“Wasn’t my decision,” Cipher says with a shrug. “I’m just filling in for now ‘cause it’s short notice.”

“Cerces help this sinking ship of a company,” Anaxa mutters.

“That’s what I said!”

“Just keep an eye on him,” Anaxa tells her. “I don’t care about what you do as long as you do a better job than the no show parasites leaving us high and dry.”

He shuts the door after that. The middling thump it makes is either an attempt to restrain his anger or the best slam his feeble arms can muster. And to think he always refuses Phainon’s invitations to work out…

“Man, you have these people under some Jedi mind-shit,” Cipher says, striding down the hall.

“I don’t know what you mean,” Phainon replies as he follows her out of Anaxa’s hair. “I just keep it honest, is all.”

Cipher cackles. “You’re in the entertainment industry, kid. You gotta keep some cards close to your chest to strike it big, and you’re not exactly a small-fry, are you?”

Pearls of wisdom from a lifelong cynic. Phainon thinks he’s got too much joie de vivre for Cipher’s preaching to land, but there are times where her experiences are too universal to shrug off.

“It helps to help people,” Phainon puts it simply.

“And that’s why you’re cyberstalking someone on company time.”

“I’m starting to think you’re doing this on purpose.”

“Took you forever to figure that out, genius.”

___

“-You’re listening to thirty three point three FM and that was ‘Had I Not Seen The Sun’ from Robin’s new album, ‘Inside’!”

As one red-headed sister makes her announcements, another presses a button on the soundboard to summon a sound bite of noise makers and cheers. The last is busy flipping through a set of handwritten notecards, perhaps revising their questions for the segment to come.

A radio show is more like Mydei’s speed. There’s less witnesses for one, which means there’s no dress code that requires Mydei to be professionally groomed for an hour straight. It’s also closer to Mydei’s interests, with its old-fashioned set-up supplemented by state-of-the-art equipment. The console must be at least twenty years old now, whereas the Rode mic pointed at Mydei’s face was only made available for purchase a month ago. Mydei is predictably amused by the living history at play.

The one thing that leaves Mydei at a loss is the radio hosts themselves. He’s known since forever that the hosts of Janus’s Table are a set of triplets, but it’s sort of a non-sequitur when listening to the show, where their distinct voices keeps them recognizable. If not for their hairstyles, the three sisters would be indistinguishable from one another in person. Mydei could just about tell them apart from their clothes, but their matching names stumps him completely.

“Welcome back to Janus’s Table!” One sister roars into the mic. Her hair is the shortest of the three, with an undercut so severe it almost comes off as a mohawk. “We’ve got a guest today that might be familiar to most of you-“

“-And a guest that we’re proud to re-introduce to new listeners,” adds the second sister. She has a perfect bob that bounces with every girlish giggle. “Together they make one of the bands that influenced the pop boom in the late aughts! Let’s all give a warm welcome to Sun and Thunder’s Phainon and Mydei!”

The three hosts forgo the soundboard to manually shower Phainon and Mydei in applause. Mydei is slowly re-learning the staples of a press tour, but it might be a long while before he gets used to the outrageous claims about their one-note boy band.

Phainon’s response, as always, is to laugh it off. “Thank you, thank you. A pop influence, huh? I don’t hear that everyday.”

“You definitely did something to pop music,” says the loud sister.

“Considering where you started, we think it applies to Sun and Thunder,” says the least talkative of the three. She’s nearly covered from head to toe, hiding behind her overgrown bangs and a long dress that spurns summer.

The friendliest sister picks up on what her withdrawn counterpart refuses to elaborate, “We still remember watching the announcement live like it was yesterday! Everyone and their moms picked up an instrument after that finale.”

“For those not in the know, Sun and Thunder is the reason we’re still respected in Asdana,” the brash one jokes.

“They represented Amphoreus in the Astral Fantasia Music Festival ten years ago,” explains the nice sister. “I think many people know this about you, Phainon, but I don’t think the youth today are as interested in the Fantasia as we were back then.”

“They’re definitely not,” Phainon concurs. “Nowadays most people say my biggest honor is winning the Golden Nymph or getting an album to platinum.”

The loudest of the sisters snickers. “They used to say it’s the Fantasia, huh?”

“Yeah, they did,” Phainon answers. “I think they’d be right anyway. The Fantasia is my biggest honor.”

Damn it. Did he have to smile at Mydei right then? “It’s my only honor,” Mydei deadpans to will himself back to reality.

No one laughs though. The peppy sister even takes offense to it. “Don’t say that! We loved your work on Swan Song!”

It figures that the hosts of one of the nation’s busiest radio shows would be well-informed about music news. Mydei bites back a groan. “That was a good album and I enjoyed working on it. I hope Lady Hysilens didn’t hear that.”

“She’d forgive you,” Phainon says, despite not having any basis for that statement at all. “You were just trying to say that you really, really like working with me, right?”

“That’s one interpretation,” Mydei diplomatically answers.

“We hope that means this reunion isn't the last we hear from you guys…”

“Me and you both, Miss Tribbie,” Phainon says. “But I think that speaks to how hard we fought for this. Both Mydei and I are incredibly busy with our careers - which I’m thankful for - but it doesn’t leave us with a lot of space to think about collaborating again. I’m glad that Euphrosyne's anniversary put us back into the zeitgeist, because that helped justify the reunion to the naysayers, y’know?”

While not technically wrong, Phainon still twists the facts to fit into a nice digestible package. Mydei almost laughs out loud at the idea that Phainon

wanted to work with him before this debacle. He should leave the hapless act to the truly pathetic among them, such as the man seated cautiously at Phainon’s side.

“All we’re hearing is that there’s still a chance!”

“Don’t pressure them, Trianne,” the one called Tribbie scolds, though her smile looks too jubilant to mean any harm. “It could be a surprise for all we know!”

“Now look who’s putting on the pressure,” Trianne huffs.

“How long have you two been planning for a reunion?” The last unnamed sister asks.

“Not long to tell you the truth,” Phainon admits. “It’s difficult to plan for the future when our schedules clash so much. We focused more on getting everyone on board than any real planning, but Mydei and I still work really well with each other, so it came together a lot more smoothly than anticipated.”

The noise gate would take care of the small scoff Mydei had instinctively let out, but there’s no chance of downplaying it in the station, where the triplets glance at him as if they’ve sensed blood in the water.

Sure enough, the unruly triplet, Trianne, turns to Mydei with exaggerated aplomb and asks, “Was it easy breezy all the way or did the new songs give you guys some trouble?”

“There wasn’t more trouble than there usually is,” Mydei says. Phainon could and probably would answer for him, but blatantly ignoring Trianne’s expectant gaze would be rude, even for Mydei. He did ask for it, after all. “It’s nice to have someone to bounce ideas off.”

“Sounds like it’s the first time you two worked together again,” Trianne concludes.

“We always thought you two kept in touch! Scapegoats sounded a lot like Symplegades off the second Sun and Thunder album! We wondered if Mydei worked on it,” Tribbie says.

“I, uh, never did,” Mydei says, side-eyeing Phainon. “Phainon is half of Sun and Thunder. It wouldn’t surprise me if the sound stayed with him.”

“It stuck out to us because the songs you write today keep plenty of elements from Sun and Thunder,” says the third sister. “Would we be right to expect the new material to feel as familiar to the fans?”

Phainon takes this chance to jump back in. “Definitely, yeah. The new Euphrosyne is self-explanatory, while the other song basically picks up where we last left off. It’s a song we probably would have worked on if we were still together, but with years of foresight packed into it. Like a glimpse of what could have been.”

“This sounds like the perfect time to remind our listeners what Euphrosyne sounds like,” Tribbie says. “Again, for those catching up, this is the song that won us the Astral Fantasia ten years ago-“

“-But remade!” Trianne cuts in. “If you’re curious about how that sounds, then keep your ears peeled. You’re listening to thirty three point three fm and this is Euphrosyne by the one and only Sun and Thunder!”

Trianne slaps a button on the console to run the queued track. The meekest of the sisters mutes their mics while the song plays, giving everyone the go-ahead to talk outside the show.

“That was really good, De!” Tribbie says to Mydei. “Agy says that you haven’t done a lot of shows together yet, but you kept up with Snowy really well!”

Mydei had only begun to tell their names apart when he’s suddenly lambasted by a new cast of characters. He makes an educated guess that ‘Agy’ must be Aglaea and that ‘Snowy’ is the walking, talking marshmallow on his left.

“Tell us if we’re getting too scary, okay?” Tribbie says.

Mydei doesn’t hear that very often from women who are a foot shorter than him. Granted, the triplets much older than Mydei’s paltry 27 years, but he’s not an animal going around taking note of women’s ages.

“I’m just following Phainon’s lead,” Mydei says. “Thank you for not making it difficult.”

“Oh we wanted to ask soooooo many questions!” Trianne proclaims. “Like are you guys sticking with retro-pop even though you guys were technically just pop back then? Did you not use the old samples because of licensing or because of artistic choice? How was it meeting Naxy? Did he tell you guys how to do that thing with the bass? Is West Wind actually a recycled Sun and Thunder song or was it-“

“-There’s a lot we were curious about,” the reticent sister summarizes for Trianne. “But might be closer to gossip than promotional material.”

“I don’t mind answering them,” Mydei says. He glances once again at Phainon, who nods his head encouragingly. “…Maybe privately. In case it strays from Sun and Thunder.”

The three sisters share a look. They say that twins possess a special kind of telepathy, so Mydei wonders if triplets have a stronger signal than the standard twofer. The synchronized nod between the three sisters seems to corroborate with that theory, though Mydei’s more focused on trying not to be scared shitless when he sees them riffling through their question cards.

“Don’t worry, De!” Tribbie reassures him, her telepathy extending to minds beyond her sisters’. “Think of this as practice before we go live again!”

“Um…”

Mydei glances at Phainon, who leisurely reclines in his seat without a care in the world. He takes it as a sign that things haven’t been derailed. Or maybe they have and Phainon is waiting to see how Mydei gets himself out of this one.

Trianne clears her throat to catch Mydei’s attention. “What was your impression of the new Euphrosyne’s mixdown?”

“It sounds good,” Mydei says.

“…Any perspectives as a producer? Since you weren’t directly involved in the post-production side this time?”

“I was on board as a performer, and as a performer I think I should focus on my musical performance.”

Unlike when the show was on, the three sisters cringe. Before Mydei’s confidence could plummet too far, Tribbie intervenes. “Let’s try another question!”

Trianne hastily searches their notecards. “Uh, from the name of the band to the titles of your songs, it’s clear Sun and Thunder is inspired by Amphoreus’s myths. Many fans suspect it’s because you were meant to come out with a concept album. Is that true?” She reads out loud.

“No,” Mydei immediately denies.

“So why the theming?” Tribbie asks when Mydei falls silent.

“It was… a prompt from the label,” Mydei answers, attempting and failing to spruce up the truth. Grove said they needed a name and gave Phainon and Mydei a list to choose from. That was prudent of them, because 12 year old boys aren’t known for naming things with taste, but saying it as it is makes it sound like the band was a product of Grove Records. Which is true, but it doesn’t work well with the inspirational organic success story they’ve cultivated for Sun and Thunder.

Mydei tries to pick out the interesting facts like he’s seen Phainon do. “We had to name ourselves, so Grove threw out some options for us. We went with Sun and Thunder because we thought Seliose was cool. Everything else fell into place after we chose the name.”

“You two were interested in myths as kids then?” Tribbie asks.

“I guess,” Mydei says. He remembers sitting with Phainon and looking up stories about the warrior, ultimately finding the history of Cloudedge Bastion intriguing. “A lot of Amphorean myths sound like something out of an action blockbuster or a Sunday morning cartoon. The kind of things kids like.”

Phainon’s breath catches in his throat the moment the journalist finishes his question.

Mydei’s hands curl into tight, hard fists, though his answer come out in nothing more than a worn-out monotone. “I wouldn’t say I based my career off of anyone. My father was more interested in growing his enterprise by the end of his life anyway.“

“So you were more influenced by his business-sense?”

The laugh Mydei forces out has more in common with a snarl. “I’m influenced by nothing of his.”

“Mydei’s a self-made man,” Phainon quickly intervenes. “It’s why his songs sound so unique.”

The interviewer refuses to segue, either out of malice or ignorance. “It sounds like his father had a hand in his career, considering how his company had gone to Mydei.”

“If you know that much, then you should already know that Bulwark was restructured and bought out by its own employees,” Mydei shoots back.

Phainon sees the moment Mydei knows he’s messed up. There was nothing false about what Mydei had said, but it was the way he said it, the

unmistakable venom of his words and the threatening tic of his jaw. Remorse settles in the tiny quiver of Mydei’s lashes, just as a gratuitous shock grips the interviewer’s guiltless face.

“If I recall correctly, it went to Mydei automatically because of how inheritance laws work in Kremnos,” Phainon says, calmly and lightly. “Mydei only wants to write songs, so he stepped away as soon as possible and left it to people who know what they’re doing. It’s old news by now really.”

This is not the way to respond. Correcting a magazine correspondent on his research makes Phainon look arrogant. Speaking on behalf of an alienated party risks tying Phainon to controversy. Sharing his real opinion in a backhanded comment illustrates Phainon as a petty diva. Yet he does it anyway, exuding with enough bonhomie to deflect immediate criticism. It works, but not on everyone. There will definitely be consequences for this later. For now, Phainon allows himself to savor the journalist’s flustered backtracking under his steady gaze.

Phainon blatantly takes point over the rest of the interview after that, as if to block the magazine from addressing Mydei directly again. Every now and then he makes sure to ask for Mydei’s opinion on more neutral topics, cracking twice as many jokes when the blond falters. It’s too early to call it a bust. Perhaps the divine light of providence could shine on them once more, inspiring their editorial team to keep their articles spic-and-span in the spirit of humanitarianism. They are a fashion magazine, not a gossip rag.

By the end of it, Phainon is beyond exhausted. He spits out a brittle ‘thank you’ as the reporter cuts the recording, hoping to quickly grab Mydei and leave. To his surprise, it is Mydei who delays him, taking the time to follow Phainon in thanking the journalist and the rest of his crew.

This is the first time he’s ever done this, so Phainon’s confusion is understandable. The anger though? Phainon doesn’t know where that comes from.

“Hey, I’m sorry about earlier,” the interviewer says, pulling Phainon out of his navel-gazing. “People are going to be curious about these kinds of things, you know? We were just trying to give you a fair shake at defending yourself.”

He appears and sounds apologetic, curling in on himself slightly to make himself look small. Mydei would normally punch his way out of a problem like this, or curse the other person’s entire bloodline until even their ancestors are begging for mercy. It’s rare for Mydei to silently nod and walk away, knowing that little else is more shameful to a proud Kremnoan.

Phainon hastens his steps to catch up to Mydei. The interview had taken place in a posh lounge, the type to invest in wainscoting for the walls and Chesterfields for seating. It would have been a lovely place to unwind in after work, to knock down a few shots with a fellow band member or something like that. Unfortunately Phainon feels nothing but contempt for it now, though he appreciates the quiet alcove that grants him a private word with the songwriter. The vacant expression hasn’t left Mydei’s face since his father had been brought up, so Phainon naturally starts with, “You’re not your dad.”

“I know,” Mydei mutters. “I should have handled it better.”

There’s that strange anger surging through Phainon again, but he brushes it off for Mydei’s sake. “If someone said my life’s work is based of some supreme asshole, I would have been arrested on the spot,” he says.

The corners of Mydei’s lips make a valiant attempt, but a genuine smile is still too heavy for him to pull off. Phainon will have to try harder.

“Coming from a guy with an uneven mustache too,” Phainon says. “He’s lucky they’re not gonna film him and put him on tv or anything.”

“…Maybe it’s what’s hip these days.”

“I’ll be dead before you catch me rocking the Tetris Z-block on my face.”

Finally, a real laugh slips through, light and husky from caprice. “That’s not what they call it.”

“You caught me. They actually call it a ‘skew tetromino’, but I didn’t think you’d care about the professional lingo.”

“I meant they probably just call it a mustache,” Mydei says. “The fuzzy caterpillar or something.”

“That’s way worse than what I said.”

Mydei chuckles again, though he hides it with a shake of his head. Silence creeps in once more, as does the dim melancholy in Mydei’s eyes.

“…Sorry,” Mydei sighs.

“For what?” Phainon says, fixing the part of Mydei’s fringe where the pomade had slackened. “Everyone fucks up sometimes.”

“The reporters.”

“…Your publicist.”

“And do you think she would have given Amphora Style the exclusive scoop on your infamous dad?”

“Not really.”

“The answer is no, not at all,” Phainon stresses. “So you don’t have to look so scared.”

“I’m not scared,” Mydei says, crossing his arms.

“You were! You totally were!”

“I was not,” Mydei insists. “I was thinking of how to explain it to her.”

“She’s used to that kind of thing. A lot of people want to keep their privacy, just as a lot of people want to be a scumbag about it,” Phainon says. “…She does it for me too. Bringing up my parents is taboo in interviews now.”

Mydei’s dour expression eases, like a startled cat sensing the danger is gone. Phainon doesn’t usually get the urge to speak about it, so his stream of consciousness barrels through the frail defenses he’d put up.

“I used to get a lot of questions about my old folks,” Phainon finds himself admitting. “I used to answer them all too, but they were really, really interested in how they died and everything that surrounded it. I didn’t want to answer them in the first place, much less give them material they could use against the people I love.”

“So Aglaea put an embargo on the questions,” Mydei states.

“After my tantrum in Ladon, yeah,” Phainon says, embarrassed. “She was real mad at me too, because she could have prevented it if I just told her how much the questions pissed me off. Fun fact about celebrities? Apparently all of us have some kind of Achilles’ heel we hate talking about.”

Mydei leaves Phainon’s words to sit, letting their thoughts simmer as he stares at the pop star without comment.

Then he says, “If I asked the cashier at my corner store about the exact circumstances her husband died, she’d punch me in the mouth.”

A sudden laugh wracks through Phainon’s body. “Fuck,” he says. “She would, wouldn’t she?”

Later, the two of them would slip into their dressing room, grab the rest of their belongings, and leave the premises together without informing anyone else. The twenty minutes that they would spend ranting in Mydei’s car would inoculate Phainon against the posts he reads later that evening, the memory of Mydei’s rakish smirk holding more meaning than any libel charged against him.

Aglaea doesn’t scold them on accounts of bad publicity still being good publicity. Some real frustration does seep in, however, when she dresses down a blogger for trying to insinuate a relationship between Mydei and his father’s cronies. Phainon assumes it’s her natural protectiveness at play, along with the sudden pep in his manager’s step. Anaxa wouldn’t dare miss the chance to dangle a disappointing incident above her head. “About time,” Anaxa says when he verifies the gap in Phainon’s schedule. “I thought that woman was going to keep this dog and pony show running on fumes.”

“I’m sure she would have let you add to the schedule if you just spoke with her,” Phainon says.

“I did. Then she added another talk show appearance.”

“To be fair, he did call Miss Aglaea a ‘serendipitous thief’,” Hyacine tells Phainon as she waters one of the many plants flourishing in Anaxa’s office.

“I called her a meritorious thief,” Anaxa corrects. “I was complimenting her on succeeding where I could not.”

At that point, Hyacine could only shrug at Phainon.

As hands-off as his management style might be, Anaxa has been hard at work getting Sun and Thunder’s new songs to the right ears. He’s been vetting early reviews and arguing with digital distributors on top of everything he’s been doing so far in regards to Phainon’s solo material. Anaxa’s latest quarry is a set of music videos that he himself insists on. That’s how Mydei finds himself in a fancy coach bus the very next day, munching on a bag of trail-mix he packed for the trip. In a rare reversal of priority, Amber Dawn’s video would be the first one to be shot to give its release a bigger push. It’s also partly in consideration for the traveling Phainon and Mydei have to do. Could Mydei have made this trek alone? Absolutely, but although Anaxa might have learned to trust his songwriting, Mydei’s punctuality was a different matter altogether. A chance to catch some shut-eye isn’t too bad either.

Mydei had been mostly left alone by the small army of assistants and attendants accompanying him on this journey. The seats around Mydei are comically barren, but it’s not like he gets to bask in his solitude for long anyway. It was only a matter of time before a well-known white mop graces Mydei line of sight.

“You shouldn’t walk around on a moving bus,” Mydei warns his new neighbor.

Phainon shrugs, folding his aviators to hang it onto his bright polo. “I don’t think you should be eating on a bus either,” the pop star says.

Mydei holds out the trail-mix bag, from which Phainon automatically pilfers a few nuts.

“Now we’re both complicit,” Mydei accuses.

The bus is yet to reach the toll gate exiting Okhema, but the scenery outside the window is already greener than it is in the city limits. It’ll only get wilder from here, where Okhema’s jurisdiction falls short. Mydei decides he might as well get that nap in now, not trusting the bus’s suspension to hold as soundly over the rockier roads. He nods off in the middle of an argument with Phainon, begrudgingly accepting the contractual agreement that salads are the perfect snack food.

Mydei thinks he might have had a nightmare about lettuce and thousand island dressing, but he forgets about it the moment he snaps to consciousness. The first few seconds of wakefulness leave him horribly disoriented, as if he’s been tilted on the wrong axis. Instead of sitting upright in chair like he remembers, Mydei finds himself curled up across two seats, his head cushioned by Phainon’s thighs. The clawing on his scalp that he had mistaken for Figgy turns out to be Phainon’s hand braiding itself into the knots of his hair. Phainon doesn’t seem to be aware that Mydei has awakened yet. He’s busy staring pensively out the window, fixated on the landscape rolling on by.

The slightest of motion from Mydei reminds the absent-minded singer of the weight on his legs. He looks down at Mydei, immediately wiping off the somber emotion from his face in favor of a familiar smirk. “Rise and shine, sleepyhead.”

“Are we there already?” Mydei grumbles, unable to keep the grogginess out of his voice.

He doesn’t get up yet, only lifting his head enough to regain his bearings. Phainon’s answer doesn’t give him much reason to rise either. “We’re about thirty minutes away, give or take.”

Mydei grunts in acknowledgement before dropping his head back onto its impromptu pillow. Phainon tries to muffle his reaction, but Mydei still hears his tiny ‘ow’ slip through his teeth.

“Wake me up when we’re there,” Mydei orders.

“Do you need anything else, your Majesty?” Phainon asks. “Want me to sing you a lullaby? Give you a massage?”

“You’re the one who put me here.”

“Your head was getting scrambled by the window,” Phainon says, leaning over Mydei. The setting sun bounces off the rhinestones on Phainon’s collar, shining onto his face like dappled sunlight. “Can’t risk you battering your precious brain now, can we?”

“Haikas,” Mydei mutters, pushing Phainon’s face away from him. “I’m going back to sleep.”

Despite closing his eyes, Mydei stays awake on Phainon’s lap. Maybe Phainon also knows he’s pretending, slotting his fingers back in Mydei’s hair to irritate him. When Mydei cracks an eye open out of curiosity, he finds that Phainon’s attention has drifted back outside the window, a stranger’s expression sitting where anticipation should have been.

Coming home is always difficult. Even more so when there’s no home to welcome you back. Mydei might know what that feels, but that doesn’t mean he has any clue of what to say.
