While the finer details of minor stardom have taken some getting used to, filming music videos are apparently much easier for Mydei to come to grips to. Not because he's particularly talented at it, but because he remembered the process being much more grueling when he was a kid. It might be that he’d gotten used to early mornings as an adult, or that people are much less likely to tell a grown man to jump around half-a-million times for a single shot. Maybe it’s a sign that Mydei’s getting used to posturing on camera.

Mydei breathes in, savoring the sting of the chilly country air. If anything, it's the locale that’s making the shoot bearable.

Amber Dawn’s music video takes place deep in the countryside. The closest town is about forty minutes away, with stretches of verdant hills between the film site and proper civilization. Summer would usually make outdoor shoots difficult, but with the higher elevation and the sea being a hop-and-a-skip away, the weather hasn’t anything less than pleasantly balmy. If Mydei rises early enough, he could even start the day off with a refreshing jog through a track shaded by stately cypress trees.

“Mister Mydei!”

Alas, there aren’t enough mojitos on set to convince Mydei that this is nothing more than relaxing excursion. The songwriter turns at the sound of his name, acknowledging the girl bounding towards him with a nod.

“Mister Mydei,” Hyacine repeats as she catches her breath. “They’re checking the dailies at the director’s tent! Would you like to check it out?”

Mydei hands her his water bottle, but she seems to have misunderstood, stowing it away in her bag full of essentials she’s been carting around for other people. Too embarrassed to correct her, Mydei simply moves on to answer her question, “No, thank you.”

“Are you sure?”

“Positive.” Mydei holds out his towel to her. “To wipe your sweat,” he clarifies, miming out the action.

“Huh? Oh! Thank you!” Hyacine beams at him. “Be careful though. Sharing towels is one of the leading causes of ringworm infection!”

“Oh.” Mydei looks down at the towel in his hands, still unclaimed. “… Do you know where Phainon is?”

“Mister Phainon? He should be in the director’s tent by now.”

Great. “…Can you lead me there?”

Today, the tent in question has been set up at the edge of a clearing, a mild trek away from where Mydei had been loitering. Hyacine kindly updates

him on the walk over, something she’s only paid to do for Phainon’s behalf. She laughs when Mydei brings it up, telling him that a good deed costs nothing. It must be her first month working in the industry, Mydei thinks. She would have swindled a remuneration out of Mydei otherwise.

There’s no door on the tent for Mydei to knock on, so he and his pastel pink cohort barge in unannounced. They find three people crowding around the largest monitor on set, reviewing a scene that makes Mydei cringe.

Phainon is the first to notice the new arrivals. “You’re just in time,” he comments as Mydei and Hyacine approach. He doesn’t sound as exaggerated or humdrum today. “We were just getting to the good parts.”

“Why is my face so big on the screen?” Mydei asks.

“We’ll zoom out in post,” the director explains. “We were checking the composition.”

“You look great either way though,” Phainon comments. “In case you were feeling insecure.”

Mydei scoffs. “What I look like doesn’t matter to me.”

It would have been a problem for the production if Mydei cared about how he was depicted on screen. There’s not a lot of good he could say about the domineering, pugnacious dope swaggering about in all their footage, but as long as no one else takes umbrage with him, Mydei would consider it a job sufficiently done.

That doesn’t make it any less horrifying to see. Mydei steps back from the rest of the watch party with barely concealed grimace. “I get the gist,” he says, making a big show of stretching his arms. “It’s getting too cramped in here, so I’m heading out.”

“We haven’t even gotten to the shots in the field yet,” Phainon protests.

“I want to be surprised.”

Mydei unceremoniously leaves the tent. Phainon turns to the rest of their audience. “He actually hates surprises,” he warns. “So don’t jump at him when you see him around.”

Hyacine giggles. “Mister Mydei is right though. Music videos lose their magic when you watch them before they’re ready.”

“I mean I think the stuff we have is already worth watching,” Phainon says, turning back to the monitor. On screen, Mydei shreds on his guitar, arcing his back to get a better purchase on those higher notes. It would make for an spectacular visual once they edit the actual music in, but even a single soundless frame is enough to exemplify the ferocity unique to Mydei.

“That kid is something, isn’t he?”

Phainon glances over to the director, who strokes her chin in deep thought. “Presence like that is hard to imitate. Especially now that the age of rockstars has passed us by,” she says.

She’s not wrong. Mydei does look exquisitely edgy thanks to the make-up and costuming, though it’s obvious that his all-consuming gaze has nothing to do with the kind of eyeliner he has on. Calypso isn’t one of Anaxa’s longtime collaborators for no reason. Mydei must have really impressed her to be worth mentioning.

“For someone who’s been out of the public eye for years, he can sure work a camera,” she continues.

“Mydei’s full of surprises,” Phainon touts.

“It wouldn’t be much of a surprise after this,” Calypso says, smirking at him. “I suggest that you and your manager lock him up in a studio soon.”

Suddenly, Phainon doesn’t feel like gloating. “What do you mean by that?” He asks with as much boylike confoundment as possible.

“Nothing for you to be envious of, Phainon,” she replies. “He’ll still have to prepare a hell of a campaign to catch up to your popularity.”

Isn’t that still impressive? In the span of a single decent project, Mydei could have what Phainon took a decade to accumulate, and no one would be able to contest it. It wouldn’t matter if it ate into Phainon’s fame. As long Mydei gets what’s been owed to him, as long as it earns him an iota of the admiration that he deserves, Phainon would consider it a sacrifice worth making.

Phainon forgets exactly what had annoyed him by the time they finish reviewing yesterday’s rushes, but he remains contemplative, as if that one question had excavated an ancient problem. He supposes that’s what he gets for engaging in discussion with Anaxa’s acquaintances. As Hyacine starts inquiring the director’s team about today’s shooting schedule, Phainon quietly steps out for further introspection, hoping that the morning breeze could help clear his mind.

A roll of bread ambushes him as he exits the tent. “What the-“

“Eat,” a man gruffly orders.

Phainon opens his mouth to object, giving Mydei the opportunity to shove an entire buttered roll into his gob. Unless he wishes to choke, Phainon is forced to chew, leaving him to frown at the triumphant Kremnoan and the assortment of samples he had picked up from catering.

After a mild jaw workout, Phainon manages to gulp down his breakfast. “Have you been sneaking around here the entire time?” He accuses.

“I obviously haven’t,” Mydei says, waving a danish right in Phainon’s face. Phainon chomps down in retaliation, but Mydei doesn’t seem to mind one bit.

“Good boy,” Mydei praises. He has no idea that he’s about to give Phainon a boner.

“You’re going to give me a boner,” Phainon says out loud.

Instead of grossing him out or pissing him off as intended, Phainon’s words magically draws a laugh out of Mydei.

“Is that how easy you are?” Mydei teases. “Good boy, Deliverer, good boy. Who’s a good boy? You’re a good boy.”

“I was joking you know.”

“Excellent boy.” Mydei smirks. “Did that make you cum in your pants?”

Phainon elbows him in the gut, sending a few of Mydei’s bread rolls tumbling to the ground. Mydei would usually follow it up with a headlock, but Hyacine had materialized right then, stopping them in their tracks with an unyielding pinch of the ear.

Mydei’s beautiful fantasy of a vacation in the country ended before it could have a chance to begin. As a consolation prize, everyone is treated to a free stay in the nearest town, courtesy of the shoot ending later in the afternoon than intended. It would be irresponsible to make their bus driver work through the evening, though Mydei suspects it has more to do with Phainon’s manager happily requesting reimbursements from higher management.

As long as it’s not coming out of Mydei’s pockets, he’s not going to complain. Complaining is currently the last thing on his mind, what with the smorgasbord of tarts and delicate puddings sitting in front of him.

“Hmm!” Hyacine exclaims. “This orange blossom custard is really good too!”

Mydei digs his spoon into the ramekin she’d pointed at. Hmm, she’s right. “It’s delicious, but simple. With some cornflour and milk, we could remake this at home.”

“The syrup looks difficult to find though.”

“Kremnoan markets have something similar,” Mydei says. “If I could find it, I’ll make you some.”

Hyacine cheers. “Then we won’t have to travel half a day for a cup!”

Mydei and Hyacine had initially set out to find souvenirs to bring back home, but it didn’t take long for them to get sidetracked at the sight of a display case filled with pastries and sweets. Since there’s no telling when they’ll be back, they ended up ordering half of the café’s entire stock of desserts on the spot. So far, it’s been worth it. Mydei almost wishes they dragged more people into their trip to justify buying more, but at least with only him and Hyacine, halving a slice of pie doesn’t require a protractor.

Some ice cream would be the perfect thing to end their lunch on a high-note, especially since they were seated outside in the sun. Hyacine doesn’t like being cooped up indoors apparently, and Mydei doesn’t like saying no to people who say ‘may we’ and ‘please’. The only thing Mydei prefers about being inside is the lack of rude cat-callers.

“Hey hot stuff! Mind giving me some sugar?”

Hyacine frowns, which is about as threatening as a puffed-up chinchilla. “You shouldn’t be parking on the street, Cipher.”

“It’s fine, shortstack,” Phainon’s bodyguard says, patting the dashboard. “I got the lights on.”

She does have her hazard lights on, but it probably also helps that there isn’t a lot of competition on the road at this hour. Still, that doesn’t stop Hyacine from attempting to goad her out of traffic’s way. “If you find a real parking spot, we’ll save you some cake,” she says.

“That’d hit the spot, but you know how it is. Boss on your ass, telling you to run around shopping for crap while you’re stuck in some podunk town…”

“Phainon's making you do errands?” Mydei asks.

Cipher blows him a raspberry. “That dweeb ordering me around? Is the sky falling on our heads? Nah, it’s Ags. She got me hunting down bargains on

leather. Wouldja believe that? Normal people would just ask for a magnet or something. What the hell do I know about traditional tanneries?”

“Take a break with us first then,” Hyacine keeps trying. “What do you think I’m doing? Just throw a piece of wafer in my mouth. I’m good for it,” Cipher requests.

She opens her mouth wide, which Mydei automatically humors with a small gooseberry.

“Mister Mydei!” Hyacine says admonishingly.

“Nice throw,” Cipher says. “Next time, try not shooting at the rental.”

The berry had missed Cipher’s head by a couple of inches, landing right onto the passenger seat instead. Mydei is sure he could make the next shot, but Hyacine’s stare shames him into giving up.

“I wanted her to know what she’s missing,” Mydei says.

Obviously not a great excuse, but Hyacine accepts it anyway, recognizing that there are other people more deserving of her ire.

“If you’re not going to join us, then you best go back to finding quality leather for Miss Aglaea,” she tells Cipher. “Mister Phainon might need you soon, you know. Who knows if something’ll happen to him?”

“Whoa, no need to call on bad omens, Cinny,” Cipher says. “Nothing’s going to happen to Phainon dearest. I even asked him if he wanted to hit the road with me, but he said he’s fine cooped up in his hotel suite. And I already baby-proofed his room twice over, so I got nothing to do back there but get bored outta my mind.”

Phainon content to be a shut-in? Maybe the sky is falling, because the only person that hates being inside more than Hyacine is the Deliverer himself. It’s clear there’s something that’s been eating at him this whole trip, and it’s even clearer now that there’s no job to occupy his mind. Mydei shouldn’t be

the only one to notice, yet neither Cipher nor Hyacine seem to react to the news. Is it that common for Phainon to have off-days? Or is Mydei overthinking it, worrying about issues are above his station?

A car honks at Cipher as it passes by, to which she responds with a furious toot of her own horn.

“I got my lights on!” She shouts at the retreating Accord. Hyacine just shakes her head.

Maybe it’s fine if Mydei overthinks this one time. Once does not constitute a pattern. It’s barely more than a coincidence, no further insinuation or significance to be made of.

“Cipher.” A vague shape of a plan forms in Mydei’s head as the bodyguard lowers her middle finger. “Where did you rent the car?”

Phainon’s back hurts from lying in bed for so long, but he refuses to get up anytime soon. Especially for an incessant ringing that the sign on his door should have discouraged. If someone wanted to play Flight of the Bumblebees on the doorbell then by all means, go nuts. There’s no one inside the room that cares. No sirree.

…Oh, fuck it. Life’s too short for Phainon to pretend he’s got a longer fuse.

He marches to the door and throws it wide open, exposing his tousled self to all and sundry. “Real sorry, but I’m not doing autogr- huh?”

“I don’t want an autograph,” the intruder deadpans before yanking Phainon out of his hotel room by the neck of his pajama shirt.

“Mydei? What are you- Wait! I can’t go anywhere like this!”

Mydei answers him by slotting a helmet right onto his dome. No words necessary as the blond continues whisking him away to Kephale knows where.

Oceanview Inn may not have an ocean to view, but their free slippers hold up swimmingly through the journey from hotel room to parking lot. Phainon’s psyche fared a lot less nicely, buoyed only by his trust in Mydei and his surprisingly reassuring grip. It’s almost like one of Cipher’s mafia shows, except instead of taking him out back to be executed, Mydei drags Phainon to a hotel parking lot to show him… a motorcycle?

In a display of great trust, Mydei lets go of Phainon’s arm to grab the other helmet hanging from the bike’s handlebars. He dons it on, looking a lot more put together than Phainon does with only a sleeveless shirt and a pair of dark wash jeans. Phainon notes the fit of his pants as Mydei slings a sculpted leg over the motorcycle with ease, the stiff waistband leaving a gap between skin and denim as he sits down. It seems that Mydei’s tattoos really do go all the way south.

“Hop on,” Mydei says, his voice dampened by the helmet.

Perhaps it’s not a mob film. Phainon swears he’s seen this same kidnapping plot in a Liam Neeson joint.

“Hop on,” Mydei repeats. This time Phainon obeys, which may or may not be a result of Mydei’s voice dipping into a low rasp. He’s not quite sure what that says about him just yet.

“There’s no seatbelt,” Mydei says as Phainon settles behind him. “So you’ll need to hold on to me.”

Phainon finally understands what’s happening. He must have fallen asleep in his hotel room, where he’s dreamt up of permission to grope Mydei. He’d be a fool not to accept.

Courtesy keeps Phainon’s touch light at first, but the speed at which Mydei tears out of the parking lot forces Phainon’s arms to tighten around his driver’s midsection. Whatever remained of Phainon’s fogginess didn’t last a minute into the ride. The roar of the engine and the wind buffeting around them had sobered Phainon up instantly, just in time for him to recognize the insanity of Mydei weaving through car after car on the road.

Phainon feels Mydei chuckle more than he hears it, and that’s when Phainon realizes he’s been screaming throughout the drive so far. Phainon would have pinched his abductor’s side, had he not been afraid of crashing into a lamppost.

A more attentive person would have asked their questions much earlier, before conversation becomes a tedious shouting match over the whizzing traffic. Those obvious questions only occur to Phainon now, when he observes lesser and lesser buildings around them. Where did Mydei get the bike anyway? Why did he decide to take Phainon with him? Where in the world could they possibly be going?

That last question is Phainon’s final attempt at ignorance. He should know their destination from the exits Mydei takes, but would it be so selfish to take this moment as it is? A simple drive down the country for the sake of seeing Amphoreus in her most scenic? The view certainly helps distract from the fundamental truth, as does the rugged body in his arms, keeping Phainon warm through the cold draft. A patchwork of greens and browns blankets the distant hills, stitched together by winding rivers and streams. Wispy streaks of white break up the vast blue above them like seafoam on the shore. It’s breathtakingly picturesque. It’s a painting on the back of a postcard. The concept of mafia movies and action thrillers have long departed from Phainon’s mind. He wants instead to reside in the same line of thought as Roman Holiday and Fallen Angels, but without any of the trifles that made either film interesting.

“Take the dirt road to the left!” Phainon shouts over the noise.

He admits to doubting Mydei’s compliance for a brief second, but his honorary chauffeur obliges without question. The path may be bumpier and the insects more relentless, but Phainon swears it shaves minutes off their perilous journey.

Mydei slows the bike as the road opens up to a village. Or what remains of it, it seems. What awaits them is nothing like Phainon’s stories, or the mock-ups Mydei found while searching for directions. What they find is a barren land, a flattened plateau of sand and concrete. The back roads had hidden the worst of it, interspersed with rickety old huts that may or may

not be mostly vacated. At least there Mydei can make out a faint resemblance to Phainon’s stories, where the lanky growths of ryegrass and foxtails mark where the sprawling fields used to be.

It’s the main boulevard that is indistinguishable from the Aedes Elysiae in Mydei’s imagination. There, a four lane road bisects the tiny settlement, running over the village green where Phainon used to chase down other kids with a makeshift sword. The shops where Phainon used to spend his hard-earned allowance have been converted into fast food chains and gas stations. In place of the trees Phainon used to climb are tall utility poles and their tangled cables, and in place of everything else is gravel and dust from abandoned construction sites.

It occurs to Mydei that he might have done a cruel thing. No one wants to see the desecrated corpse of their hometown, but before Mydei could work out the best way to apologize, Phainon points out to a store and says, “That’s where I skinned my knee running after Rini.”

“…When she stole your wooden effigy?”

“It was an action figure,” Phainon corrects. “I got scolded at home for it too. I’m glad this place got turned into a Soulglad’s.”

The buildings, despite being newer, are already starting to show signs of wear. They’re already not too impressive to look at - a line of flat uniform cubes dumped out in the middle of nowhere - but the chipping paint, the muddy windows, and the faded signs make up the final nail in the coffin. The sweltering heat beating down the main road is not only detrimental to humans. Shade is important for a hastily constructed strip mall too.

“Hey, can we stop here?” Phainon requests.

At his request, Mydei obediently parks in front of a grocer’s, the myriad of advertisements taped over the front telling him nothing about the store. Phainon nearly stumbles as he jumps off the bike, ignoring Mydei’s snort to shove the helmet back in his arms. He looked to be seconds away from dashing inside, but the bird nest his headgear had left forces him to pause. Phainon nearly scalps himself trying to tame his hair, only the shop’s door

to open wide before Phainon could even reduce the number of cowlicks down to his usual two.

The man that steps out has a stoic brow and a heavy footfall. He stalks toward Phainon as if he intends to pummel the singer’s face in, alerting Mydei enough to get him hopping off the motorcycle in panic. The man unfortunately gets to Phainon first, accosting him with a terrible and brutal bear hug.

“Phainon!” The man bellows. “You rascal, you didn’t tell us you were coming by!”

“Hrk- Probably because it was last minute…” Phainon says. One of his ribs is probably dust by now. “…Could you put me down, Uncle Galba?”

This so-called ‘Uncle Galba’ lowers Phainon to the ground at his command. He also gives Phainon a hearty smack on the back that almost unseats his lungs.

“You shoulda tried ringin’ up. I got nothing ready for you,” Uncle Galba says disapprovingly.

“Aw, you don’t hafta, y’know,” Phainon tells him.

“For you, maybe. But what about your guest 'ere?” Uncle Galba gestures to Mydei. “I know you too, by the way. You’re the other kid that’s singing and dancing with our Phainon!”

Mydei had no idea what Uncle Galba would do next, but he definitely didn’t expect a weathered middle-aged man to start singing his own song back to him. A deep cut from the Sun and Thunder discography no less.

“That one’s my favorite,” Uncle Galba says once he gets enough of that. “Phainon said you wrote that one on your own, so he made you sing most of it.”

“Okay, Uncle Galba, let’s give Mydei some space,” Phainon interjects. “Can we continue this inside? It’s blazin’ out here.”

“Of course, of course.” Uncle Galba nods. “Can’t have you city boys frying in the sun now.”

Mydei had planned to stay outside while Phainon attends to his own matters, but he can hardly turn down an invitation from Phainon’s elders. He follows them into the store, awkwardly third wheeling their warm greetings and well-wishes.

A rotating fan welcomes them with a blast of cold air. It’s a lot less brighter indoors, Mydei finds, as he blinks furiously to acclimate to the sudden shift in lighting. Not that there’s much of the store to look at once he opens his eyes, being small enough for Mydei to survey the entire room from the entrance. It makes it a bit of a tight squeeze for 3 men of their stature to make their way through the aisles, though it could be worse. Mydei tries not to be too thankful for the shop’s lack of customers and other employees. He’s not trying to jinx Uncle Galba’s source of revenue.

“Make yourselves at home,” Uncle Galba orders as he opens up one of his display coolers. “Find somewhere to sit or somethin'.”

There’s only one stool in the entire store. Phainon takes it at Mydei’s insistence, forgoing the usual quarreling and subjugation. He’s more subdued today, Mydei thinks, before Phainon starts patting his thighs in invitation.

“Seat yourself here,” Phainon offers with the panache of a used car salesman.

Mydei would have loved to make Phainon regret saying that. Unfortunately, he has no desire to out himself as a scoundrel in front of Phainon’s Uncle Galba, something that Phainon himself has no qualms with.

“There’s plenty of space,” the bastard continues to needle.

“On those twigs?” Mydei says. Phainon’s legs aren’t the least bit skinny, but his ego’s already inflated enough without hearing Mydei’s real opinion.

“You liked resting on them last time.”

“Probably because I was unconscious.”

Uncle Galba thankfully had been too busy sticking his head in a cooler to witness Mydei’s rudeness. When he finally withdraws from the store’s icy depths, Phainon’s hair has mysteriously gained some new unruly flyaways.

“Here. To cool you off,” Uncle Galba says, pushing a can of soda into each of their clutches.

“I’m fine, thank you,” Mydei refuses.

“No you’re not,” Uncle Galba says. “You’ll need this if you rode all the way here on that two-wheeler."

“It’ll hurt his feelings, Mydei,” Phainon warns as he opens his own can.

“I-“

“You don’t ‘ave to pay,” Uncle Galba clarifies.

“…I don’t want to impose,” Mydei says, accepting the can in defeat.

“Trust me, you’d be doin’ me a favor,” Uncle Galba says. “That old thing’s just gonna go bad sitting on the shelf. You see anybody tryna fill their larders up in here?”

“It’s ‘cause you keep talking like that,” Phainon points out. “No one wants to shop anywhere where the owner’s mouthing off their own service.”

“That’d make sense if there were actually people around to hear me talk.”

Uncle Galba steps behind the counter and begins rummaging through its shelves. It takes a few seconds and a couple of drawers before he finds what he’s looking for.

“Hey kid,” he calls out to Mydei. “Check this out.”

Mydei lowers his soda can to see Uncle Galba proudly holding up a bare cassette tape; no sleeve, no case, no label, no nothing. The plastic is a little

dinged and a little grimy, and it takes a little elbow grease to shove it into the radio currently blasting some staticky 90’s hits. The music dies out at a push of a button, replaced moments later by another song that’s just as geriatric.

“Wow,” Mydei says. He doesn’t sound like it, but he does genuinely mean it. Who wouldn’t be astonished to hear their old debut single out in a remote village?

“D’you need money for a real stereo, Uncle Galba?” Phainon asks. Phainon wouldn’t be surprised by something like this. This is his home turf. “Our stuff sounds a whole lot better on CD.”

Uncle Galba huffs. “CDs compress the sound. Listen to that. ‘ear how the wah-wahs ring? You can’t get that on CD.”

“It’s a bootleg recording,” Phainon says. “You can’t hear jack.”

Uncle Galba waves him off and turns to Mydei. “You get what I’m sayin’, right kid?”

“It sounds very authentic,” Mydei says.

“See?”

“You can literally hear the radio announcer doing commentary on it,” Phainon argues.

Mydei shrugs. “It’s authentic like a home movie.”

“I like this kid,” Uncle Galba says. At some point, he had picked up a phone receiver and started dialing. “Bring ‘im over more often, would you?”

“He’s a kissass,” Phainon says.

“I learned it from you,” Mydei retorts.

“Learning from the best? You’re welcome.”

Mydei kicks his stool in response. The jolt spills a few stray drops of Phainon’s soda onto the singer’s pants.

“Oops,” Mydei says, automatically leaning over to wipe off the mess.

“Whoa Mydei, not in front of Uncle Galba,” Phainon exclaims.

Mydei immediately takes his hand off Phainon’s leg and glares at him. “Do you want me to kill you?”

“I’d like to live a long happy life, if you don’t mind,” Phainon says, grinning. The sugar from the soda must have shot up straight to his head. “You could join me if you like.”

“Join you? That’d kill me.”

“Well no need to be dramatic about it.”

If Uncle Galba notices their exchange, he doesn’t say anything. Instead, he starts cackling at someone on the phone. “Yeah, yeah, but this ain’t a social call. Guess who’s sitting in the store right this very second?” Uncle Galba’s merry expression suddenly drops to a scowl. “No I ain’t in trouble! I paid for the damn- Can you get in ‘ere already? Phainon’s waiting for you!”

“We’re actually just passing through,” Phainon corrects. “I don’t think we-“

“And bring leftovers. Phangry ‘ere doesn’t have time for a real meal,” Uncle Galba says before setting the receiver down. Then he picks it up and starts dialing once more.

“You’re not escaping that easily,” he tells Phainon. “You don’t know how many people you’ve pissed off staying away for so long- Hello? No I wasn’t talking to you, I was talking to Phainon!”

“Uh,” Phainon hesitantly looks up at Mydei. He doesn’t say anything, allowing his apologetic smile to do the talking.

Mydei clicks his tongue. “It’s fine,” he says with a half-hearted reproach.

“You spoil me.”

“You’re the one who’s going to explain your absence to Hyacine.”

Phainon’s brow furrows. Mydei knows he would have opened his mouth to say something incendiary had he not been interrupted by Uncle Galba’s voice. “Yes, our Phainon! Do you know any other Phainons running around?”

Phainon eyes Mydei, who nurses his soda awfully slowly. “That’s a lot of people to meet,” he tells the blond.

“So?”

“So are you gonna be okay? Or would you like to hide it out somewhere?”

Mydei clicks his tongue. “Don’t patronize me. I’m a fully grown man.”

The crushing grip on his can being indicative of nothing, of course.

Phainon’s first visitor arrives much earlier than anticipated, though the bags hanging from her arm suggests she might be in the store for another purpose. Her double take at the door solidifies that theory, and for a moment Mydei fears she’s gone into cardiac arrest with the way she clutches at her chest.

“Oh my stars,” the woman quietly breathes. “Do my eyes deceive me?”

She approaches slowly, as if reality would crumble at her next step and send her tumbling out of bed. Her hand reaches Phainon’s face first, confirming his existence through sight and touch. For all his bravado earlier, Phainon now appears to be no better than a bashful child.

The woman stares at him wide-eyed in disbelief. “You haven’t been mailing lately,” she says.

“Neither have you guys,” Phainon replies.

The woman throws her arms around the pop star and laughs. “You keep changing addresses! It’s too complicated for simple folk like us.”

“As if the Aunt Doli I know could be stumped so easily,” Phainon says, sounding slightly out of breath. Everyone in Aedes Elysiae seems to be aggressive huggers, which explains a lot about Phainon’s proclivities.

The door bursts open just then, ushering in a stream of people carrying tributes of fruit and bread. “Where’s the boy?”

Phainon buries his head into Aunt Doli’s embrace, but Uncle Galba readily betrays him. “He’s over here!”

No one dares to miss out on the chance to see Phainon, no matter how much Phainon assures he’ll get to everybody eventually. While everyone has retained the good sense to line up and wait their turn, they’re utterly remorseless with their questions, drilling him on how he’s been, if he’s had the chance to try this-and-that, or if he even remembers them at all. Sometimes the question opens up to the floor, and everyone gets the chance to excitedly update Phainon about how their own lives are going.

Seeing the hubbub around the star, Uncle Galba silently gestures for Mydei to join him behind the counter, far from the madding crowd of aunts and uncles. As much as he’d love to be safely behind a barricade, the hand gripping onto his shirt tethers Mydei to Phainon’s side. He’s aware this makes him look like a security guard hovering over his charge - and he acts a bit like it too - but Mydei did drive all this way for Phainon’s sake. It would be incongruous of him if Mydei deserted Phainon at such a critical junction.

“How’s your folks?” Asks a woman as she places two wet kisses on Phainon’s cheeks. “Sorry we couldn’t make it to your ma’s birthday.”

Phainon laughs. “Yeah, that drove her crazy! She even took down your cross-stitching from the living room wall!”

“Oh that shrew! I oughta drive down there and give her piece of my mind!”

“What about Rini?” A man with an obtrusively large sun hat asks.

“She’s doin’ great!” Phainon answers. “Maybe a lil’ busy these days cause of the new book. That reminds me, I started raising a plant recently, and I can’t tell if the leaves are too yellow or if I’m seein’ things-”

“You got too much sulfates in the soil!

“You don’t know that, dummy! We needta check a photo before we start making that call!”

The population of Aedes Elysiae is a piddling number compared to any other town in Amphoreus, but the crowd that Phainon’s presence draws is still too much for Uncle Galba’s humble store to handle. Some villagers appeared to have foreseen this, hauling in plastic tables and chairs to set up outside. All the food they’ve brought for Phainon have been arranged out on the tables to be shared, while those who are sick of Uncle Galba’s radio have gathered around a guitar to entertain themselves. Anyone not hungry or musically inclined have taken to card games or discussion with a neighbor. Someone even props a chair against the shop’s door to keep it open, the fan on the counter working overtime to spare everyone a little relief.

Phainon lets go of Mydei’s shirt by the 30 minute mark, either no longer in need of his presence or aching from a terrible case of cramped fingers. Not that Mydei is itching for a chance to wander off, though the festivities happening right outside the door does pique his interest. He clearly put too much stock in Phainon’s magnetism if he thinks his curiosity isn’t obvious, because a group of ladies catch on to his wandering eye and decide to do something about it.

“Come, dearie,” says the woman tugging at his arm. “It’s no fun being a wallflower.”

“I am having fun, ma’am,” Mydei insists.

“Oh indulge us, would you?” Another woman says. “We don’t want you to think these four walls is all there to see in our little township.”

“Especially after Phainon dragged you all the way here,” the first woman says.

“…I was the one who brought him here.”

“Then the more you oughta enjoy yourself!” She replies.

Mydei looks back at Phainon, who pauses his conversation to shoot him a toothy smile. He’ll be alright without Mydei, and Mydei can survive a few minutes without him. With their consent, the women hoist Mydei around the gathering, introducing him to the various people who took a hand in raising Phainon. Each time, Mydei is taken aback to be recognized at first glance. His name might escape most of them, but everyone happily regales him with a performance they remember Mydei from. To be Phainon’s fan is to be a fan of his collaborators, apparently.

“‘cept for that song he did with that Belobog hip-hopper,” one of the village’s fishermen says. “She was alright, but Amphorean musicians are on a different level.”

“But that song he did with that tee-bee person was really catchy!”

“Yeah but see, they made that song in Amphoreus,” the fisherman says. “Phainon did not take a single step outside the country, which makes it a good song.”

“Men.” The lady holding on to Mydei clicks her tongue. “Allergic to feelings.”

“I’m also a man,” Mydei reminds her.

The woman pats his arm. “That’s why I’m tellin’ you, sweetie.”

Time passes exceptionally quick. Mydei gets to try a slice of bread or two, too full from his trip with Hyacine to stuff himself with more. He gets a sight of Phainon with his own entourage across the improvised reception, carefully examining a painting of large fluffy dog on the side of a truck. Mydei gets intercepted by a handful of curious people, and for once Mydei

doesn’t get snide or skittish about answering a simple question. He gets an explanation on Phainon’s beloved childhood friend, and when Mydei tells them he’s met Cyrene, he gets an aunt shouting at the crowd about how ‘it’s serious!’.

The guitar finds itself in Mydei’s hands at some point, and everyone instantly cajoles their two visitors into singing a song. Mydei meets Phainon’s eye, and with an amused shrug, they decide to premiere Amber Dawn right there and then. It’s difficult without all the instruments and without ever rehearsing an acoustic arrangement, but the audience is forgiving and the song is sincere. The performance earns them laughter where Phainon had promised tears, so Phainon naturally makes a show out of looking upset and seeking appeasement.

“He’s always been a sensitive boy,” Phainon’s old teacher tells Mydei.

“…I think he’s just joking,” Mydei says, watching Phainon feign offense with someone’s apology.

Phainon’s teacher laughs quietly. “I was referring to your song,” she explains. “Phainon can be very… transparent with what he feels. There isn’t a single soul here who wouldn’t immediately get what he was singing about.”

“Is it too on the nose?” Mydei asks.

“I think it’s just right,” Phainon’s teacher says. “ For what it’s worth, I liked it. You both wrote a lovely song.”

“…But?”

She smiles up at Mydei. “But Aedes Elysiae doesn’t really merit that kind of sentiment anymore.”

“You can blame the council for that,” the woman behind her mutters. “They sold a pretty lie about turning’ this ‘ere region into a moneymaker, then fled when the goin’ got tough.”

Mydei had read about it when he was looking up directions to the village. Aedes Elysiae was part of a grand renovation plan to turn the coast into a series of resorts, with hopes of boosting tourism and Amphoreus’s GPD. It had fallen through after 5 stagnant years of development, in which the Council of Elders slowly came to realize the true magnitude of the project and how idealistic their projected budget had been. The plan had left nothing but rotting structures and displaced families in its wake - footnotes in Amphoreus’s quest to catch up with the wider world.

A car crash had taken Phainon’s parents around the very start of the demolition period. The kind of loss he experienced at such a young age shouldn’t result in a man so eternally sunny, and yet here he is, laughing and grinning at a pun too lame to repeat.

“It’s not so bad,” Phainon’s old teacher says, looking out at the desolated buildings across the street. “All the important bits are still here.”

The lady from earlier, the one who Phainon called ‘Aunt Doli’, approaches the singer while the others are distracted. Whatever she says to him makes him smile meekly, to which Aunt Doli answers with the universal gesture for ‘shoo’.

“I hate to be the bearer of bad news,” Phainon says loud enough for the entire yard to hear. “But clock’s a tickin’. Mydei and I gotta go get while there’s still light out.”

A chorus of ‘aw’s ring out from the gathering. Everyone surges once more toward Phainon, seizing their last chance to bend his ear. A few stragglers even take some time to approach Mydei with a promise to welcome him in their homes whenever he comes back. The farewells stretch on for minutes on end, coming to a stop when Phainon sees enough teary eyes in the crowd. He steps his foot down and pulls Mydei back to the bike, much to Mydei’s insistence on independence. The villagers all boo while Mydei revs the engine, but as the two begin to ride off into the sunset, a horde of arms shoot up in the air and wave them off as zealously as they can.

Phainon waves back until their faces are mere blurs in the bike’s side mirrors. His arm drops and quickly returns to Mydei’s waist, adhering his

body to Mydei’s back.

“…Did you have fun?” Phainon asks.

“I did,” Mydei answers.

“Good,” Phainon says. “Because I need you to take that next right before we head back.”

Mydei is yet to defy a direct instruction from Phainon today, and there’s no reason for him switch it up now. Despite the creeping fatigue from their merry-making, Mydei follows the directions he’s been given, even as the path leads them up a hill through a battered road. They carefully navigate through the obstacles until reach the top, where they’re greeted by a tiny cloister ravaged by snaking vines and wild ivy.

Mydei parks the bike under the building’s shade. The symbols etched into the stone should be enough to clue him in, but Phainon beats Mydei’s memory to the punch. “It’s a temple to Oronyx,” he explains. “Defunct, obviously, otherwise Cyrene woulda been a priest by now.”

It’s hard to tell if he’s joking. Mydei might not know what a priest of Oronyx does, but solemn prayer and religious piety doesn’t strike him as something Phainon’s sprightly sister would enjoy. Then again, she is a really good storyteller. She’d probably be really good at preaching.

“Keep up, will ya?” Phainon says when Mydei stops to examine the roughened masonry. “That’s not why we’re here!”

Mydei grumbles to himself as he hikes through years of untamed shrubbery. A piece of bramble causes him to stumble out of the thicket and trip right onto Phainon, who steadies them both right before they end up tumbling down the hill. Mydei would had an unkind word to say, had the vista behind Phainon not stolen the complaint right out of his mouth.

Aedes Elysiae is no longer the beautiful tranquil village from Phainon’s memory, but it’s less obvious from up on high, where that garish highway is a trivial part of a wider picture. The ramshackle huts they passed earlier

envelop the lifeless thoroughfare with color, their brightly tiled roofs appearing like a meadow of flowers from afar. A wave of porch-lights flicker on in preparation for evening, despite the faint sounds of revelry still echoing in the air. On the outskirts of the village, young sycamore trees brace against the wind blown in by the sea, its waters shimmering brilliantly in the late afternoon.

Mydei turns to Phainon, who has wandered off to a pond beside the courtyard. Mydei follows him in squatting by its edge, following his gaze to a sprinkle of duckweed.

“All the kids used to bike up here in the summer to watch the frogs hatch,” Phainon says.

Mydei searches for said frogs and finds none. “We must have missed them,” he says.

“Summers are getting warmer. Wouldn’t surprise me if the frogs moved it up to spring.” Phainon skims his hand over the pond’s surface. “One year we found salamander eggs in the water too. That caused a big commotion, ‘cause we were worried the larvae would eat the tadpoles or vice versa.”

“Did you move them?”

Phainon shakes his head. “Nah. Our parents didn’t want a bunch of amphibians running around our houses, so we just let ‘em be. They all survived anyway. I think.”

“Is it only frogs and salamanders in here?”

“I don’t actually know. I haven’t been here since Rini’s folks moved away,” Phainon confesses. “How ‘bout you? Been to Kremnos lately?”

“Naturally,” Mydei says. “Krateros and I go back whenever it gets too cold in Okhema.”

“Must be nice.”

“You don’t know that. You haven’t been there.”

“But you sounded like you liked it.”

“It’s my city,” Mydei says. “I’d like it any way it came. You don’t have the same perspective.”

“I mean we like most of the same things,” Phainon points out. “Like music, for starters. And working out and… civilized discussion.”

“Hmm.” Mydei taps his knee in thought. “Then I suppose it’s no surprise that I like your village, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon scoffs. “Do you really?”

“Yes,” Mydei replies. “I do.”

Phainon stares into Mydei’s eyes, ready to latch on to the first sign of a lie. He stares at Mydei, who has never been anything but honest, and who’s nothing like Phainon’s cabal of timid admirers, shrinking away from the slightest bit of recognition.

The singer's withdrawal is a foregone conclusion, but the hysterical laughter is something Mydei would have never predicted.

“What’s wrong with you now? Mydei mutters.

Phainon wipes a stray tear from his eye. “How come I never remembered you being so presumptuous?” He asks with a juvenile grin.

“You say that as if I presumed wrong,” Mydei challenges.

“Okay, well, you got me,” Phainon concedes. “There’s still a lot to like about Aedes Elysiae. I just forgot for a second.”

“Remember it well then,” Mydei warns. “Or those poor women would be left waiting for letters that would never come.”

“You make me sound like a playboy.”

“So it’s funny to you? Playing with old women’s hearts?”

Another bout of laughter grips Phainon before the world around them takes over the conversation. Chirping crickets keep them company as the gentle wobble of the pond remains bereft of frog or salamander. The rustling grass fetes a creaking swing with lilliputian applause, rivaling the zeal of the tree branches above. The sky blooms into oranges and pinks, like bruises from a nasty spill orchestrated by your adopted sister.

Beside him, Mydei hears Phainon sigh. He turns to the pop star, wondering if his legs are also burning from squatting for so long. Instead of sore muscles and tetchy words, Mydei finds Phainon already looking back at him.

“You made my dream come true, you know?” Phainon says with a quiet chuckle.

Phainon’s wayward locks flutter in the wind, gilded with the citrine shine of noon. He doesn’t exactly smile, doesn’t grin in that open boyish way of his. Instead, catharsis squares his shoulders and lights a resolute glint in his eye, maturing him in spite of the rumpled pajamas and the flush of red from the sun.

What a sight to behold. Here, in the most perfect location with the most perfect of weather at the most perfect of timings.

“I mean in my dream I think I was the one taking you home, except th-mmpf?!”

There’s a name for the type of contact people make with their lips, but Mydei can’t remember it right now. He only recognizes it as a spark firing repeatedly in his synapses, overwriting his body’s directives until his mouth connects with the handsome face in front of him. It’s softer than he could ever imagine and sweeter than he could ever hope.

Mydei’s brain restores its functions too late. Kissing. The word is kissing. He’s kissing Phainon, and good Mydeimoses never kiss Phainon.

It’s a feather-light touch, nothing more than a vestal graze reserved for schoolchildren and ceramic tchotchkes of plump cherubs. Mydei pulls back

the moment he senses a pressure against his mouth, but he’s still too slow. His lips already tingle from Phainon’s absence, and he’s overwhelmed by the urge to swipe his tongue over the thin film of chapstick that had been left behind.

Mydei doesn’t do that, however. Not when Phainon’s wide eyes meet his and reflects Mydei’s doomed expression back to him.

“There’s a frog,” Mydei says. “On the tree. Behind you.”

Phainon turns and nearly jumps. There is a frog behind on the tree him. It’s a damn big frog too. Nearly the size of a handball.

“That is a frog,” Phainon says. “Or a toad. What the hell is that?”

That is the sound of Mydei getting away with it scot free. Kephale, Oronyx, or whoever it was who listened - your newest believer praises your mercy.

How they got back to the hotel is a foggy memory to Mydei. He’d been too focused on keeping his cool and distracting Phainon from what just transpired, telling himself that it could easily be mistaken for an accident. He comes up with all kinds of excuses - he had a cramp in his leg, he was trying to hear him better, he was too excited to see a huge frog - but he doesn’t dare neglect to prepare his apologies either. An apology would be the kindest thing Mydei can offer, and perhaps if he were a better person, it would have been the first course of action he takes.

And Phainon? Phainon stays the same old Phainon, badgering Mydei on the way back to their hotel rooms like he always does.

Nothing explicit happens in this story at all but I do want to say that you may not want to read this in public. I mean I can't stop you. I've read a kpop fanfic over someone's shoulder at a guns and roses concert so maybe that's the move

Kissing Phainon is a problem for all of one day, because Mydei soon remembers about the interview coming up two days after. The thought of ruining another televised appearance and the thought of Phainon secretly despising him had cancelled each other out in his head, leaving Mydei at peace once it came time to head into the studio.

Mydei had been so calm and prepared that he arrives at the set earlier than he’s ever been. Typically that means sitting put in a corner and scrolling through his phone for an extra half-an-hour, but today he’s feeling energetic enough to try something productive. He decides to take a page out of Phainon’s book and boldly approach a crew member out of his own volition. To no one’s surprise, Mydei is not as skillful at talking up uninterested strangers, but he’s good at lifting things, and there’s apparently a lot of equipment that needs to be carried around on set.

“Mydei?” Phainon calls out as he arrives. “What are you doing?”

It’s hard for Mydei to look at Phainon when he’s holding up a large metal stand, but it’s not as hard as he expected days ago, when Mydei was still tortured by a certain fiasco in the mountains.

“Helping out,” he answers.

“I assumed that was the case,” Phainon says, raising an eyebrow. “Because it’ll be pretty difficult to sneak something that noticeable out of here.”

Mydei would have shrugged if his arms weren’t occupied. “So why’d you ask?”

The stand was starting to get in the way, so Mydei plods on to get rid of it once and for all. He places the stand down on the indicated spot, setting it up as instructed. This film crew is easy to please. They happily shower Mydei with praise and gratitude for a task that only takes him a few minutes to complete - and that’s with their assistance. Mydei is quick to rectify whatever false impression they might have, telling them that a few bicep curls a day would allow them to carry twice the weight of a plain old stand. Everyone weirdly loses interest after that, but they do wish Mydei good luck once he makes to leave.

Phainon hasn’t moved at all from where Mydei had left him, watching Mydei with his arms crossed as if he disapproves of what he sees. When Mydei gets close, however, he finds nothing but Phainon’s trademarked cheer.

“Got up on the right side of bed today, I see,” Phainon chirps.

“Can it,” Mydei says. “You’re not the only one allowed to talk to the production team.”

“I didn’t know you were trying to compete me on that.”

“We aren’t.”

“Yeah, because I’d kick your ass so bad,” Phainon boasts. “But that’s alright. That’s what makes you so cute.”

Apart from the tiny twitch of his eye, Mydei remains wholly stone-faced. “…That’s the kind of thing you’d say while hot mic’d.”

“Not this time,” Phainon claims, despite visibly reaching back to check. “But if I am, so what? Do you have something against getting called

‘cute’?”

“Only if you don’t want people to think you’re out of your mind,” Mydei says.

“Well okay, you’re not being very adorable right now,” says Phainon. “You’re so sweaty that even Phagousa’s basin can’t hold you.”

Mydei instinctively wipes off the dampness on his neck. “Haikas.”

“You should get to the dressing room,” Phainon says as he slaps Mydei’s shoulder. “Your make-up artist is getting restless back there.”

Mydei sets off as advised. He throws Phainon a customary glare, but in reality he couldn’t be any more relieved. If Mydei wasn’t sure before, then that exchange certainly makes it clear that the worst is behind them. For once, Mydei is grateful for Phainon’s leniency to every transgression made against him, because he doubts the singer would have given him a second chance otherwise.

Or perhaps kisses like that are just too commonplace for Amphoreus’s national sweetheart to take seriously. A little peck on the mouth between two estranged co-workers is probably a regular Monday for Phainon. In that case, all the more reason why Mydei should forget everything about it as soon as he’s able.

As Mydei gets freshened up for the camera, Phainon remains standing in the middle of the sound stage, staring down at his own palm. That felt like the right about of force for a friendly pat, not too weak and not too grabby. He clenches his hand ever so slightly and recalls how firm and supple Mydei’s deltoid was under his touch. Then he immediately shoves his fist into his pocket when a technician passes by. Yeah, this interview will go well, Phainon thinks.

At least the musical performances are guaranteed to be good. After being stuck in the mountains pretending to pluck a guitar for hours on end, Mydei is itching to give his six-string a real run. It makes even Euphrosyne sound refreshing to his ears, despite being the only song they’ve played on the

promotional tour so far. If it helps to distract him from his more unsavory thoughts, then Mydei would give it all he’s got until only Euphrosyne is stuck in his head. He even remembers to smile and wave at audience when it ends.

Mydei’s high spirits carries over to the interview portion, where he sits cordially without a single sardonic bone in his body. His answers still lack the charm and sharpness of a tolerable celebrity, but he’s become more forthcoming with information, politely sharing his opinions before the host has to wrestle it out of him. He refrains from talking down at Phainon and adds relevant details to his stories without obnoxiously derailing them, keeping them both on equal terms as the interview goes on.

“Just to be clear, you two aren’t going for this year’s Astral Fantasia, right?” Asks Diogena, the show’s host. “Because sign-ups are still open if you want to try defending your title.”

“It’s tempting, but I think we’re all Fantasia’d out,” Phainon jokes. “This year’s entries are unbelievable too. Proi Proi gave me goosebumps, wow.”

“I like Clouds and Snow more,” Mydei says. “It’s very festive, which is also part of the competition.”

“Festive, huh? Is that why you submitted Euphrosyne?”

“Kind of,” Phainon answers Diogena. “It was the best song we had so far.”

“It was distinctive, I can tell you that much,” Diogena says before turning to Mydei. “What made you write that kind of song anyway? You would have been too young to be in a discotheque back then.”

The audience laughs politely at her soft jab. It’s a common question, played-out way before Sun and Thunder broke up and got back together. If you look back at old interviews, you’d hear Mydei regurgitate the same worn out anecdote about wanting to write a party song. ‘I wanted to hear more fun tunes on the radio’ or something along those lines.

No one ever believed it even when he was a moody teenager, much less the crotchety man that Mydei grew up to be. The truth’s not that sordid, but Mydei still hems and haws on his way to tell it. “It’s, uh, it’s a funny story.”

He glances over at Phainon, who’s as supportive and encouraging as ever. He might not be as understanding once Mydei spits it out, but hey, Mydei tried to warn him.

“It came to me one day,” Mydei starts. “In the most literal sense. A bug that flew in through the window and scared the daylights out of Phainon.”

“I don’t think I would have been that scared of a bug,” Phainon interjects.

“It was a wasp. A really, really big wasp,” Mydei clarifies, approximating its size with his hands. “When you saw it you let out this insane scream. The whole building probably heard it. It was a high C sharp, I think.”

“I see,” the host says with a snap of her fingers. “You were inspired to test Phainon’s voice.”

No, Mydei was inspired to test himself. The shriek Mydei heard that day was the stuff of dreams, a sound that the most accomplished of singers would spend their whole lives chasing. It’s the reason why he makes Phainon jump from crooning to belting on the same line. Sometimes, when Mydei thinks the song he’s writing isn’t going well, he likes to look back on that memory and remember the way everything clicked into place.

But Mydei’s not going to admit that out loud. What is he, crazy?

“Yes,” the songwriter answers.

Nothing conveys serious and assured more than a pair of crossed arms, but what Mydei had missed is an expression to match it. He doesn’t look as bold and audacious with his downcast eyes refusing to meet another’s gaze. Whatever it is occupying his mind clearly makes him flustered, and no amount of lip-biting could conceal the smile threatening to erupt.

Beside him, Phainon calmly takes stock of the room. A camera or two pans over to focus on Mydei while the host nods slowly in contemplation. Some members of the audience begin to whisper and giggle amongst themselves, reminding Phainon of the production runners that had been eyeing Mydei earlier.

It’s a breakthrough, the one that Phainon’s been waiting for all this time. Yet somehow, for whatever reason, Calypso’s warning rings in his ears once more.

It’s rare for Phainon to be one of the least sought out figures in any room, but here he is, blending in with the fine folk of Okhema’s Dawn Banquet.

That’s not to say that Phainon hasn’t captured anyone else’s attention this evening, especially after Aglaea spent the entire day getting him ready. It just so happens that everyone else is also dressed up to the nines, and unlike Phainon they don’t have to lease the spiffy designer clothes they’ve got on. These are the crème de la crème of Okhema’s upper crust, a crowd that can afford to look past Amphoreus’s beloved Deliverer in favor of gorging themselves on cold finger sandwiches.

Tonight, Phainon is carrying out his annual duty of being Grove’s talent representative. In other words he’s schmoozing for investors, which would have been a drag if Phainon wasn’t already familiar with the guest list. He knows who would be willing to hear him out without being a chore to converse with, and as impossible as that may sound, Phainon has been to enough of these banquets to find certain exchanges enjoyable. Phainon always imagined that he would have studied business or management or something similar had he pursued higher education, and listening to some VIP explain their financial ventures is sort of like a college lecture.

Unfortunately, they’re not interested in speaking about finances tonight. “A toast to your label and their recent undertaking!”

Their modest group of five raise their drinks in celebration, with Phainon’s neighbors going so far as to clink their glasses against his. They stand off to the side of the busy ballroom, closed off yet mobile enough to mingle elsewhere.

“Grove’s gambles never fail to pay off,” says a man with a navy pocket square. “I though Lycurgus had lost it when news of the reunion broke out.”

“It wasn’t Lygus’s idea,” Phainon states lightly.

“Whoever it was, they must have been a fan,” another man comments, tugging on his bowtie.

“Or eager to prove themselves,” a lady with a glittery shawl counters.

“Either way, he or she had a lot of faith in Sun and Thunder,” Bowtie says. “No one even knew if the other lad was still doing music!”

“He’s actually done a lot of producing in the past years,” Phainon points out.

“Yes, but who would know that?”

“Anyone who’s typed in his name on the internet,” says the man next to Phainon. He sips on a glass of deep red wine, unconcerned about the havoc it may wreck on his beige dinner jacket. “Being aware of the boy is just Grove’s due diligence.”

“Speaking of, why isn’t Mydeimos here with you?” Shiny Shawl asks Phainon. “I would have loved to meet him. He seems like such a charming boy!”

Phainon laughs. “He’s still too shy. He needs more time to get used to being known.”

“Aww, how adorable,” Shiny Shawl says. “But isn’t it rude of him to leave you here hard at work?”

“Not really? Chatting with you doesn’t feel like work to me,” Phainon says.

Everyone laughs politely. “Oh you,” the lady purrs.

“It’s better for Mydeimos to keep his distance,” Navy Pocketsquare remarks. “His family has plenty of enemies in this room alone.”

“So I’ve heard,” Bowtie says. “But it’s old news now, isn’t it? Hardly fair on the boy to hold up old grudges when there aren’t any profits to protect.”

“Eurypon was a plague,” says Beige Jacket, swirling his wine. “He should have been happy making his silly jingles, but he had to be greedy. Keep an eye out on Mydeimos, Phainon. Bad apples never fall far from the tree.”

“Haha, I’ll keep that in mind.”

“I always presumed he was more like Gorgo,” Shiny Shawl chimes in. “He looks like her and does music like her.”

“More reason for Phainon to watch out,” Beige Jacket warns. “If it wasn’t for her, Eurypon wouldn’t have been nearly as ambitious.”

Bowtie shakes his head. “Phainon’s safe. Mydeimos isn’t a woman.”

“It’s a shame. Gorgo was a gorgeous creature,” Navy Pocketsquare jokes. “Maybe if her son eases off the ‘roids, I wouldn’t mind looking the other wa-OW!”

“My deepest apologies,” a cheerless voice apologizes.

If looks could kill, Navy Pocketsquare would be charged with several counts of manslaughter. He grabs his leg as if to make sure it’s still connected to him, glaring down at the lavender-haired culprit that ran him over. All around him, his comrades laugh, with only Phainon to offer him a look of condolence.

“Please forgive her, Mister Liluder,” Phainon implores as he sets his half-empty glass on a server’s tray. “It was an honest accident.”

Navy Pocketsquare glances at the wheelchair and the young woman bound to it. “…I forgive her.”

“She didn’t even graze you,” Beige Jacket says.

That earns Navy Pocketsquare more ridicule and jeering. Phainon decides to make an exit before his colleague gets into real hot water.

“I’ll see her out,” Phainon promises before turning to the interloper. “Do you need help, miss?”

“Please,” she says, holding up her plate of canapés for Phainon to carry.

With one final apology, the two abscond from the group to head to a quiet corner alone. The wide berth people give them makes it easier, even if it

does feel demeaning. Phainon’s contrite face lasts up until they’re out of sight, where he is free to sigh out in relief.

“Thank you so much Polly,” Phainon whispers. “I’ll make sure they don’t complain later.”

“It’s alright. They wouldn’t dare,” Polyxia assures him. “You were cueing me pretty frantically, so I assume they deserved it.”

“No, they-” Phainon thinks back to the discussion and clenches his jaw. “… Maybe they deserve it a little. I owe you big time.”

Polyxia silently laughs. “You have already paid me back. I usually have no problem keeping things on my lap, but my dress makes it difficult tonight.”

The aforementioned dress is a sleek gown made with purple organza or something similarly slippery. Polyxia wears it well despite its simplicity. It’s one of the three formal outfits she owns, all gifted to her by Aglaea. Polyxia and her sister would have had more if Grove were willing to either lessen Aglaea’s workload or invest in proper marketing for the twins’ music. It’s the least they could do, considering how they’ve made the two sisters a mandatory presence in fundraisers and the like.

Phainon doesn’t recall seeing Polyxia’s sister around though. Polyxia must have lied to her again, as if Castorice wouldn’t be able to piece two and two together. For her sister’s peace of mind, Phainon decides to loiter with Polyxia a while longer, sharing bites of amuse-bouches while they observe the clandestine meetings taking place in the ballroom.

The Dawn Banquet is known for its ironic name, but as dark as it may be outside, the ballroom itself is kept bright and vivacious, with large crystal chandeliers spread out to maintain the appearance of daytime. The all-encompassing brightness makes it challenging to hide yourself away, but between large tables with ostentatious centerpieces and tall vases bursting with floral arrangements, there is bound to be a shadowed corner for someone to take advantage of. In a moneyed hall like this it means intrigue of the boring kind, like debating a company’s line of succession or sniffing

out stocks to short sell or ingratiating with their betters like Phainon’s supposed to be doing.

Rarely is it anything truly salacious, like two unlikely people necking in some overlooked cranny. When Polyxia first points to that exact sight, Phainon’s immediate reaction is to choke on a piece of lox.

“That’s… brave,” Phainon says once he’s evacuated his airway of cured salmon. “Who is it?”

“It must be the general’s son with one of our sponsors’ daughters. How Shakespearean of them,” Polyxia quips.

“As long as they’re keeping it above the belt, I guess it shouldn’t matter,” Phainon says, turning away. “I never really understood the appeal though.”

“Of kissing?”

“Of making out in public.”

“Oh.” Polyxia sweeps some stray crumbs off her skirt. “If Cas was here, she might be able to tell you.”

Phainon can’t help but chuckle. “I don’t know, I feel like having an audience is a turn-off for most people.”

“It’s not about who’s watching I think,” Polyxia says, squinting at the intimate couple. “Affection is at its purest when you live in the moment. It could be the most inopportune and unromantic circumstances, and all you can think of is how nice it would be to kiss them. That’s how you know it’s real.”

In the moments to follow, a pair of feuding mothers would storm into the scene to discipline their unruly children, making use of whatever physical and verbal means available to pry the two apart. It would be humiliating, infuriating, and a great deal of trouble for everyone within its immediate radius.

But for now, under the cover of lush hydrangeas, a lovestruck girl tenderly holds her sweetheart’s face in her hands. She tucks a stray strand of hair behind his reddened ear, beaming at what she sees.

“That’s how Cas would see it anyway,” Polyxia continues. “Her favorite rom-coms always turn kisses into a spectacle. Personally I feel it would be embarrassing, but I guess they do provide insight into the characters’ emotions. Films are about exaggeration anyway, right? Mister Phainon?”

Polyxia looks up at her unresponsive companion, who gingerly hands her back her empty plate before ambling off. It’s a concerning response, but Polyxia has no reason to believe that Phainon would do something irrational. He’s probably just checking in to see if he remembered to turn his stove off.

Phainon walks until he’s out of the ballroom, ignoring the people who call out to stop him for a chat. He pads through the long carpeted hallways and waits patiently on the lengthy elevator ride down. He nearly slams into a family of 4 once the doors slide open, making the concierge eye him with disdain as Phainon jogs pass his desk.

The pandemonium of late-night traffic welcomes Phainon outside, but the pop star doesn’t even pause to acknowledge it. He runs past the valet, past the restaurants and bars and the lines of people waiting to be let in. Phainon’s lungs and legs burn as he breaks into a full sprint. He refuses to stop until he… until he gets to… to what, exactly?

Phainon skids to a stop in front of a startled couple. The two hapless pedestrians warily walk around this strange man, who’s left bent over and panting after his mad dash to nowhere.

In his late night dreams, Phainon always imagined their first kiss to happen after some type of impassioned confession. The kind where there’s a choir and a pergola and a candlelight dinner that would soften Mydei’s answer. Sometimes he imagined it happening in the pouring rain, after a screaming match that wrests the truth out in the open. One of them would have enough and grab the other, and the ensuing kiss would almost be punishing if it wasn’t such a long time coming.

Phainon never envisioned it to be so tangible and it stunned him. He hesitated - so used to toeing the line that he fails to recognize when it’s been crossed - and now his window is gone. What’s the plan now? Continue clambering for Mydei’s favor when he knows Mydei isn’t the kind to look back? Phainon should know by now that Mydei doesn’t mind moving on, that he doesn’t care one bit about glancing back to see what he’d left behind.

Phainon’s throat seizes. At the end, Mydei still leaves. History repeats itself, as if there was any other ending for Phainon. As if the stupid, immature boy who can only piss him off and waste his time could ever be a real contender for Mydei’s heart.

…No.

No, that’s not true. Phainon’s feelings are not so shallow that they could be buried so easily. He was the first one to see beyond Mydei’s pretenses and the first one to appreciate him whole. Phainon learned how to make him laugh and how to make him cry, and in turn Mydei indulges him with the care Phainon never deserved. All of Mydei’s little concessions and thinly veiled generosities aren’t for nothing. There is a part of Mydei that felt the same, and if Phainon could only ignite it again…

Before Phainon could act on his renewed conviction, his phone rings. He picks it up and immediately regrets putting the phone so close to his ear.

“Where the fuck did you run off to, you damn mutt?! You’re a dead man when I find you, and I WILL find you. Stay where you are! And DON’T do something stupid, for the love of-“

Too late for that. Phainon mentally apologizes to Cipher as he looks around at all the people with their phone cameras out. He knows it’s dark out, but the flash photography a little egregious.

“…I don’t suppose I could convince you to keep this a secret?” He asks the crowd.

“Are you seriously asking me that? Oh man what the- are you OUTSIDE? I’m gonna get your ass so bad! What the hell are you doing you-!“

It’s not a stretch to say that Mydei doesn’t mind spending time with Phainon. Maybe he tolerates it greatly. One could say that Mydei looks forward to each new meeting like a child restlessly waiting for their birthday. Maybe.

Lately he’s been a frequent victim of this type of anticipation, with Phainon appearing at Mydei’s side every so often with some kind of peace offering. Like a box from a dessert cafe he did an ad for, or a fuzz pedal he thought would be fun to mess around with. On days where they’re not scheduled to see each other, Phainon would blow up Mydei’s phone with photos and videos of cute animals being cute, and he won’t stop until Mydei replies with an interesting fact about his day.

In short, Phainon has been nothing but pleasant company, which is a sign that something has gone wrong. Something like a catastrophic stage dive resulting in a cracked head and Phainon losing his sense of self.

“He’s trying to get close to you now that you’re popular and actually valuable,” Ptolemy hypothesizes without looking away from his computer.

Mydei frowns. He wasn’t a fan of Phainon getting injured in a freak accident, but even that’s more optimistic than what Ptolemy had proposed.

“You’re the one who said the music industry was a cutthroat environment,” Ptolemy says when he sees Mydei’s expression.

“It still wouldn’t make sense,” Mydei argues. “Phainon’s popularity dwarfs mine multiple times over.”

“Didn’t you say Phagousa Ent’s been trying to get you to sign a permanent contract?”

“To write more songs for them. Not to turn me into a public figure.”

Ptolemy lowers his reading glasses so Mydei can take in the full breadth of his skepticism. “You are a public figure,” he reminds Mydei.

“Yes but-“ Mydei waffles for an elegant rebuttal. “-I’m really bad at it.”

“Yeah okay, sure. It’s possible your popularity is a short-lived fluke.” Ptolemy returns his attention to the computer. “Acting like you’re close is still good publicity. Phainon’s people would definitely recommend it to him in the meantime.”

It’s still a lot of effort for a publicity stunt. Phainon only gets so many hours in a day, and he decides to spend it on Mydei?

“You could use it to your advantage too, you know?” Ptolemy advises. “You scratch his back, he scratches yours?”

Mydei scowls. “And what would I gain from that?”

“I don’t know, fans who’d follow you to your return to anonymity?” Ptolemy shrugs. “Point is, I’d prefer if you looked out for yourself too. The more you tell us about how this system works, the more we worry.”

Mydei knew that. It would be impossible not to. It would be naive of him to think that Phainon would remain unsullied in the entertainment business. That doesn’t mean it’s the only conclusion he can make. Even if Mydei owns up to his fanciful fantasies, there has to be some personal benefit for Phainon to seek him out so frequently, right?

The door cracks open. “Doctor Ptolemy…? I have a question about the Daneshnam- Oh!”

A young girl stands gasping at Ptolemy’s office door, nearly dropping her laptop and a stack of loose papers.

Without missing a beat, Ptolemy turns to Mydei and says, “It was nice talking to you, young man. Good luck, and remember to do the reading for Wednesday’s class debate.”

“Thank you. Doctor,” Mydei stiffly says as he gets up and flips his hood on.

“Wait! Please!” The girl begs, blocking Mydei’s path. “Could I, uh- Are you…?”

“Stop delaying this completely normal student, Erin.”

“Just one moment!” The girl pleads. She tries to search her bag, but she’s carrying far too much for it to be a smooth motion. In the end, she gives up and thrusts a random piece of paper into Mydei’s hands. “Please! Signature!”

Mydei looks down at the essay that’s been handed to him. Ptolemy groans.

“Come here,” Ptolemy says, beckoning Mydei over. “I’ve got a pen and paper you could use.”

After monopolizing a solid chunk of Ptolemy’s office hours, Mydei sneaks out of his university feeling  moderately enlightened. Simply looking at the students’ reaction to him proves Ptolemy’s theory to be plausible. There’s a chance that Phainon could be using Mydei, but is that really as bad as it sounds? A part of the reason why Mydei agreed to reuniting was to uplift Phainon’s image, and he knew from the beginning that it would require a lot of staging and playacting to pull it off. Considering that Mydei gave Phainon sole access to Sun and Thunder’s legacy, he’s obviously fine with being Phainon’s stepping stone. He signed multiple contract stating so for Kephale’s sake.

So why does Mydei still feel upset? Perhaps he’s mad that he was never clued in, but a person who’s been so thoroughly rejected shouldn’t have expectations.

If there was a pebble to kick, Mydei would have launched it into the stratosphere by now. Unfortunately, Ptolemy’s place of work is a decently prestigious university, which means it has the funding to sweep the sidewalks clean of debris. Its reputation also means that fancy cars with heavily tinted windows are a common sight around the area, though it’s not common for one to stalk commuters on the street. Mydei is at a loss with the Lexus deliberately matching his walking speed, and he’d been debating

on confronting the driver when one of the back windows suddenly rolls down.

“Hey, Mydei! Need a ride?”

Ah, the devil. He comes a-clip-clopping.

“No,” Mydei answers tersely.

Usually Phainon would take any opportunity he gets to drag Mydei into a meaningless argument, but recently he’s been really into empathy and compassion. He only hits Mydei with the barest hint of his sad puppy dog eyes before asking, “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. I don’t need a ride when I have my bike,” Mydei says. Feeling a little bad for being short with him, he tries again. “…They let you out on your own today?”

“Nope!” Cipher’s voice calls out from the driver’s seat. “Still under probation!”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Then why is this one here?”

“Oh, Anaxa’s an advisory board member for the media production program,” Phainon explains. “He booked me in as a guest speaker.”

“I was just in there. Why didn’t I hear about it?”

“Cause it’s not today!” Cipher says. “He had to go meet with the eggheads running the place first.”

“Exactly,” Phainon concurs with a nod. “What about you? Are you visiting the library or something?”

“It’s where I’m parked,” Mydei says, speeding up to get to his motorcycle. “It was nice to see you, Phainon. You too, Ci-“

A drop of water falls onto Mydei’s head. Then, a shower.

Despite being safe in his cozy SUV, Phainon looks troubled by this turn of events. “You should catch a ride with us,” he says. “You might catch a cold.”

Mydei scoffs. “A light drizzle can’t enfeeble m-“

Thunder cuts him off once more. The gentle summer rain quickly turns into the first stirrings of a storm, and Phainon’s distressed expression deepens into proper dejection. He gazes up at Mydei, eyes round and glassy with pity.

Mydei firmly shuts the car door behind him as he joins Phainon in the backseat. He’s dripping water all over the expensive leather upholstery, but he hardly notices when he spots the tragic sight outside.

“Kokopo…”

“Huh? You say something?” Phainon asks.

“No,” Mydei quickly replies.

It’s okay. He left Kokopo under a sturdy awning, and Ptolemy is around to take care of it if anything were to happen. He is not deserting his bike, Mydei tells himself. Leaving Kokopo behind is far better than risking battery corrosion or damage to the carburetor.

“Look at that downpour,” Phainon says. “You could have gotten hurt on the road if we weren’t around!”

There’s that too, though Mydei is still pretty sure he could handle a bit of water.

…Perhaps not this bit of water, which is shaping up to be one of this year’s heavier rainfalls. It’s hard to believe the sun was out only minutes ago. The sky is so thoroughly clogged that it appears as if evening had struck early.

“Turn on the heater, would you Cipher? Thank you so much,” Phainon requests before turning to Mydei. “We’ll try to get you home as fast as

possible, but I’m guessing the traffic report’s not looking too good right now.”

There was something in the air that night. The stars were bright, the city even brighter. Phainon and Mydei burned brightest of all, full of want and

none of the inhibition. Kisses turn out to be better with two active participants, and Phainon and Mydei’s competitiveness translates a little too well to this kind of give and take.
