“Souvenirs,” Leonnius replies, his arm buried deep into one of the bags. “Mostly candy and fridge magnets. I also got some chew toys for my girl Figgy, even though she forgot say ‘hi’ to me. Is she mad at me for being gone for so long?”

“Uh-“ Mydei glances at the dog slumped against his bedroom door. “- Something like that.”

“I got her like a squirrel that squeaks and this crunchy milk box thing,” Leonnius says. “If only I could find them-“

From the corner of his eye, Mydei spots a pair of blindingly neon boxer briefs peeking out from under his television stand. Mydei tactically shifts to block it out of Leonnius’s line of sight.

“Are you staying for long?” Mydei asks. “Should I get you something to eat?”

“I’ll pass,” Leonnius says, giving up on his search with a sigh. “I gotta head back to the garage soon, but I didn’t want the candy to melt in my locker while I’m at work.”

“Hm.” Mydei tries not to look too relieved. “Good luck.”

“… You got any of those lemon cookies for the road though?”

“Ah.” Mydei baked up a batch yesterday for Phainon, imparting his home with an damning scent. “…Yes, you can take some.”

Leonnius stares expectantly at Mydei, who stays rooted in his spot. It takes a second for Leonnius to figure out he’s not planning on moving.

“Okay,” Leonnius says. “I’ll just… get them myself I guess?”

“The cookies are in the blue jar and you can find tupperware in the usual spot,” Mydei says as Leonnius heads into the kitchen. “Don’t finish them off!”

“I won’t! Sheesh…”

While Leonnius raids his kitchen, Mydei rushes to grab the offending article of clothing and anything else that might bust their dirty little secret. Thinking fast, he opens the bedroom door and inadvertently causes the man plastered against it to stumble with a silent yelp. Any other day and Mydei would have laughed at Phainon’s wide-eyed bewilderment, but the sound of Leonnius banging around in his kitchen might as well be the ticking of a bomb. Mydei barely manages to chuck the evidence into Phainon’s arms as Leonnius returns with his loot.

“I only got a couple, okay?” Leonnius says, shaking his box of cookies. “And maybe a little extra for the road, but the candy should make us square.”

“Only if the candy tastes as good as my cookies,” Mydei says. He’s left leaning oddly against his doorjamb, which Leonnius doesn’t seem to notice.

“I don’t think you realize how difficult it is to browse an entire aisle written in a language you don’t speak,” Leonnius says, apparently more occupied with defending his honor. “I could have just given you straight up pinecones but no, I took the time to personally handpick everything I bought for you guys.”

“I’m guessing that’s why you took a long time to come back.”

Leonnius groans. “Don’t get me started. One thing led to another and I ended up owing money to some other guy and- It’s a whole thing, okay? Open the chat sometime and I’ll tell you all about it.”

“Of course.”

“And in return you tell me what’s up with you,” Leonnius says as he finally gets ready to leave. “I can’t believe I have to follow PopZine just to find out… huh?”

The way Leonnius trails off has Mydei’s heart plunging into his stomach. “What?” He asks as calmly as possible. “See something?”

On Mydei’s shoe rack, chucked haphazardly between his combat boots and his beat-up trainers, is a pair of colorful chunky sneakers. Mydei’s forehead starts beading with sweat.

Leonnius picks one up and gives it a close inspection from multiple angles. Murkily yellow with electric blue trim, the sneakers clash with the entirety of Mydei’s wardrobe. The only person with the confidence to wear such a thing is the pop star hiding out in Mydei’s bedroom, the one that Leonnius has seen live in concert at least twice.

After the longest minute of Mydei’s life, Leonnius opens his mouth to ask: “Are these the new J’s?”

“Yes,” Mydei answers all too quickly.

Leonnius lets out a low whistle. “Where’d you get them?”

“It was-“ Behind a dumpster. At a clearance sale. At a crafts fair. “-a gift from-“ A fan. Krateros. Myself. “-the record label. On account of the good job I did.”

“They’re clean as hell, man,” Leonnius says, examining its sole. “Mind if I try them on?”

“Uh-“

“Please?”

After this, Mydei swears to physically remove Leonnius from the building himself. “Knock yourself out.”

Leonnius pops his shoes off the instant Mydei agrees. Mydei could only hope that Phainon doesn’t mind, though he supposes this is an apt punishment for swiping something from Mydei’s closet every time he visits.

“Damn, I thought we were the same size,” Leonnius says as the sneakers slip on effortlessly.

“This was the only pair available.”

“That sucks. Still fire though.”

Leonnius paces about, testing the fit and snapping pictures. He drains all of Mydei’s patience to pose with shoes that look like overboiled eggs.

Eventually Mydei forgets about the importance of staying on Leonnius’s good side. “I’m calling your boss if you don’t take those off in the next ten seconds.”

“Chill, this is the last one,” Leonnius promises, taking another quick photo before pulling the sneakers off. “I’m out of here, but remember what I said!”

That he owes money to a stranger…? Oh, the other thing. “Hey, I open the chat everyday-”

Leonnius peaces out before Mydei can attest to his online presence. The apartment goes still for a solid second after the door closes, easing only when Leonnius’s footsteps could no longer be heard.

The bedroom cracks open once the dust has settled. Phainon pokes his head out and peers around the apartment. “Is he gone?”

“Take a guess,” Mydei says, sinking into his couch.

Phainon joins Mydei on the sofa, still mostly in the buff. Mydei much prefers Phainon sans underwear for obvious reasons, but Mydei can tough it out if it saves him from contracting a cold or a UTI. Hyacine won’t be too happy if Phainon came back with a viral infection, he thinks.

Thankfully Mydei still has his pants on. He takes his phone out of his pocket and starts browsing on the web.

“Are you that bothered about what he said about your group chat?” Phainon asks.

“No,” Mydei mutters, scrolling furiously. “I’m looking for a new door-lock.”

Phainon chuckles. “A little too late, methinks. You might as well put it off a bit longer.”

“And why should I do that?”

Phainon answers by plopping his chin in the crook of Mydei’s elbow, peering up at him with a perfect facsimile of Figgy’s downtrodden expression. Like Figgy, Phainon is instantly placated by a few scratches to the underside of his jaw. He falls limp in Mydei’s masterful hands, replacing the phone that Mydei once deemed more important.

Before Phainon could get too comfortable, Mydei grabs hold of his face and pulls him close. “Needy. Demanding. Insatiable.”

Phainon eagerly nods with each growl. When Mydei falls back onto the couch, Phainon follows, slinking over his supine body like a predator staking its claim. As beastly as ever, even after such a close call. As if Mydei ever wanted him tamed.

“Sorry man, but I think I forg- AGH!”

Leonnius’s shriek forces the two intertwined men to scramble off each other in panic. Phainon falls on the floor ass first while Mydei nearly pops his hip pivoting upright. There’s enough common sense in Leonnius to have him turn around for the sake of decency, but not enough to have him scurrying out the apartment.

“Either that’s who I think it is or that’s a really, really old man,” Leonnius rambles, covering his eyes. “Whatever it is, you gotta hit me in the back of the head, De. I can’t be walking around with this knowledge!”

“So why would you come back?!” Mydei yells. He loves and cares for his friend deeply, but there’s a limit to how many times a man can get blue-balled in the span of 30 minutes.

“I needed my keys!” Leonnius says. “I think I left them here!”

“Then knock?!”

“Your door’s always open, man!” Leonnius exclaims. “It’s not like I was thinking you’d be getting it on right there! Sue me for not thinking that was a possibility!”

Mydei massages his temples. In the end, it comes down to his own negligence.“…You can have the rest of the cookies. Just don’t tell anyone else about this. Please.”

“You don’t need to pay me off, you know,” Leonnius grumbles.

“I mean it Leonnius,” Mydei stresses. “Not even to Hephaestion and the others.”

“You didn’t tell them? Holy shit- Am I the only one who knows?”

“I’ll get the cookies,” Phainon volunteers, getting up. He’s taken one of the blankets off the couch and wrapped himself up a nice new chiton. “Mom always said you can’t ask for favors that you can’t pay upfront.”

With a reassuring pat, Phainon leaves Mydei to stew in a hell of his own making. Mydei can blame a lot of this on Phainon, but he can’t really blame him for escaping. There’s not much he can contribute to whilst in his birthday suit, though that’s not saying that Mydei is in a better spot.

Still, Mydei has to say something. “It’s not what it looks like.”

“You said that last time,” Leonnius points out.

Mydei groans. “It’s complicated.”

“Tell me if you’re being blackmailed,” Leonnius says in Kremnoan.

“I’m not,” Mydei replies accordingly.

“Are you blackmailing him?”

“Fuck no.”

“Are the record execs blackmailing you?”

“No one is blackmailing anyone,” Mydei says. “And don’t stick to Kremnoan the entire time. He’ll get paranoid.”

“So let him?”

“Don’t try to convince me that you’re anti-Deliverer again.”

“I’m trying here, man!” Leonnius cries. “Hephaestion should’ve been the one to walk in on you! He’ll know if this is a bad idea or not!”

Mydei looks down at the ground and digs his toes into his rug. “…What do you think?”

“I think that maybe you shouldn’t be doing this,” Leonnius admits. “Do I think people who date super-popular high-profile celebrities usually have happy endings? Not really. Do I think it’d be cool to get an RSVP to the Deliverer’s wedding? Hell yeah.”

“We’re not dating and we’re not getting married,” Mydei clarifies. “This is a temporary situation.”

“You keep saying that, but look who’s sucking face with who whil-“

“Leonnius.”

“Look, it sounds like you’ve made up your mind,” Leonnius concedes, switching back to common Amphorean. He turns around to give Mydei a once-over. “I thought that maybe the glow was just movie magic, but seeing you now, I stand corrected.”

Much to his chagrin, Mydei feels his face heating up and proving Leonnius right. “Up yours.”

“Aw loosen up, De. It’s not like I get the chance do this often.”

“Why not?” Phainon suddenly chimes in, plundered goods in hand. Keep this up, and they’ll relieve Mydei of all his precious storage containers. “I thought Mydei would be popular considering that body of his.”

Mydei has to will himself not to react, lest he encourage Phainon.

Leonnius side-eyes his friend’s paramour as the cookies switches hands. “I’ll kill you if you break Mydei’s heart.”

The pop star nods back in understanding. “I’ll kill myself first though.”

“I could kill you on my own,” Mydei states before turning back on their intruder. “Is there anything else, Leonnius? Or are you planning on barging in again?”

“It’s not like I wanted to see that,” Leonnius huffs. “My keys. Did you guys see them?”

Phainon and Mydei haven’t, having been obviously distracted. Perhaps sensing the answer and not wishing to hear of it, Leonnius carries out the task himself and finds his keys in one of his paper bags. Needless to say, Mydei wasn’t amused.

Mydei remains unamused even after Leonnius leaves for good. The mood is beyond salvaging, regardless of how shameless Phainon is willing to be. The best he could do is stick by Mydei’s side as he recovers from his mental anguish. The resulting sigh Mydei lets out sounds anything but auspicious, but Phainon could work with it.

“We should meet up less,” Mydei concludes.

“Why?”

Mydei frowns. “Are you seriously asking?”

“Yeah,” Phainon says, adjusting his make-shift mantle. “I mean that wasn’t great, but it’s not like we weren’t being careful.”

“I don’t think any of this is being careful,” Mydei deadpans.

“That was an outlier,” Phainon says as he throws an arm around Mydei. “Like what your friend implied, it’s impossible to predict every single outcome of every action. Forty thousand people die every year from car crashes. That doesn’t mean we should live our lives hiding at home forever.”

Mydei stares at him, pensive. “…You’re not upset.”

Phainon grins and gives Mydei’s cheek a light pinch. “Aww. Is that why my schnookums is sulking?”

Mydei smacks Phainon’s hand off. Not his schnookums apparently, but his objection had been suspiciously swift. “Be more serious. You stand to lose more than me.”

“Would I lose anything as valuable as you?”

“Drop it for one second and listen,” Mydei warns, stepping away from Phainon. “If what we’re doing here gets out there, you’ll be ruined. You won’t be the Deliverer of Amphoreus anymore. You’ll be the guy who has gay sex with his colleagues. Excuse me if I think we should do what we can to keep that from happening.”

Phainon nods his head. “You trust Leonnius, right?”

The question takes Mydei aback. “It’s not about trust-“

“Do you trust him or not?”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “Yes, I trust Leonnius.”

“And I trust you, therefore I’m not worried,” Phainon concludes. He interrupts Mydei by pressing a finger to his lips. “Getting caught sucks, I know. I was there. But now that we’ve experienced how it could happen, we know exactly how we could be more careful next time.”

Surprisingly, that does not convince Mydei.

“Troubleshooting,” Phainon calls it, complete with jazz hands.

“And what brilliant innovation have you concocted for your illicit hook-ups?”

“Kephale, you make yourself sound like my mistress,” Phainon comments. He ducks out of Mydei’s punching range in the nick of time. “Don’t hit me! I think it’s hot! I’m just saying that you don’t have to be the other woman. We can just go to my house, simple as that.”

That gets Mydei to drop his hackles. “Your house?”

“Highly secure, highly classified, and highly recommended,” Phainon boasts. “It’s got at least three locks.”

“You want me to go to your house?”

“Yes. Is this thing broken?” Phainon asks as he taps the shell of Mydei’s ear. “I want you to come home with me sometime. Is that too much to ask?”

“No, you surprised me. I thought-“ Mydei shakes his head. “…Whatever. I accept. Next time, you’re hosting.”

Phainon lights up like a firework. “You better get ready then,” Phainon says. “Because you’re about to learn what real hospitality looks like.”

Mydei scoffs. “Sorry my apartment doesn’t have enough scented candles for you.”

“And yet I keep on visiting. Curious.” Phainon claps a hand on Mydei’s shoulder. “Maybe you’ll get extra points if you turn the TV on while I get dressed. We stopped at a cliffhanger last time, remember? We gotta find out what happened after Detective Hanu got shot.”

“I’m sure the main character can survive a bullet from a one-off episode.”

“It’s about the how, not the if!”

Since Mydei doesn’t seem to be getting undressed any time soon, Phainon finds there’s no use in staying chilly all day. Before he could reach the bedroom, however, Mydei asks him one last question. “Are you sure you’re alright?”

Phainon turns back to look at him. A life mapped out in newspapers and magazines could only be so private. Mydei’s carelessness would only blur the lines Phainon had drawn, leaving his world louder and narrower than it already is.

So Mydei had no way of expecting Phainon’s jubilant smile.

“Yeah,” Phainon answers truthfully. Mydei may not have family in the traditional sense, but that doesn’t mean Phainon wouldn’t be happy to meet them all the same. “I’m feeling awesome.”

On Tuesday, Phainon and Mydei model for a photoshoot.

On Tuesday evening, Sun and Thunder plays at The Imperator’s Centre of the Arts, complete with encore.

On Wednesday, Phainon films an endorsement for a soda company. Mydei takes Figgy for a walk.

On Friday, Sun and Thunder plays on the Chrysalis Festival’s main stage. That same evening, Phainon brings Mydei back to his humble abode.

“This is the place where you hide your affairs, isn’t it?” Mydei says.

Phainon looks aghast at the accusation. “This is my actual house. I’m not the pervert you think I am.”

Actually, Mydei has a pretty good idea of how much of a pervert Phainon can be, though perhaps not in the way they’d been discussing.

“My house looks normal, right?” Phainon continues pestering Mydei. “It’s not gonna be on Better Homes and Gardens, but it’s not a Leisure Suit Larry den of iniquity or anything like that.”

It was not. In fact, Phainon’s alleged home is quite welcoming and domestic for a bachelor pad. The rattan furniture and their linen accoutrements harken back to Phainon’s clean image, both strangely old-fashioned in spite of their contemporary minimalism. The wooden veneers warm up what would have otherwise been a dreadfully pale living room, conveniently matching with the ceiling fans that spoke a little too much of the building’s age. If it weren’t for the few Phainon-esque baubles displayed throughout the house, it could have been mistaken for a timeshare on some Styxian island.

Somehow, the place manages to both meet and subvert Mydei’s expectations. Perhaps it’s the fact that Phainon’s house isn’t some secluded mini-mansion or a glittering penthouse in the sky. It’s not even a townhouse in a gated community. Apart from a slightly glitzier location, Phainon’s apartment couldn’t be that much different from Mydei’s or that of his other

friends. Mydei’s apartment is probably bigger, considering Phainon only has one bedroom to speak of.

“This can’t be your only house,” Mydei says as he examines a frame on the wall.

Phainon laughs. “Nope. Just the one. Why? Were you hoping I was some kind of land mogul?”

“No. I just thought a hoarder would prefer to have more space,” Mydei says, picking up a weird yellow geode sitting on Phainon’s shelf.

“For the last time, they’re investments,” Phainon argues. He slides in to take the rock back from Mydei. “These are all rare pieces that’ll grow in value as time passes, watch.”

“Funny, I thought I saw a ‘Made in Jarilo’ label on that.”

“I mean as long as I’ve touched it, it pretty much becomes a collectible.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “I must be worth millions by now.”

“You’re priceless,” Phainon says, adding to Mydei’s value with another passing kiss. “Experts would tell me to get you insured as soon as possible.”

This insurance would soon come in the form of vivid red marks following the line of Mydei’s hip bone, making it appear as if his tattoo had begun snaking upward. He would gain a few more around the swell of his chest, on the meat of his thigh, and on an awfully ticklish spot on his back - all of which Mydei pays back with equal vehemence.

“I win,” Phainon declares as the two of them lie breathless on his bed. “I got more bites than you.”

Mydei responds by rolling over and attacking his wrist twice. Phainon laughs at this awful display of sportsmanship.

“I meant I have more bites on my body than you do,” Phainon clarifies. “But thank you for sealing the win for me.”

It’s not like Mydei ever counted them in the first place. They could only ever last so long before Phainon has to make use of miscellaneous balms and icy spoons to erase all trace of him in the morning. Tallying them up is an insanity reserved for Phainon.

Mydei might have double checked it anyway, had he not been so exhausted by the day’s events. The next thing he knows, he’s getting jolted from his sleep by his bladder, which forces Mydei to fumble about in the morning in search of a bathroom. Mydei is wide awake by the time he finishes what he has to, leaving him to realize exactly how early he’d risen.

The curtains flutter gently as Mydei approaches the balcony. Even before he’d pushed the drapery aside, the blue of the outside world had already seeped through the open weave of the linen, dyeing Phainon’s once lively home. The flat, dim lighting makes everything appear as if they were suspended in time, much like the hazy skyline and empty streets that await beyond the window.

Waking up earlier than Phainon isn’t anything new for Mydei, though waking up in Phainon’s apartment is certainly a first. Usually Mydei would already be where he needs to be, resulting in the two of them always meeting in the morning. Sometimes with breakfast, sometimes not. Perhaps that’s where they’re going wrong. Right now, Mydei could slip out of the apartment without alerting Phainon, and it wouldn’t be strange or discourteous. It would be exactly how arrangements like theirs were meant to operate. Perhaps if they left things in the evening instead of carrying it onto the next day, this charade would finally lose its luster and allow common sense to reign once again.

A pair of strong arms suddenly wrap around Mydei’s waist and pulls him out of his doldrums. “Why’re you up?” Phainon sleepily slurs in his ear. “I thought you didn’t ‘ave work right now?”

“Toilet,” Mydei answers.

Phainon nuzzles Mydei’s neck. “Hm.”

They linger there for a moment, staring out the window and swaying gently to an absent beat. Out on the balcony, Mydei spots the plant that Phainon had bought weeks ago, now touting a fresh set of blooming buds. Despite the sweltering weather, the flowers had retained their vibrancy, being the only things colorful enough to stand against the monotonous blue backdrop.

“Come back to bed,” Phainon mumbles. Mydei’s entire back shivers from the light kiss Phainon leaves on his nape. “It’s warmer with you there.”

“… You big baby,” Mydei says, sighing.

Yet he relents, helpless against such an eloquent argument. The snapdragons persist in Mydei’s peripheral vision, even as Phainon successfully drags him back to the confines of his silk duvet.

“You’ve been in a good mood lately, Mister Phainon.”

With a practiced hand, Phainon puts his phone aside before Hyacine could connect the dots. “What makes you say that?”

“For starters, you pointed out that Mister Anaxa’s bolo tie was crooked the other day,” Hyacine says as she sits down by the conference table. “And this morning, you asked me if you could have the last bran muffin!”

Phainon tilts his head, wondering if he’s hearing her right. “Sorry, I don’t think I quite understand…?”

“What she’s really saying is that you’ve finally graduated from being a human doormat,” Cipher says. She practically sprung out of thin air, occupying a seat that Phainon swears was empty. “Congratulations on becoming a vertebrate like the rest of us.”

Hyacine shakes her head at Cipher, who’s too busy with the phone to notice her disapproval. “That’s not what I was trying to say. I think it’s great that Mister Phainon is respectful towards everyone, but sometimes he can get stuck on work mode for way too long.”

“You want him unemployed? Not very nice of you, Cinny- Oops!”

Phainon takes the phone away from Cipher. Just as he thought, she’d pinched his phone when he wasn’t looking. The closest he gets to an apology is a shrug.

“Didn’t see anything interesting in there,” Cipher swears. “I only saw some Z-Bay listings for some dusty ass vinyls. Which is, yawn, borrring.”

“What else are you expecting?” Phainon asks.

“I don’t know, something that dudes your age would normally look at?” Cipher nudges Hyacine with an elbow. “Like maybe a fucked up dating app or a freaky sext or two.”

To her credit, Hyacine holds her head high, and doesn’t gasp and clutch her pearls like her furious blush warrants. “Mister Phainon’s not like that.”

Cipher grins. “You’re right there, cupcake. I was just curious about why Wonder Boy over here has been smiling and giggling at his phone these past few days.”

Oh fuck, he was? Judging from how Hyacine’s look goes from indignant to inquisitive, Phainon has not been playing it as cool as he thought.

Hyacine, bless her heart, still attempts to defend his good name. “Maybe he’s excited to see some rare vinyl records. He makes music, you know?”

Cipher shakes her head. “Tell me the truth, Hyacine.” She drops her pitch low and leans in, almost intimidating in her sudden seriousness. “You think he’s a virgin, don’t you?”

You could pinpoint the second the question sinks in for Hyacine. An almost audible crack seemed to ring out in the room, as if Cipher had taken a chisel and a hammer to a Fabergé egg. Phainon could only stare at his temporary bodyguard in stupefied horror.

The moment passes when Hyacine gets up, brushes some lint off her peplum shirt, and smiles at Cipher. “I should see what’s taking Mister

Anaxagoras so long,” she says.

Hyacine’s gait is steady for someone who appears to have her whole world rocked. Phainon glares at the perpetrator as Hyacine exits the room.

“What?” Cipher asks. “Was I wrong?”

“I’d say corrupting the youth is pretty wrong, yeah,” Phainon says.

Cipher cackles. “Please. Cinnybuns has a bunch of nerdiac degrees over the both of us combined. She knows what s-e-x is. She just probably couldn’t believe that you get any tail, so you should actually thank yours truly.”

Phainon thinks back to Hyacine’s terror-stricken face. “No, I don’t think I will.”

“I think you would,” Cipher shoots back, turning her chair around so she can prop her head on the backrest. “I basically got the red carpet out for you and loverboy. Assuming you’ll get Blondie to bite anytime this century, that is.”

Cipher pantomimes the gnashing of teeth to complete her metaphor. Sometimes, Phainon wonders if he had to make his impossible love-life more convoluted by throwing Cipher into the mix, but it’s impossible to deny her resourcefulness and quick-thinking. Or so he tells himself.

“I’m taking it one step at a time,” is what Phainon ends up saying.

“Widen your stride then,” Cipher advises, shedding her carefree tone. “Because someone up top’s thinking about putting the kibosh on your little side venture.”

“Aglaea said they’re looking to extend the contract.”

“You know Agy’s a soft touch when it comes to you,” Cipher says. “She’s not going to tell you that the board room’s split in two, especially if it’s around seventy-thirty in your favor. Doesn’t change the fact that your little lion’s had a hell of a family dynasty. Ever wonder why you haven’t heard much from the big time investors lately?”

Phainon frowns. “Grove’s heads are always talking about moving on to the next phase and becoming a self-sustaining business. What happened to that?”

“Same thing that happens to every good intention.” Cipher rubs her thumb and index finger together in the universal sign for- “Money.”

Suddenly, Cipher straightens from her lackadaisical slouch, signaling that she’s heard the same sound Phainon did. The hollow thud of a square heel thunders through the hallways of Grove Records’ headquarters, stopping at the conference room Phainon and Cipher are squirreled away in. The door dramatically slides open to reveal a woman with a posture as rigid as her stiff brow. A scowl lurked in the shadows of her face like a shaky photograph, making her smile appear derogatory no matter how much teeth she puts into it.

“Good afternoon, Phainon.”

“Good afternoon, Miss Caenis,” Phainon replies.

If Cipher was less concerned about her job, she would have argued that the only ‘Miss’ that Caenis counted as is misanthropic. Alas, there is no use in picking a fight so early, not even as she walks pass Cipher without a single word of greeting.

“You must be looking forward to this meeting,” Caenis says to Phainon. She lobs her laptop onto the conference table, gently rolling her wrist after dropping a thousand-dollar machine.

“I always am,” Phainon says.

“Hm. Some people should learn from you,” Caenis remarks as she sits herself near the head of the table. “But of course, this is only a perfunctory briefing. There’s no use in getting a headstart with your… think tank.”

“Just killing two birds with one stone,” Cipher chirps. She stands up as Caenis sits down, like two pistons in an engine keeping things trotting

along. “Your golden boy here was looking for some advice while waiting, so I stopped by to give him some.”

“How kind. I’m sure you had something enlightening to say.”

“Don’t you know it.” Cipher rounds up to Phainon and pats him on the shoulder. “Remember to floss your teeth and wash your hands. Oh, and make your bid on the last day of online auctions. Keeps the final prices low. Toodles!”

Cipher makes a quick getaway before Phainon could say anything, let alone beg her to stay. Somehow, with only two people left, the room has only gotten stuffier.

“I didn’t believe it when they said you’ve been a diligent worker lately,” Caenis says to Phainon. “Apparently you’ve been enjoying yourself with your new project.”

“I have. The fans would notice if I wasn’t sincere,” Phainon reasons.

Caenis chuckles as she organizes her files. “There’s no need to pretend when it’s just the two of us. We’ll get you more profitable projects after the summer.”

Despite her high position in Grove’s hierarchy, Caenis and ‘listening’ have never gone hand-in-hand. It’s a wonder how Phainon has never heard of her getting kicked out of a boardroom for insubordination.

“…Are you feeling thirsty, Ma’am?” Phainon asks. “I could get you a coffee if you want?”

“Coffee’s too acidic for me,” Caenis says without a single glance at him. “Get me some earl gray with a single teaspoon of sugar. Not one packet of sugar. Not one sugar cube. A teaspoon.”

“Right away, Ma’am.”

“And don’t use the garbage they stock in the pantries. Make sure to get it from the cafe on the fourth floor.”

Phainon hopes his spirited nodding hides his eagerness to scramble out of the room. He slows down once he’s out of sight, fully intending on taking his sweet time to complete his errand. It’s pathetic of him to flee, but his discussion with Cipher had left him short of patience towards Grove’s decision-makers. The reunion was their idea in the first place, and now they’re retracting their decision? After Mydei has proven himself to be nothing but beneficial?

The countless appearances, interviews, and shows have been received with high praise and higher sales. Years old material previously gathering dust in Grove’s copyright graveyard are now generating revenue once more. Demographics that Phainon could not charm on his own are now buying merchandise in droves. Hell, some of Mydei’s own songs had even reappeared in the charts despite him not singing or performing in any of them.

It’s torture for Phainon, who has to be there for every meet-and-greet, who has to watch people sidle up close to Mydei to touch and grope him as they please. He has to watch interviewers harass Mydei with innuendos and unsubtle flirtations so they may profit off of his flustered reactions. Photoshoots and film shoots dress and pose Mydei in all the vulgar ways that Phainon’s virtuous reputation safeguards him from, often bordering on pornographic. It’s madness.

And when asked about his thoughts, Mydei only replies with: “It’s alright.”

Next to him, Phainon grits his teeth under his tight-lipped smile. The host of the variety show proceeds to laugh at essentially nothing.

“With muscles like those, who wouldn’t be showing off?” She says to the camera.

The show has Phainon and Mydei competing on who can split the most firewood. An insultingly simple competition, seeing how the producers have chosen logs with prominent cracks in its centers. Phainon breezes by with ease, whereas Mydei, who comes down on the wood with too much height, struggles to keep up.

No one corrects Mydei’s awful technique because the way he heaves his maul high and puffs his buxom chest out is entertainment. Halfway through, the host trips on a wedge and is caught in time by Mydei, who drops his maul precariously close to his foot to get to her in time. Phainon happens to know that the host is a happily married woman, but her job still requires her to ham it up, exaggeratedly fawning in Mydei’s arms as if he’d crossed mountains and seas to save her from an excruciating boo-boo. She gives his bicep a honk in farewell, because of course she does.

It takes the joy out of Phainon’s victory, whittling his smile back down to another brittle imitation.

Mydei had woken up after the program’s taping feeling like roadkill. He expected as much with the amount of manual labor he’d done during the day, but Phainon’s peculiar exuberance had been a complete surprise that evening. To apologize, Phainon volunteers himself for breakfast duty, and Mydei refrains from reminding him of his participation in his own exhaustion.

While Phainon struggles to put together something edible, Mydei peruses his shelves for something interesting. Perhaps even incriminating. He finds the perfect item bound in maroon buckram and frizzy twine, and as he leafs through the hefty volume silently musing the nth picture of a doting family, a delectable smell starts to take over Phainon’s apartment. Phainon reappears in time for Mydei’s grumbling stomach, his proud swagger immediately faltering at the sight of the tome in Mydei’s lap.

Phainon scrambles to grab the photo album, but Mydei holds it away from his reach. “I already saw the pictures of your second grade play,” Mydei informs him.

Phainon groans. “At least tell me you thought I was cute.”

The second grade play had, for some reason, dressed all the schoolchildren as miscellaneous animals. Whoever painted Phainon’s face for his oryx costume had turned him into a Rorschach test instead, and the boy had been

so immersed in his role that he was photographed munching on a weed. It was adorable. “Cyrene was cuter.”

“Oh. Yeah, I get it.” Phainon nods. “She went as a lagomorph, by the way. In case you got her confused with a bunny like everyone else.”

“I don’t know what that is.”

“They’re not pink and fluffy in real life. That’s Cyrene’s twist on it. I went for realism, so my costume wasn’t as small and cuddly.”

“Mm hm.”

“I actually did a lot of research for it, you know,” Phainon boasts. “I helped carve the horns so they had realistic rings. I didn’t paint them, you can check.”

Mydei pats Phainon’s cheek. “That’s nice, deer boy.”

For a moment, Phainon stands there gawking at Mydei, mouth hanging agape before slamming shut into a pout.

“I was clearly an oryx,” Phainon corrects as Mydei hands him the album and leaves him for more appetizing matters. “They’re a kind of antelope. They kill predators!”

Breakfast awaited Mydei on Phainon’s kitchen island. Maybe the toast had browned too much at the crust and maybe the omelettes were two shakes away from being scrambled eggs. That didn’t stop any of it from calling out to Mydei’s stomach. By the time Phainon catches up, Mydei is already fork deep in a plate of eggs and cheese.

Phainon doesn’t immediately join him. Instead, he picks up a carafe and fills up two cups close to the brim. Phainon generously slides one over to Mydei, who doesn’t think twice before washing his meal down with whatever’s inside. A balance of tart fruit and rich cream meets his tongue, completing what was already a decently nourishing breakfast.

Mydei looks up. “You can cook.”

“Just because I don’t use your fancy knife tricks doesn’t mean I don’t know how to feed myself,” Phainon says casually, as though as he’s not suddenly aglow from winning some unspoken competition.

“You always made it sound like you’re helpless in the kitchen,” Mydei says as he swirls his cup. “You really made me drink unmixed protein powder to mess with me.”

Phainon smirks. “I wasn’t trying to prank you.”

“You were just trying to remember what juice I drink.”

“That’s not it either,” Phainon insists as he balances a piece of egg on his toast. “Four-fifths pomegranate and a splash of milk. You drank that everyday, how could I not know?”

Mydei shrugs. “It’s a normal thing to forget.”

”Well I didn’t. I only made something else because I didn’t know if I could use the goat milk in your fridge.”

“When did I give you that impression?”

“It’s a pricey milk,” Phainon says. “And I didn’t want to waste what you had. At least a scoop of protein powder is, y’know, a scoop.”

The clinking of their cutlery carries the conversation forward as Mydei mulls over what has been said. Stray pieces from different puzzles gradually come together in his head to form one single conclusion.

“Grove’s not skimping on your cut, are they?”

Phainon bursts out laughing. Thankfully he hadn’t been chewing, because Mydei didn’t feel like testing his knowledge on the Heimlich maneuver. “They’re paying me really well, don’t you worry.”

Mydei simply stares at him, as if he’d find the real answer on Phainon’s forehead. His eyes might have dried out if Phainon hadn’t continued. “I promise I’m not a money laundering scheme.”

“You live in a shoebox,” Mydei points out.

“Come on, it’s a decent apartment,” Phainon defends his home. “Sure I could live in a palace, but I’m one guy. I don’t need that much space. And I don’t want to have to clean a bazillion rooms. I get that some guys hire people for that, but I’d rather have my own place to myself.”

“You also used to pay for everyone’s lunches when we were recording.”

Phainon shrugs. “It’s not that crazy. Don’t give me that look. I’m Grove’s highest earning artist, and I think it’s fine to give back when I can afford it. Most of my co-workers are my friends anyway, so I’d prefer that Grove save that money for the other artists under the label.”

Mydei taps his fork. “It sounds like you’ve got stock in the company.”

“I don’t. Again, not that weird! I just don’t really have a lot to spend on,” Phainon admits. “I have my antiques, I guess, but I don’t buy them that often. Could you imagine? A single earthquake could tank my entire life’s savings.”

Phainon pauses for a bite of bread. “I think most of my paychecks end up going to the clinics in Aedes Elysiae. The people back home are getting up in age, so they need it even if they don’t want to say it. Cyrene’s folks don’t like taking any of my money, and let’s face it, Rini’s more successful than me anyway. What else… I give to charity whenever I can, but volunteering is better I’m told. It’s better publicity for what the charity actually does, which results in better fundraising at the end of the day.”

Mydei allows Phainon a moment to munch on his breakfast. When his toast is gone, Mydei asks, “So the only thing you want is a bunch of paperweights?”

Phainon meets his eye. A strange light dances in his blue irises before vanishing in the next blink.

“They’re valuable antiques,” Phainon haughtily tells him. “If you’re nice, I’ll get you one for your birthday.”

Mydei scoffs. “No thanks.”

The two proceed with their meal, making light work of the omelettes with its fresh tomatoes and gooey cheese. Throughout the meal, Mydei catches himself watching Phainon more often than usual, thinking back to the little boy in all those photos laughing and rolling in the dirt. Despite being the poster boy for everlasting adolescence, it’s easy to chart the ways Phainon had grown. Straighter teeth, a more prominent brow… Life in the city has even taken that little boy’s once golden tan, and with it went the sprinkle of freckles that dotted his precocious face.

And yet, when Phainon falls asleep and Mydei gets a chance to nestle close, he could just about make out a few stubborn flecks hiding out in the bridge of Phainon’s nose. The boy still walks among the living, splurging thousands on a single dinner and scrimping on scant millilitres of milk.

Mydei gathers up his used dishes. “Just for the record, you can use anything in my refrigerator. You don’t need my permission.”

“Huh?” Phainon impatiently swallows his food, but Mydei has already made off with the dishes before he could catch Phainon’s sheepish response.

A dubbing error calls for Phainon to hop back in a sound booth and re-record a line for his latest commercial. Luckily for him, Grove has a recording studio of their own, so he doesn’t have to travel too far that morning for a single line of dialogue. It does, however, mean that Phainon is much more likely to bump into his co-workers.

“Oh, Hyacine.”

Hyacine acknowledges Phainon with a smile and a tiny bob of her head. They haven’t had a proper conversation since their run-in with Cipher, which makes getting into the elevator a daunting notion for Phainon. He perseveres anyway, too fond of the pink-haired girl to let the awkwardness

simmer. The way Hyacine shuffles to give him space implies that the feeling is mutual.

The doors close, and Phainon automatically blurts out, “I’m so sorry about Cipher.”

“Huh? Oh, that,” Hyacine waves off his apologies. “I’ve forgotten all about that day, Mister Phainon. We’ve been working with Cipher long enough to know how she’s like. It’s part of her charm by now.”

“I mean, as long as you’re not bothered…”

“Not at all,” Hyacine assures him. “I’m not put off by the thought of you engaging in sexual congress. It may have caught me off-guard to hear out loud, but I never once thought that you were actually celibate!”

Is Phainon’s chastity that hot of a topic amongst his social circle…?

Nevertheless, he clears his throat. “Still, if you’d like me to have a word with Cipher, I’d be happy to step in,” Phainon offers.

“Uh, what bases?”

“The safety of you and your sexual partners, of course!” Hyacine chirps. “My assistance might be limited, but if you ever find yourself in need, I’ve stocked up on some of the most reliable contraceptives on the market!”

For some reason, Hyacine’s fondness for horror movies comes to mind. “… Thank you, Hyacine.”

“I didn’t have any specific details to work with, so I sourced a bunch of different condoms and lubricants to accommodate for common allergies and preferences. I’ve also got hygiene products and toiletries that can be useful even if you’re not planning on having coitus,” Hyacine says, counting each point on her fingers. “I did include emergency contraceptive pills too, but

those expire much faster, so I didn’t bulk up on them. Obviously proper birth control medication has to be prescribed, but if your partners are struggling to find a reliable doctor, I’d be happy to help!”

“That’s very considerate of you, um-”

“-I’ve also started drafting confidentiality agreements and consent forms if you or your partners want a safety net. I haven’t ran them through legal yet to avoid circulating gossip, but this way you won’t have to wait as long. I can’t do much about security leaks beyond that, but I did update my RSS feed with more comprehensive terms and common shorthands.”

“It would’ve, but we do have a tiny budget leftover for our first aid supplies,” Hyacine says. “After checking we have the essentials, I went ahead and added to it.”

Anaxa’s department must have the strangest first aid kit in the entire building. “I see.”

“It’s more costly to fall sick anyways,” Hyacine lectures. “Or to have a secret love child. Don’t forget, prevention is better than cure!”

She’s not wrong. Despite Phainon’s discomfort, he recognizes that Hyacine is simply looking out for him the best she can. Hyacine may like to maintain a degree of formality while they’re at work, but it doesn’t erase the fact that they’re friends at the end of the day. Perhaps she senses that Phainon is keeping secrets from her, and this is her way of dealing with the disappointment of being kept out of his personal life.

“You should also get a PrEP prescription when you can! It’s not just about anal sex, although anal sex is no different from any other kind of intercourse once you take the proper precautions.”

Phainon looks at the elevator display. There are 12 more floors.

Fortunately for him, the doors open before Phainon has to walk Hyacine through his own medicine cabinet. A single sullen man joins them in the elevator, impatiently tapping on the button that Phainon had already pressed previously. The suit and the slicked back hair had made the man difficult to recognize, but his thick facial hair is too impressive for Phainon to mistake for anyone else.

“Hello sir,” Hyacine greets politely.

“Hello,” the man replies.

Phainon follows suit. “Good morning, Mister Krateros.”

He gets a click of a tongue in return. “What’s so good about the morning?”

Phainon’s wish for silence in the elevator had been granted, but at what cost?

“I think what makes a good morning is the smell of freshly brewed coffee,” Hyacine suddenly says. Either she’d missed the acrid backnote of Krateros’s rhetorical question or she was intentionally sidestepping it altogether. “Have you had some yet? We get really good coffee around this hour.”

“…I’m leaving your office now,” Krateros murmurs. “I appreciate the offer, but I don’t want to outstay my welcome.”

There’s a chance that he just came out of a particularly awful meeting, and that’s why he’s glaring at Phainon like he’s looking at the man who’s besmirched his godson. That’s not good news for Phainon either. Phainon needs Mydei and Grove to have a good relationship, and that won’t happen if his agent isn’t on board. That begs another question: how best to broach the issue without further getting on the man’s nerves?

The answer: the polite and optimistic personification of a fluffy cloud. “You’re always welcome to take a quick break,” Hyacine says. “We won’t turn away anyone who needs it, even if they’re not affiliated with us.”

“I am not that closely affiliated with your company,” Krateros says.

“We wouldn’t mind working closer with you,” Phainon chimes in. “I mean a lot of us already love working with Mydei. He’s a really talented person.”

“Yes, Mydeimos is a skilled musician,” Krateros iterates. “So I refuse to be pressured into a decision.”

“Oh dear.”

“The negotiations have been balanced so far,” Krateros hastily replies to Hyacine’s reaction. “We’re just finalizing the details before we sign.”

That’s a relief. It doesn’t answer anything about his attitude though. Unless sound can travel down an elevator shaft and he heard something that makes Phainon sound like a sex pest.

“Please take your time in deciding,” Hyacine tells Krateros. “Things that are important are worth being patient for, and rushing to a decision would only reflect badly on us.”

Phainon has no idea if Hyacine actually recognizes who she’s talking to or if she’s that adept at extrapolating context. Considering how Anaxa avoids small talk by any means necessary, it makes sense that Hyacine would be well-practiced in filling in the gaps in any conversation.

At the very least, it makes Krateros nod civilly. “I will answer your director correctly and sincerely, this I promise.”

“If there’s anything we could do, Mister Krateros, feel free to tell us,” Phainon offers.

Once again, Krateros reacts as if he’d just discovered a mosquito buzzing in his ear. Phainon takes offense to that. His voice is not that shrill.

The elevator dings, and out steps Hyacine and Phainon. Phainon continues trailing her down the hall until she suddenly stops to look at him.

“Weren’t you headed to the basement parking?” Hyacine asks.

“Was I?” Phainon says, sounding surprised. “Ah, well. All that coffee talk made me want one of your lattes.”

“Oh! I’ll get some ready then!”

The two of them resume walking, with Hyacine picking up the pace for Phainon’s consideration.

“… Hypothetically, if you have to impress an older man who’s pissed at you for some reason, what gift would you get him?”

“Hmm, I think I’d get him a nice tie.”

“A tie, huh…”

“It might be safer for you to stick to fruit baskets instead, Mister Phainon.”

The loop plays on, repeating the same bar of music in Mydei’s headphones. It sucks to admit, but the song isn’t shaping up how he had expected, and it’s taking too much time for him to pinpoint why. Is it too bare? He tries layering one more piano track and- no, now everything sounds a half-step off. Mydei might have slammed his finger a little too hard on the delete button, toying with the idea that maybe he should also delete everything else while he’s at it.

Mydei closes his eyes and takes a deep breath. It’s a song for a PSA about crossing the road. He needs to relax.

Getting his work done is far more important than writing something he’d actually like listening to. The reason Mydei even brought the project home with him is because it was the type of assignment he could bang out in an hour. He’d forgotten that every time he’s home, he gets haunted by big, unnecessary ideas that go nowhere. It’s a new development, one that he forgets until he contracts a migraine from staring at the screen for too long.

There’s no particular reason for this change, but the likeliest cause has coincidentally chosen that exact moment to call Mydei. Mydei reaches out

for his phone immediately, though he pauses to let it ring for a few seconds more.

Once he’s deemed it credible enough for someone of his sangfroid, Mydei finally picks up the call. “Hello.”

“Hey,” Phainon’s voice answers from the other line. “You busy?”

“Yes.”

“For the road safety ad? Can you take a break soon? Please?”

“No,” Mydei grumbles. “I’m at work, haikas.”

“Really? But both your car and your bike is parked at your place.”

“How did y-“

Mydei cuts himself off with a swear. He gets up from his desk and marches to his door, where he finds Phainon waiting patiently outside. The only response the pop star has for Mydei and his glare is an excessively flattering grin.

“Bye, honey,” Phainon says into the phone, dropping the call with one last ‘mwah’ before addressing the Mydei in front of him. “I have a surprise for you.”

Mydei tries to object, but Phainon happily sweeps into the apartment without his say so. “Great,” the owner of the house deadpans. “You and your surprise can wait in the living room until I’m done.”

The grocery bag Phainon is holding does not exactly inspire excitement for Mydei. If anything, it irritates him to see what their time is being wasted on.

“Trust me, you’ll like what I got you,” Phainon promises. He hangs his hoodie on the correct hook and tosses his crocs almost correctly onto the shoe rack. “It might even help you out, actually. I just need you to get your record player ready and-“

“I’m not doing that.”

“Okay, then I’ll prepare your record player while y-“

“Most people would usually tell their victims what they need their sound system for before abusing it,” Mydei says.

Phainon shoots him a classic pout. “Play along this once, please? It’s a surprise.”

“Is that suppose to fill me with confidence? Letter bombs are surprises too.”

“For Kephale’s sake- I’m not bombing your apartment.”

“And Brutus still stuck a blade into Caesar’s back.”

Phainon groans, but he obediently thrusts the plastic bag towards Mydei. “Alright, fine. Here. I was trying to build up some anticipation, but you don’t have a single romantic bone in your body to appreciate my efforts.”

Mydei smirks. “I fail to see what Mnestia has to do with… this…”

His voice fades off. In Mydei’s hands is a vinyl record dating back to at least forty years prior. A protective sheathe has been fitted over its outer sleeve, which is already yellow and grody despite not being particularly old. The edges of its paperboard housing are barely hanging onto its last fibers, and if Mydei were to pull the record out with any significant force, he suspects he would have ripped the sleeve apart into two separate pieces. Only the album art survived the passage of time, its inks bold and clear for Mydei to read. A thousand thoughts zip through his mind, of which none shows through his blank face.

“Just thought you should have that,” Phainon says, markedly less enthused. “I’ll see myself out now.”

Mydei’s hand stops him before he could grab his jacket. “Wait. Sorry,” Mydei apologizes. “Please stay.”

Phainon glances back.

“… You need to hear if there any defects you need to ask a refund for.”

Ha. Only a weaker man would let that slide.

“Sure,” Phainon says. “I’ll give it a listen.”

Mydei’s turntable is naturally located in his music room, where Figgy had been sleeping when her owner and his complication decided to barge in and start a ruckus. Phainon eventually joins her by the dog bed after bungling up the wires one time too many, leaving the two of them to watch as Mydei meticulously rearranges the room.

Soon, the needle is placed very carefully onto the spinning record, with only a small fizz from the speakers to indicate that everything is working as intended.

“I was lucky to find it,” Phainon says as Mydei makes his way to where dog and guest are congregated. “I’m told that this is actually from the original pressing.”

It takes the needle some travel before it reaches the first song, and when it does, it is immediately shit. It’s absolutely awful to hear. It sounds like it was recorded on a roll of zippers instead of the traditional tape, with furious crackles and pops nearly drowning out the music underneath. No amount of brushing and microfiber cloths could possibly salvage this record, let alone improve its sound.

It’s even harder to hear with Mydei laughing so hard. “That’s an original, alright,” he says in between guffaws.

“Great,” Phainon says dryly, finding it significantly less humorous. “I guess I’m getting that refund now.”

“Don’t,” Mydei says with one last laugh. ”It hasn’t skipped so far. We should hear it out.”

Mydei is biased, of course. Everyone has always known Mydei’s mother to be this untouchable genius producer, forgetting that she had to have made,

at some point, a first album. Hearing this record, Mydei could almost see her, excitedly running out a dirt cheap recording booth that cost her half her savings to rent. The rest of her money would go to the most affordable manufacturer willing to give an unknown amateur a quote, because what other form would her work take other than high-fidelity vinyl? She probably changed her mind on her pièce de résistance after hearing it herself, but it was also the moment where Gorgo got to feel the weight of her music for the first time, and everything afterwards would be summarily set in motion.

As for the music itself, well, Mydei has already heard it. The album was re-released years into Gorgo’s established career, with everything re-recorded because the masters were in too much of a sorry state to use. It performed as well as expected, which is to say only critics and niche enthusiasts had bothered listening to it. While she was held in high regard, the greater public wouldn’t seek out a producer’s personal work. Gorgo was not a particularly smooth singer either, though she possessed a memorable timbre and exceptional skill with the guitar. Equipped with only those two things, she filled her sole performance album with covers of old standards and torch songs, all of which were already decades out of fashion before she even recorded it the first time.

“I have the exact guitar she used on this record,” Mydei comments offhand. The classical guitar had cost him a pretty penny at an estate sale. It was the most self-indulgent thing Mydei had done so far, up until he found himself embroiled in an irresponsible and torrid affair.

“Is the guitar listening with us right now?” The irresponsible and torrid affair asks.

“Yeah. Probably cringing at how it used to sound.”

“Hey, it’s not bad when you actually get to hear it,” Phainon argues. “It’s got some jive.”

Phainon snaps his fingers to the song. Cover albums like these were a dime-a-dozen, and Gorgo had chosen to differentiate hers by arranging these classic foreign songs in a style traditional to Kremnos.

“Jive is an interesting way to describe it,” Mydei remarks.

On the speakers, Mydei’s mother plucks the Gershwins on her nylon strings like a poem on a barbiton, almost as if imagining Dux Carminum dancing in place of Astaire. Phainon slots himself somewhere in the middle of that image, with only the faintest idea of a box step to guide him. There are hundreds upon hundreds of videos of Phainon’s concerts online, and in those videos he performs choreographies that require incredible athletic skill to pull off so smoothly. It’s apparently much more challenging to lead Mydei into a shuffle, but Phainon laughs along as if each little trip is a great thrill.

Mydei tightens his hold on Phainon. “This is not how Kremnoans dance to this kind of music.”

“Really? But this is how we dance in Aedes Elysiae.”

“Oh, is that so-“

“I’m joking,” Phainon says, pulling him close. “In Aedes Elysiae, we just move how we like.”

A snicker slips out of Mydei. “That’s a nice way of saying you dance out of beat.”

“It’s tough to hear the beat right now,” Phainon excuses himself. “But it’s still pretty danceable all things conside-Whoa!”

“I don’t know,” Mydei drawls, holding Phainon in a low dip. “Maybe I’ll figure it out after a couple more turns.”

Mydei graciously yanks Phainon right-side up again, unaware of the toll he now has to pay. As Mydei steps to the side, Phainon uses the momentum to lift him into the air with a move that Swayze would have been proud of. Mydei yells, though his resistance is undercut by the airy peal of his own laughter.

In the background, Mydei’s mother continues to sing about daffodils and candle lights while his dog continues to wag her delightful tail up at her foolish owner. Phainon squeezes Mydei tight as they slowly spin in place, gazing up at him with something approaching reverence but cannot be.

Just this once, Mydei allows himself to close the gap. It would be a shame to ruin a good thing.

for more information, and while Mydei might have wrung him of something, it was nothing that Krateros would have considered educational. The most that Mydei has gleaned is that Grove headhunted this man to supposedly lead their artists and repertoire division. Most people say supposedly, because he’s also got his fingers in mergers and subsidiaries and company restructuring and other things that have been speculated on but never confirmed. It seems that even if Mydei were to ask, he wouldn’t have learned much anyway.

The doors eventually crack open, allowing a neat secretary to beckon the two of them inside. Mydei and Krateros follow the secretary pass his little antechamber and to another set of doors that he pauses to knock on. An austere voice invites them to enter, and the secretary opens the way forward into an impressive sophisticated office. A similarly debonair man sits behind a robust executive desk, his lank figure appearing almost feeble next to the solid mahogany.

“Your eleven thirty five, sir,” the secretary announces.

The man stands up to greet his appointment, rising to a height far taller than Mydei would have guessed. “A pleasure to see you again, Mister Krateros,” the man says. “And a pleasure to formally meet you for the first time, Mister Mydeimos.”

Mydei doesn’t really like being called that, but he still shakes the man’s hand. “It’s nice to meet you too, Mister Lycurgus.”

“Please, call me Lygus,” Mist- Lygus says. He motions them toward the plush chairs facing his desk before returning to his own seat. “May I interest you in any refreshments? Something to nibble on or to quench your thirst?”

Lygus speaks with a peculiar slowness, his lilting syllables stretching out with the weight of his gravitas. It’s unexpected enough that Mydei is left slightly off-kilter.

“No, thank you,” Krateros replies to Lygus’s question as he sits down. “Mydei?”

Mydei shakes his head and follows Krateros’s lead.  Lygus nods at his secretary, who leaves the room at his signal. The man moves his head with a mechanical stiffness, reminding Mydei of an old analogue clock.

Lygus claps his hands together. “Well, gentlemen. Let us not tarry. We convene today because we are of the same mind, and further contemplation has strengthened our convictions about the proposed partnership. If our aspirations have since diverged, please, feel free to correct me.”

“Our minds haven’t changed,” Krateros assures him. “We also think this is right for us.”

“Mister Mydeimos? Have you been kept up to speed with our entreaties?”

“I am.”

“Excellent,” Lygus says. “With your consent, the only variable that remains are your signatures.”

After briefly thumbing over the documents on his table, Lygus slides a thick contract towards Mydei. A bony finger taps on the paper. “You are required to sign in several places, but please start here.”

Mydei reaches for the pen propped up on his desk, but before he could even uncap it, Krateros stops him.

“Hold on,” Krateros says, gripping Mydei’s wrist. “Can I scan through it first?”

“You may,” Lygus says as he folds his hands together. “I commend your prudence. Us humans are prone to error, no matter how learned and competent.”

Krateros nods perfunctorily, already taking out his reading glasses to review the contract. Usually when people scan through documents, they don’t actually take in each and every line. That would be called reading. Krateros, who is examining the words printed with utmost care, is most definitely

reading a contract that he could have requested a copy for any time in advance.

Mydei glances at Lygus, who appears nonplussed by Krateros’s slow crawl. If he recalls correctly, their appointment is only supposed to last 30 minutes maximum. The contract seems to be about 50 pages, and judging by where Krateros’s eyes are, it’ll take the whole day just for him to reach page 4.

“There is no need to be concerned, Mister Mydeimos,” Lygus suddenly says. “Such occurrences are commonplace for negotiations.”

Mydei frowns. “Are you going to refuse us automatically when you kick us out?”

“Of course not. You and your agent may use my settee or the lounge outside should it suit our needs. I promise the time spent won’t have any bearing on our subsequent agreements.”

Krateros coughs lightly. “I’m not going to take that long. I just thought that important things are worth taking time on.”

“Aptly put,” Lygus comments.

No one has anything else to say after that, though Mydei notices Krateros’s pupils moving marginally faster. Without anything else to do, Mydei looks out to the windows to check out the view. It’s not much more interesting, he finds, being mostly occupied by other office buildings and the like. Peering closer only makes Mydei feel like a dirty voyeur, which makes the whole wall of floor-to-ceiling windows feel a tiny bit wasteful. Their only contribution to the room is perhaps sunlight, and Lygus’s opinion on that is apparent with the thick curtains that dim his half of the room.

“Would you like me to explain the contract in greater detail, Mister Mydeimos?” Lygus asks. “Seeing as we are both idle for the moment?”

Mydei snaps to attention. “I think I’m good, thank you.”

“Such confidence. What a boon to have you within our ranks.”

“Actually-“ Mydei stops. “…No. Nevermind.”

“Please, do not suppress yourself for my sake. Your understanding is vital for our co-operation.”

“I already understand what I need to,” Mydei tells him. “I was going to ask something personal.”

“Oh? Of what matter piques your interest?”

“I was wondering if anyone in the company has a problem with me.”

For a second, it almost seems like Lygus hadn’t been prepared to hear Mydei’s query, losing the prescience in his smile. Then his processing unit kicks in again, and he starts nodding all-knowingly once more.

“You refer to your unfavorable background, correct?” Lygus asks. “There is no need to fret, for we live in a world outside clear cut binaries. Your advantages do not become obsolete because an opposing force has introduced dialectics.”

“Biases still exist,” Mydei points out.

“Another uncomfortable truth to contend with,” Lygus concurs. “But one without foundation. Tell me, does a single dust rose constitute a garden? Or is it the grass, the soil, or the life that it implies?”

Mydei ponders the question, even though Lygus answers it for him. “The answer is all of it. In myth, the Grove of Epiphany flourished in its diversity, and thus so too shall ours. Whether you are a blossoming rose or a voidshroom sprouting in the dark, our modest Grove shall benefit greatly from your involvement.”

If Mydei were given the chance to think it over, he might have realized that Lygus did not actually answer him at all. Unfortunately, he’d been distracted by Krateros’s rapid flipping of the contract, the older man’s grimace growing more distressed with each page he passes.

“Is there a definition of Sun and Thunder anywhere?” Krateros asks.

An odd detail to nitpick, but Lygus directs him in his search anyway. Krateros temporary hands back the contract, and it takes Lygus no time at all to flip to the front page and find what he’s looking for.

And yet, Krateros does not look relieved. “Is that all there is?”

“Yes,” Lygus says. “Have you spotted an issue?”

Mydei peers over Krateros’s shoulder. From what he can read, the contract states that Sun and Thunder is a band under Grove Records and that they comprise of the musicians Phainon and Mydeimos. It’s reductive, but accurate. Perhaps Krateros is wondering about the other live musicians they have to perform with…?

“I don’t know if I’m reading this wrong, but I thought we agreed that Sun and Thunder should be able to work together without Mydei being signed to Grove,” Krateros says.

“That is what the contract stipulates, yes.”

“So why is it saying that any song Mydei writes automatically belongs to Grove Records?”

“An easy misconception to make,” Lygus says. “The contract only refers to a partial ownership, and only for any Sun and Thunder song that Mister Mydeimos may write in the future.”

“But there’s no clarification on what a Sun and Thunder song is,” Krateros says. “Is it a song written by Mydei and Phainon? But why specify Mydei’s name? What’s to say Grove won’t categorize all his songs as the band’s?”

Lygus shakes his head. “We are not trying to pull the wool over your eyes, Mister Krateros. We are only trying to protect Sun and Thunder. It is not inconceivable that its main songwriter would subconsciously create more songs in a similar vein. Imagine if you will, that such a song gets sold to another artist with a bigger outreach. Sun and Thunder’s appeal and originality would come into question, and it would be nigh impossible to step out of its shadow. Why, Grove would have its hands tied if we were to

go against respected industry leaders such as Phagousa Entertainment. Our only solution would be to place these primitive guardrails in advance.”

As Lygus justifies Grove’s intentions, Mydei skims through the contract himself. Truthfully, Mydei came into this deal unsure of what he wanted, so he assumed that he’d be feel just fine if it were to fall through in the end. He severely underestimated how dispiriting it would be in reality, to see exactly how their best interests have been taken for granted.

“There’s no rubric for the songs,” Mydei re-emphasizes, ignoring the way his gut lurches.

“Is there are a need for one?” Lygus asks. “Sun and Thunder’s musical stylings are quite unique. Any reasonable jury would be able to identify its markers.”

How much of Mydei really is in Sun and Thunder? Has he ever written a song that didn’t sound like it was meant to be sang by a certain person?

“Moreover, we have no motive to claim your songs for our own,” Lygus continues. “On the contrary, we at Grove pride ourselves in our artists’ development, therefore the implication that we would recycle anybody’s music is antithetical to our mission. I would go as far as to call this an opportunity for you, Mister Mydeimos. Perhaps we’ll cultivate an intimate familiarity with your musical talents, and be inspired to work with you through the proper channels. Doesn’t that sound grand?”

“Maybe if the contract gets adjusted,” Mydei counteroffers.

For a moment, the only sound in the room is the ticking of a clock and the soft taps of Lygus’s bony fingers drumming on his table. Mydei barely catches the man’s weary sigh before he burrows back into his leather chair.

“I am ashamed, Mister Mydeimos,” Lygus admits. “Ashamed that I lack the wherewithal to assuage your fears. I believe I have elucidated our intentions to the best of my ability, but without your trust, I am afraid we are destined to misinterpret each other.”

Mydei shakes his head. “That’s not-“

“Contracts are really about trust, are they not?” Lygus interrupts. “You are willing to enter this agreement not because you believe the repercussions will keep us in line, but because you trust we will do what is right. I see now that we have failed to prove ourselves worthy of your commitment. Continuing to pursue this deal would be insulting to everyone involved.”

“It’s not paranoia to ask questions,” Krateros objects. “Why are you justified for putting in protective clauses while we can’t even get a concise description?”

Lygus holds his hands up in surrender. “You are well within your rights to seek answers for your doubts. I even sympathized with your worries, if I recall correctly. However, it is strange that you are the only ones who see this as a problem. It’s one thing for our people to hold their silence, yes, but your lawyers? They have no motivation to lie, yet they’ve attested to the contract’s fairness.”

There’s a lesson here to be learned, about lawyers and the kind that you should hire, but Mydei should have learned this back when his father’s company dragged him into a never-ending lawsuit.

“Nothing to say?” Lygus asks. “You must have arrived at the same conclusion as I.”

Though he knows better than to think this way, Mydei feels he’s to blame for everything falling apart at the last second. He tries not to make it look so obvious when they leave Lygus’s office, but all the pleasantries in the world can’t get him to do anything more than grunt.

As the doors shut behind them, Mydei recalls that most gardens convert unneeded vegetation into mulch. Only time can tell if Lygus’s promises held a grain of truth.

Phainon’s agitated pacing is beginning to wear on the soles of his shoes. The loafers were built for photographs, not pavement, but changing out of them had completely slipped Phainon’s mind. Once he set his eyes on a certain text, paying a designer’s fine became the least pressing matter at hand.

Every now and then the sound of an approaching car gets Phainon to pause, only for him to turn away from the road in dejection. It takes looping a couple more rounds before the Camry he’s looking for finally arrives, and even then he doesn’t wait for the car to come to a full stop before yanking the door open.

“Be careful,” Mydei tells Phainon as he stumbles inside.

Phainon ignores his chiding to get to the crux of the matter. “What happened back there?”

“I got a no. Just like I told you,” Mydei says, easing his car back into drive. “I’m making avgolemono tonight, is that okay?”

Phainon fumbles a tiny bit with the seatbelt and ignores the promise of chicken soup. “Was it only Lygus there? Is there going to be a follow up meeting?”

“We only spoke with Lygus and no, I don’t think we’re going to meet up again,” Mydei answers. “He spoke like the decision’s been made.”

“Lygus is only a mouthpiece,” Phainon grumbles. Never before has Phainon been so annoyed to be stuck at a photoshoot, although it was probably for the best he wasn’t around to assail his boss. “He doesn’t have the power to overrule the company’s decision.”

“Have you considered that maybe the company doesn’t want Sun and Thunder to become a real band again?”

“Impossible,” Phainon says, scowling. “Everybody’s been in favor of Sun and Thunder, either because of the money or because they like our stuff. So

many people worked to get this tour rolling, and they’re not going to be happy to be collateral damage from Lygus’s power trip.”

“The man definitely likes the sound of his own voice,” Mydei concurs. “He talked in metaphor half the time I was there.”

“The fucking metaphors. He loves it when people can’t understand him. It makes it easier for him to sneak in insults without biting him in the ass.”

“He compared me to dirt, I think.”

Phainon clicks his tongue. “Who the fuck does that guy think he is? Do you know that he can’t hold a tune to save his life? I fully believe he’s actually tone deaf, because there’s no way he thinks he’s better than you.”

Mydei laughs quietly. “He’s your superior.”

“Superior pain in the butt, maybe,” Phainon mumbles. “It won’t be long until he’s booted. Lygus is ruining the company by rejecting you.”

“That’s an exaggeration.”

“I was serious when I said there’s a lot of internal support for us,” Phainon says. “You don’t know half of what’s been invested in getting the band back together. I mean, we haven’t really gotten that far in the tour!”

“I know, that’s why Krateros was willing to negotiate,” Mydei says. “He thought it was a sign that they were taking us seriously, but they refused to rectify the one clause we wanted to change.”

“What clause?”

“There’s a part in the contract that says Grove owns all Sun and Thunder songs,” Mydei explains. “Including the ones I write outside of Sun and Thunder.”

Phainon’s brow furrows. “What does that mean?”

“It means they can strike my songs if they think it sounds like Sun and Thunder,” Mydei explains. “And they refused our request to make the definition more specific.”

“Oh. Are they asking for full ownership?”

“They’re asking for royalties and the right to refuse unauthorized usage.”

“So you can’t use your own songs?”

“They say I can, but they’ve left it open for their own loopholes.”

Slowly but surely, Phainon begins to process his words. “…Mydei, are you the one who refused to sign on?”

“Only because they wouldn’t change the contract,” Mydei says defensively.

“I know but…” Phainon pauses. “I mean, I haven’t seen the contract so maybe it’s worse than I think, b-“

“What part of what I said sounded fine to you?”

“Nothing!” Phainon immediately corrects himself. “It’s definitely bad, but compared to other contracts where people have to sign away their entire life, I think your contract was pretty forgiving.”

“You think my work isn’t my entire life?” Mydei scoffs.

“I’m talking more literal here,” Phainon emphasizes. “There are hundreds of people who are actually indebted to their companies, who aren’t credited for a single note of their music and are probably never going to see any money from it. People who’ll sign openly hostile agreements because it’s their only shot at their dream! I’m not saying Grove is in the right, but at least they’ve made your contract contestable.”

Mydei’s knuckles have gone white on the steering wheel. You could almost hear the contraction of his muscles, with the vein on his hand appearing more prominent than it’s ever been.

The tension lasts for only a second. Mydei’s grip relaxes with his next question. “Have you ever thought about leaving Grove Records?”

“Myde-“

“Have you?” Mydei presses. “You obviously don’t think Grove is a perfect entity. You talk shit about their upper management and you have to put on stage plays with your manager to get anything approved. Everyone you like in the company basically hates it there too.”

“Moving record labels isn’t as easy as it sounds.”

“You’re the Deliverer,” Mydei sneers. “You’re not a helpless little kid from the country anymore.”

“It’s because I am the Deliverer that I have to stay,” Phainon argues. “All the artists and employees in the company depend on me for their livelihood.”

“Here we go again. Acting like it’s your duty to save a company that only sees you as a cash cow.”

“Is it a fucking crime to have some loyalty?” Phainon grits his teeth. “You think I want advice from the guy who leaves other people to clean up after him?”

Mydei cackles. “That’s rich. I didn’t know it was a burden to have our entire discography and the resources of the whole company at your disposal. Fuck me for leaving you alone with endorsements worth millions!”

“You don’t know what I wanted,” Phainon interjects.

“What do I have to do with that?” Mydei says in disbelief. “If you want something, you have to take it with your own hands. Like how I wanted to make music on my own terms, and how I was willing to lose everything I have just to do that!”

“It’s not the same!”

“Yes, because I was a child. You are an adult with an established foothold on the industry.”

“Being older won’t make it easier to transfer the rights to my songs from one label to another!”

“So you choose to rot away in a company that doesn’t respect you. I’m not surprised.”

“I’m being strategic.”

“You’re being a coward,” Mydei says. “Every person you think you’re protecting would benefit much more from you pushing back at Grove. But you can’t, because you can’t bear the thought of anyone thinking negatively of you, Amphoreus’s most perfect, most brilliant, most magnanimous suck-up-”

“Your mother’s a famous record producer and no one even remembers you!”

The car comes to a stop at a red light. Neither Phainon nor Mydei make a sound, as if a vacuum had sucked the out all the atmosphere. The rest of the drive remains frightfully silent, the weight of the inevitable looming over their heads.

Phainon gets out of the car once they reach his building, but Mydei stays seated inside. He drives off the moment the passenger door slams shut, and Phainon can only watch as the Camry disappears down the street and out of his life.
