The past week has been hell, to put it lightly.

For starters, every Sun and Thunder show has been canceled for good. Half the refunds are to be settled out of Mydei’s own pocket, on grounds of being the reason the band breached their agreement with the venues. Perhaps in a fairer world Mydei would have disputed this claim in court, but recent events have left him with nothing but trepidation in regards to all things law. Whatever. If it takes draining his bank account to sever his

connections with Grove, then Mydei would give them the shirt off of his own back for all he cares.

It’s not like Grove’s going to get that money soon anyway. They shot themselves in the foot when they put out that exposé on Mydei’s father. Nobody wants to work with Public Enemy Number One or his son, adding to the suspicion that Grove did this not for the profits, but to humiliate Mydei specifically. That’s not to say there aren’t benefits to their petty article, considering they now have a convenient scapegoat for the fans’ outrage. Their own brand would come out of the scandal unscathed, and all the investors that were on the fence with Mydei’s contentious reputation are now flocking around the company once again. A big happy ending for everyone who matters.

Despite what their intentions might have been, Mydei is not the worst victim of his own downturn. That honor would go to Krateros, who has since been slaving away to recover a scrap of Mydei’s former standing. It seems that even the mediocre days preceding the comeback were out of reach, and it’s just too ironic of an outcome for Krateros to accept lying down.

So far his efforts have reaped nothing but exhaustion. Although Mydei had disagreed with him from the beginning, he had no desire to see Krateros wither away.

“Eat, old man,” Mydei orders, pointing to the lunchbox he graciously placed on his desk. “You won’t be able to make your calls if you don’t have the strength to pick up your phone.”

Krateros rubs his haggard face in exasperation, but ultimately yields. What is going to do? Say no to Mydei again? “Thank you,” Krateros mutters.

“Stop talking and eat,” Mydei repeats as he plants himself onto the couch. He stares at Krateros until the stubborn man takes his first bite in earnest.

Krateros’s office has always made Mydei cringe to be in. Most of the paraphernalia in the room are related to Mydei or Mydei’s past accolades, and it was nigh impossible to turn your head without making eye contact

with a plaque or a newspaper clipping he had minimal involvement in. Recent events only make it more difficult for Mydei to be here, but perhaps it wouldn’t be long until these embarrassing artifacts are finally stowed away for good.

“I’m waiting on a call today,” Krateros suddenly brings up. “Aquila’s Angels want to work with you.”

“Aquila’s Angels,” Mydei echoes. That was the name of the new girl group on the rise.

“I heard their manager wanted to get in touch,” Krateros says. “He said he’ll get back to me this morning.”

It is nearing four in the afternoon. Mydei decides not to pop his bubble yet; Krateros’s hair is starting to sport more salt than pepper. “That sounds great.”

“There’s-“ Krateros sighs and puts his spoon down. “I’ve gotten word back from Phagousa Entertainment, and they’ve made an offer for your pre-written work. I told them we’ll think about it, but I suppose it’s an option.”

“Keep eating,” Mydei says. “I assume you’re having second thoughts because they want to bury my credits.”

“I’m sor-“

“Don’t,” Mydei quickly cuts him off. “I’ll take their offer. I have plenty of unreleased songs I could sell.”

“You don’t have to force yourself to,” Krateros insists. “I can find a way.”

“I’m not forcing myself. I think it’s about time I stop stockpiling material.”

Krateros sighs again. “You didn’t say that the last time we had this conversation.”

“My feelings have changed,” Mydei says. “Now eat.”

The constant reminder makes Krateros grumble, but it’s what he gets for forcing Mydei to eat asparagus as a child. It takes a few more bites for hunger to properly sink its claws into Krateros, and when it does, he starts wolfing down the porridge like a man possessed. Mydei is glad he had the foresight to bring something both filling and easy on the stomach, but he might need to think about making bigger batches for the weeks to come.

“Did you know? We’ve been lied to,” Krateros grumbles into his porridge. “When I was still in talks with Grove, they said that it was us who requested for help during your writing phase.”

“…Is that so?”

Krateros almost sprays rice over his desk with how aggressively he nods. “I told them that they were the one who asked to keep eyes on you, but they laughed me off. It’s been a farce from beginning to end. Snakes, the lot of them.”

Mydei nods, having nothing of value to add. Krateros doesn’t need his blood pressure to rise any higher than it has.

Eventually, Krateros finishes eating and resumes flipping through his rolodex for someone to answer his prayers. Mydei takes it as a cue to leave him alone, though the swarm of reporters staking out his car makes him rethink his decision. Maybe Mydei could get around better if he tried disguising himself, but he won’t be surprised if the paparazzi has memorized his license plate by now.

Wigs aren’t Mydei’s thing anyway. Ignoring questions and pushing people out of his way is more his style. Sooner or later, the public is going to get tired of hearing of Mydei and his antisocial antics. Or at the very least, journalists are going to get tired of getting shoved around.

“Are you still in cahoots with Councilman Ephor? Will you address the damages caused by Bulwark to Kremnos’s trade economy?”

“Mydeimos! Mydeimos! Is it true? Is it true you attacked employees at Grove for refusing your orders?”

“How are you feeling, Mydeimos? Do you feel like an idiot for screwing up a million dollar contract or are you just living up to dear old dad?”

Mydei clips that last guy with his car door. The mortified gasps he gets are a bit unfair, considering that he gave them exactly what they came here for.

Luckily, the reporters have enough common sense to leave his car alone once he starts backing out of his parking spot. Mydei makes it onto the road without major incident, and he drives himself back home where he does the same song and dance with different set of reporters. Sometimes the paparazzi amazes Mydei with their organization. It makes him wonder if this too is Aglaea’s doing, if she took the time to learn Mydei’s weak spots so she may kick him when he’s down. Perhaps everyone at Grove is seeing this and laughing at him right now. Perhaps he deserves it.

At least Figgy still likes Mydei, judging from the way she circles his ankles when he returns. They’ve been closer than ever since Mydei started staying at home for longer. And look, Mydei has more time for himself now. He can add more reps to his workout and he can clean the bathroom like he always tells himself he would. Mydei can no longer continue the show that Ptolemy and Leonnius like, but maybe he can find another series he can start with them instead.

If none of that works, then there’s music. Once he remembers that, Mydei suddenly finds himself seated in his home studio with a guitar in hand and his MIDI controller at the ready. Everything he could ever need is here with him, and he can choose whether to make music to sell or to simply indulge. He hasn’t been given a single instruction or deadline. No time signature, no key, no genre. Only freedom.

Mydei stares at his empty project file.

The project file stares back.

Gradually, the guitar gets unmounted from his neck. The peripherals are turned off and the computer is shut down. Mydei rolls his chair away from the desk and takes in the stillness of his home.

Mydei’s parents knew each other for a sum of 20 odd years. For a time, Gorgo and Eurypon were what besotted lovers and budding rockstars aspired to. He was a guitar virtuoso oozing with stage presence and she was a musical savant who could bring any song to transcendent highs. Together they brought beautiful and glorious rock-and-roll to Amphoreus, and they believed, foolishly, that their music could be the very thing to bring the country together. Their naïve dream manifested in a media conglomerate that ate through the large majority of businesses in Amphoreus, whether through buyouts or takeovers or alliances or some other unscrupulous thing. Once the entertainment industry began to gear towards an oligarchy, Eurypon proceeded to run the company to the ground and take half of Amphoreus with it. Eurypon was eventually arrested for a litany of illegal practices, but not even his death could turn Bulwark’s fate around.

Gorgo left Eurypon before shit hit the fan, when Mydei was still a wee babe. Of their dream, she mentions a simple wish - for music to reach every corner of Amphoreus free of censorship and stigma. If Mydei could go back in time, he’d tell her to wish for something else. Music is a wonderful thing, but it can’t bring anybody together.

To his credit, Mydei does jump out of his chair when he sees the time. He chooses to get ready over replying, hoping he could make it up to Hephaestion with the microseconds his silence shaves off. Thankfully the paparazzi have yet to find a way to break into the underground parking, though Mydei tries not to be too grateful less he jinxes it. Mydei decides to prioritize speed and hops on Kokopo, praying that his boxing gloves don’t fly off on the way there.

When Mydei finally makes it to Hephaestion’s gym, he finds the man himself scrolling on his phone, a giant frown marring his face. Sadly, Mydei’s presence does not miraculously improve his mood. Hephaestion skips the well wishes and orders Mydei to prepare for the ring post-haste, hovering menacingly as Mydei wraps his hand in gauze.

“You took so long that I already cooled down,” Hephaestion grouses. “I’ll make you do high knees for an hour if you pull this stunt again.”

The clatter of gym equipment must have gotten too quiet for Hephaestion’s liking, because he goes on to turn and address the rest of the boxing club. “Are we all done with our drills?” He shouts. “Or are you all waiting for me to personally come and assist you?”

Judging from the sudden onslaught of noise, everyone is doing just fine without their coach’s assistance. Mydei on the other hand appreciates the help, though he still thinks Hephaestion should hold their sessions at a less crowded time.

Mydei warms up, hops into the ring, and proceeds to get his ass kicked for a solid 30 minutes. He and Hephaestion are sparring purely for fun - the gap between their heights and weights disqualifies any other option - but Hephaestion’s blows land like Mydei owes him actual money. Mydei deduces that it’s his piss poor timing that’s setting him off, along with a bevy of other obvious blunders that Hephaestion yells at him for.

Spending an entire match on the defensive is draining, but it keeps Mydei’s attention away from the eyes directed on him. Mydei is so preoccupied that he doesn’t realize who’s in the audience until a familiar voice calls out.

“Mydei! I brought you a booster shot!”

Between the unexpected guest, the frenzy of punches, and Mydei’s godawful positioning, the devastating strike to Mydei’s face is not as surprising as the gasps imply.

“Oh shit!” Hephaestion exclaims.

The headgear saves Mydei from crippling medical debt, but his cheek is going to smart for a couple of days at the latest. It’s lucky they have a doctor present, even if he is the cause of Mydei’s predicament.

“How is it?” Perdikkas asks once they’ve situated themselves ringside. He almost resembles a bookie, standing in the gym with his starchy button-down and loose fit trousers.

Mydei smacks his tongue as if it would help him taste Perdikkas’s homemade green juice any better. “It’s one of your better ones, honestly,” he says.

“I was talking about your face.”

“Oh.” Mydei moves his jaw from side to side. There’s a disconcerting pop as it shifts, but that’s probably normal. “I think I’m good.”

“This is not the time to play it tough,” Hephaestion says, examining his cheek in concern. “How’s your teeth? All there?”

“You’re not that strong,” Mydei says.

Hephaestion sighs. “Don’t underestimate how easy it is to get a concussion. This is why we keep our posture in mind.” He claps a hand on Mydei’s back. “But other that, you did a good job today. Well done.”

Mydei nods. Coach Hephaestion must have left the building. “Thanks.”

Hephaestion gives him a smile before turning to Perdikkas. “You should have told us you were coming,” he says. “We would have waited.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow at that.

“We could have added to our warm up while waiting,” Hephaestion amends his statement. “If you’d like, I could go for another round in the ring-“

“I’m really not dressed for it,” Perdikkas immediately refuses. “I just thought I could surprise you guys since I had a shorter day today. Can’t say it panned out how I thought it would.”

“Don’t worry,” Mydei assures him. “Next time, we’ll surprise you at work.”

Perdikkas frowns at the notion. Right, he’s a doctor. That punch must have jostled Mydei’s brain harder than he thought.

“You know, I was planning to get waffle fries with Mydei,” Hephaestion muses out loud. “But seeing as I have you two hermits with me, I say we should go somewhere a little more special.”

“What’s that rooftop restaurant with the bar?” Perdikkas asks.

“It’s a Tuesday and we’re all driving,” Mydei deadpans.

“I could tank at least one espresso martini,” Perdikkas implores them. “Please. I need this.”

They end up going to a more understated restaurant with a less comprehensive drink menu, but Perdikkas looks happy enough with his avocado milkshake. Mydei has a feeling that no matter what he ordered, Perdikkas would have still ended up slouched over the table bemoaning his job. Listening to a hospital’s petty bureaucracies turns out oddly riveting, even if it does convince Mydei to never get admitted at Perdikkas’s place of work.

The rest of Mydei’s days remain unpredictable, but adhere to a kind of routine. Usually it would start with feeding and walking Figgy, then a customary check in with Krateros. The rest of the morning would be reserved for matters around the house, and if he’s lucky, Mydei would find the time to properly sort his burgeoning archive of music.

Afternoons are the busiest. Sometimes Ptolemy would invite himself over to seek peace away from students and graduate papers, while other times it would be Peucesta dropping by to take a much needed break from his own piano. Peridikkas in particular enjoys gifting detox smoothies that Mydei shares with Krateros, who enjoys it much, much less. Occasionally, Leonnius would bring his new GameStation 6 to show off, and the workaholics in their group would suddenly be free to play a game of Galactic Grand Prix All Stars. The constant visitors are also a convenient excuse for Mydei to rediscover baking, which has the unintended side effect of Hephaestion grilling all of them twice as hard in the gym.

Going outside is still a pain, but a prominent starlet snagging a new beau has at least halved the number of reporters hounding Mydei. A few more news cycles and the public’s perception of Mydei might simmer down to a passive antipathy, and everything would be back to where they started. Even the ex-concert venues have eased their case against Mydei, perhaps coming to a realization on how pitiful his net-worth has become.

One evening, after another harsh bout in the boxing ring, Hephaestion approaches Mydei with a question.

“What do you think about holding a demonstration for the others?”

Mydei stares at his friend, still heaving from their rigorous workout.

“Most of the new members already have a good grasp on the fundamentals,” Hephaestion explains. “But they have trouble keeping their stance while on the move. I was thinking maybe we could show them how proper footwork can make or break their combos in a match.”

It’s been about a month since Mydei’s been a regular at Hephaestion’s boxing club. Whatever problem the other gym goers may have with him didn’t last past the first week, and a few familiar faces have even gone on to exchange small talk with Mydei. Watching him get consistently whaled on must have softened their views on their controversial newcomer.

“… I can see right through you, you know,” Mydei says.

Hephaestion doesn’t respond to the accusation, too busy toweling himself off. Despite his stellar winning streak, Mydei is catching up.

“You don’t have to tell us anything if you don’t want to,” Hephaestion eventually says. “I just think you should know that… We’ll be here whenever you want to move forward.”

It takes a moment, but Mydei thinks he may have smiled. “I appreciate it,” he admits.

Hephaestion answers with a grin of his own.

The status-quo continues to mold itself around a new mundane. Weekends become busier. Kokopo gets brought into Leonnius’s garage for frequent tune-ups. Ptolemy signs Mydei up for his book club. Apartment listings start appearing in Mydei’s e-mails along with miscellaneous job openings. Figgy finds a new dog park. A second boxing lesson gets scheduled over a warm serving of fries.

Everything is so normal and fine that Mydei forgets himself. On the drive home from one of Peucesta’s concerts, Mydei fails to notice where his route leads, too occupied by thoughts of tomorrow’s bills and yesterday’s chores. He barely registers the highway he’s taken until he finds himself looking up at a familiar face.

The billboard remains standing after so many months, still promoting that cologne that Mydei now knows smells of cedar and peach tea. A line of floodlights illuminate the display in the dark of night, inadvertently drawing attention to the streaks left by the errant rain. The discolored lines give the impression that the model had been weeping.

The rush hour traffic pins Mydei into place. What had once filled him with giddy laughter now leaves him hollowed and raw. It’s illogical. Mydei may not have been a pious man, but he had faith in discipline. As long as he abstains, as long as he compartmentalizes his thoughts and steels his reactions, his vices would no longer be reflex. These small pleasures would be lost in pursuit of the bigger picture, and the world would keep on turning as it always did.

And yet, Phainon remained. He was in everything; the sights, the sounds, the absence. He was on giant billboards and the television and the newspapers and strange internet gossip. He was in the music Mydei loved and in the advertisements Mydei detested. He was in the plums laid out in the market, in the floppy twitch of Figgy’s ear, in the extra shadows casted by the sun. He was in the silences that trailed every conversation, in the spaces in between Mydei’s fingers, and in the wrinkles of his pillow case when he wakes.

Mydei felt odd, like all breath had slammed out of him at once. In truth, it would have never worked out anyway. He’s seen how it plays out when two people know each other for too long. He didn’t want it for himself, and he certainly didn’t want it for Phainon. Phainon deserved better than to be shackled to a lifetime of shame, and through perseverance and hard work, Mydei ensured that would never come to pass. Mydei won. He succeeded, and it hurt.

Triumphant and victorious, Mydei crumples. His only witness continues to gaze at him from above, as unfeeling and impersonal as Kephale passing judgment.

Chapter Notes

I think it's pretty obvious that I get a lot of inspiration from romcoms but this chapter is REALLY obvious with it.

Another inspiration is What Became of the Likely Lads? by The Libertines, which is where the title came from! It took until the last chapter for me to remember to mention that, but we got there

This is a double chapter drop by the way! In case you were following along and just clicked on the recent one

“You’re leaving?”

The question hung in the air like one of the fishing lures Phainon’s dad had been so proud of. Unlike his dad’s mayfly nymphs, however, Phainon’s question failed to hook its target. The crabby teenager ignored him in favor of staring out the window like the angsty posters mounted on his side of the dorm.

“When are you coming back?”

It took a second question for the boy to finally turn his snooty face towards Phainon. “I don’t know,” the blond answered.

“Is it like a few months?” Phainon prodded. “‘Cause we just got back home, and it’d be weird if we took a hiatus right when we’re hitting it big-“

“I probably won’t return,” Mydei said bluntly. “I cut all my ties with Grove.”

“Oh.“

Phainon found himself at a loss. He heard and understood the words perfectly well, but they just didn’t sound right to him. It almost sounded as if-

“Stop making that face,” Mydei scowled. “Do you have a problem with me leaving?”

“What? No way!” Phainon pretended to gag. “If anything I’m glad to get rid of you! I mean finally, I don’t have to deal with you hogging the bathroom all the time!”

That was a close call. Something in Phainon had told him to panic, but it would have made him look really uncool.

Mydei rolled his eyes as he got down from his perch. “Great. I’m sure you’re happy to go solo way sooner than you expected.”

“I am,” Phainon blustered.

Who knows, some time apart could be a good thing. As much as he hated to admit it, Phainon has been on edge around Mydei lately, an uneasiness like an insidious creature burrowing into another’s nest. Phainon was scared it was jealousy, that he’d taken Mydei’s talent and wit and devastating prettiness personally. A break from each other could help nip these anxieties in the bud, or at least allow Phainon to catch up and do the impressing for once.

Still, Phainon can’t help but to make sure- “We can still make music together, right?”

Phainon’s words reached Mydei at the door. He lingered long enough to shoot Phainon one last aggravating smirk.

“As long as you ask nicely,” Mydei promised.

___

Sick of knocking, Aglaea finally makes use of the spare keycard and barges into the hotel room.

In hindsight, it was not the best idea to book an entire presidential suite for one singular person, let alone a person going through an inexplicable moody phase. Anaxagoras maintains that a nicer environment would chase away anyone’s blues, but he possessed as much empathy as a block of wood. Thanks to him, a throng of luxurious couches sat in the suite gathering dust, a trend that followed the generous amenities in the kitchenette and study. The wide screen TV might as well have been wallpapered over, and Aglaea isn’t even going to start on the jacuzzi tubs in the bathrooms.

Aglaea bypasses these trivial distractions to get to the only closed door in the entire suite. Growing short on time, she bursts into the guest room with an immediate demand.

“Get up, Phainon,” she orders. “You’re required at sound check.”

Taking on these extra concerts was Phainon’s idea, yet he attended to them with the most perfunctory of effort. It’s disproportionate to the labor it takes to move a battalion of crew members and equipment from city to city, not to mention the late nights spent on retooling shows at the last minute. It’s unbecoming of Phainon to behave so irresponsibly, but as Aglaea’s eyes adjusts to the sight in front of her, she finds herself unwilling to continue her rebuke.

The pop star lay on the bed facing away from Aglaea, the sheets pooling around him in a tangled mess. The curtains left no light to speak of in the room, save for a tiny sliver that bisected Phainon’s listless figure. Occasionally the ventilation would click on and blow a gust of cool air, but other than that, the scene remains as still as a painting.

Aglaea enters the room. Slowly, she sits herself on the outer perimeter of the bed, noting the steady rise and fall of Phainon’s back. She reaches out to console him, but stops once she thinks better of it.

“I could listen, if you want,” Aglaea says instead. “Though you might have to turn off the Barry Manilow playlist first.”

Somewhere within the mire of sheets, a muffled song plays on Phainon’s dying phone, droning on about farewells and lost opportunities. The lyrics are heavy-handed with its sap, but they had a better chance of reaching Phainon’s ears than Aglaea’s offer did.

She casts her gaze aside. “I didn’t know. Truly.”

Whether Phainon believes her is up to him. Aglaea can only keep talking to fill the dead air.

“I don’t believe the reunion would have been approved if it wasn’t for the timing. People wanted something to fill the gap between your albums, and it was by luck that the Fantasia was coming around again. Our shareholders could never pass on easy money, but don’t be mistaken. Opinions on Sun and Thunder were divisive from the very start.”

“I must say, I was one of the people who opposed the project,” Aglaea continues. “The proposal was preposterous, frankly. We have to put together so many moving parts in so short a time, and for what? An overseas competition that no longer holds any cultural relevance? I simply didn’t see the appeal in disrupting your rest to reunite a dated band, and to be honest I still really don’t.”

“What I did see was you on stage having the time of your life,” Aglaea confesses. “While I still can’t say the music is my cup of tea, watching you two trying to one-up the other… I liked that part.” She chuckles at the memory. “I believe a lot of people did. I thought that if my mind could change, then perhaps Grove could rethink their stance as well.”

Her faint smile evaporates. “I never intended to get your hopes up. It didn’t occur to me how important Mydeimos is to you. I’m sorry.”

Phainon remains dead to the world. Like her attempts at comfort and levity, Aglaea’s honesty also fails to rouse him, coming off more self-indulgent and preachy than she’d intended. It’s one thing to be an interloper, but to intrude and have nothing worthwhile to say?

Accepting that some matters are beyond her pay grade, Aglaea pushes herself off the bed as quietly as she can. She makes it out the room in a few brisk steps, but just as she’s about to close the door behind her, she hears it.

“What should I do?”

Aglaea looks back. Phainon is sitting up on the bed, still twisted up in his sheets.

“What should I do, Aglaea?” He asks again. His voice comes out terribly small and riddled with cracks.

The answer is to get dressed and head to sound check, but even with the distance and the awful lighting, Aglaea can see his hair matting from the build-up of grease. His two-day scruff has thickened into a patchy stubble, and half of his face sports deep imprints from where he’d been lying on the bed. He’s wearing jeans and yesterday’s undershirt, and not pajamas dyed in clashing colors or a graphic tee proudly displaying a children’s mascot. Not even a jumper several holidays out of season.

…If Aglaea is willing, there is another answer she could give him. The problem is that it doesn’t feel like the right time to enact her plans, but perhaps that may be the point.

“You should reach out to Mydeimos,” Aglaea ultimately tells Phainon.

Phainon’s eyes flicker ever so slightly, but he doesn’t comment. Aglaea leaves the door open, taking it as a sign to continue. “I’ve been working on something for a while now,” she confides in him. “There’s no guarantee it will succeed. In fact, it’ll be career suicide even if it does. The most I can say is that it might benefit you and your friend, provided that you can establish a line with him once more.”

She holds off on the details for now, in case the trade-off is too severe for Phainon to commit to. Aglaea wasn’t privy to what exactly transpired between him and Mydei, but she has a feeling Phainon’s impulsive tendencies had been burnt out in the aftermath.

“We can discuss it further after the concert,” Aglaea says, checking her watch. “Right now I need you to wash up so I can take you to the venue. I can only stall for another hour at most. ”

“…How can I get Mydei to respond?”

Aglaea looks up at Phainon, who stares at her like she’s his last lifeline. She turns the question over in her mind, pondering over every possible outcome he had asked for. If she were Mydei, what would she want to hear?

“I don’t know,” Aglaea settles on at last. “But from what I reckon, love is anything but a one-way street.”

___

“You traded Garner for my Stilott and you’re benching him?”

The weekend is on the horizon once again, which makes today another Roboball Friday. Mydei and his friends would usually spend this time at their favorite sports bar, but with the preseason winding down, getting good seats is becoming a challenge. Now they pick one of their apartments to watch the game in, and since Mydei puts in the most effort to feed them, it’s often his place that wins the draft.

In exchange, Mydei forces everyone to go to the store with him beforehand. If they were going to empty out his kitchen every time, then the least they could do is carry his groceries.

“What? Argenti’s good,” Leonnius tells Ptolemy, swinging around a bag of celery to accentuate his point.

“He’s dogwater, dude,” Perdikkas says.

“Yeah but he was intercepting like crazy last match. This could be his redemption arc.”

“Of course he did well. They were playing a bigger court,” Ptolemy points out. “It was easier to go wide, but now he’s going to be stuck with tight one-v-ones, which he sucks at.”

“You don’t understand my vision.” Leonnius taps his own noggin.

“Half a point per pass on a player that averages three assists per game?” Hephaestion says.

“He literally bodies Stilott on passes, but go off.”

Mydei’s not sure how serious they are about this fantasy league of theirs. For starters, the teams are still playing exhibition matches.

Regardless, Mydei appreciates his friends’ banter. After all, a Roboball match is not the only event happening this Friday. The Astral Fantasia Music Festival also kicks off this weekend, which marks today as the actual 10 year anniversary of Sun and Thunder’s victory. Apparently, the Marmoreal Arena is too valuable of a booking to let go, so it’s been repurposed into a solo show. Ptolemy and Leonnius’s argument about strategic stacking makes it easier to tune out all thoughts of it.

The six of them make it to Mydei’s apartment with little incident. While everyone continues with their debate, Mydei reaches for his keypad before remembering that he changed the locks some time ago. Holding back a sigh, Mydei veers his course towards his pocket and pulls out his car keys, which is the wrong key, obviously. The key to his apartment must be in his back pocke- no? He doesn’t feel it in his jacket pockets either, and another pass in his jean pockets reveals that his house key is definitely not hiding in there.

“Are you sure it’s not in your wallet again?” Hephaestion asks.

“Try the inner lining of your coat,” Perdikkas advises. “I accidentally did that in an airport once, and I couldn’t figure out why the metal detector wouldn’t let me through.”

“Oh! Maybe it’s in the groceries,” Leonnius suggests as he starts rummaging through a bag of vegetables.

Mydei goes through all of his pockets, his pouches, the sleeves of his jacket, and even the insides of his socks and shoes. Each time the key fails

to come up, Mydei starts to feel worse and worse. Figgy is locked up in his apartment alone. Who knows if something happened to her?

“It’s probably in your car,” Hephaestion assures him. “Why don’t we go take look before you do something drastic?”

And so six men welcome Roboball Friday by scouring a car for a single key. They’ve decided to divide and conquer: two to check the trunk, two to check the back, and two to check the front. So far, they’ve made zero headway into their search.

“I found out you need to get a new spare tire,” Ptolemy says, closing the boot. “But apart from that, nothing.”

“Me too,” Peucesta calls out from the rear seats.

“Me three,” Leonnius says, crouching to look under the chassis.

“What time is it?” Perdikkas asks.

Leonnius checks his phone. “Uh, eight minutes to kick-off.”

Perdikkas instinctively sucks a breath through his teeth before catching himself. “I mean, aw nuts! That’s so much time left to wait!”

“It’s not that bad,” Hephaestion says as he closes the glove compartment. "No one’s going to score in the first ten minutes anyway.”

“Don’t jinx it!” Leonnius cries.

Hephaestion rolls his eyes and turns to Mydei. “Can we turn on your radio to listen to the game?”

“It’s fine if not,” Perdikkas adds. “It’s not the same without Dei’s chicken wings.”

“Play it,” Mydei orders Hephaestion. He’s on the floor checking under the driver’s mat when he should be calling for a maintenance guy. Missing the game would be the cherry-on-top of this shitshow.

Hephaestion complies. The radio opens with a burst of white noise that he hurriedly tries to fix.

“Just for the record, I wasn’t complaining about not seeing the game,” Leonnius pipes up.

“Be quiet and keep looking for that key,” Perdikkas grumbles.

Being in an underground garage, most of the radio channels come out as nothing but straight fuzz. It’s an unbearably awkward amount of static to be subjected to, so Hephaestion naturally pauses on the first channel they can actually decipher.

“-so good to have you back with us, Phainon!”

Hephaestion jumps.

“Turn that shit off,” Ptolemy immediately says, rushing to the car’s passenger side. “I’m sick of that interview.”

“You’ve heard this?” Hephaestion asks.

“Who hasn’t? The Tribios sisters have been replaying it for weeks,” Ptolemy says, disgusted. “He’s debuting a new song to promote his ‘new’ tour. The usual garbage.”

“A new song?” Perdikkas says. “That’s fast.”

Hephaestion frowns. “Did you know about this?” He asks Mydei.

“No,” Mydei answers.

Leonnius sputters. “You haven’t? But it’s- I mean-“

“I see you have an acoustic guitar with you today,” Tribbie’s voice floats from the radio. “Something tells me we’re about to hear something really special!”

Mydei’s tinny car speaker makes Phainon’s laugh sound uncharacteristically nervous. “I was just messing around with something that was stuck in my head. I don’t really know if I did it any justice.”

“What a tool,” Ptolemy remarks with a grimace. “Shut it off already, Hephaestion.”

“No!” Leonnius interjects.

Ptolemy gives him an incredulous look. “What do you mean ‘no’? You know the game’s not going to be on this channel right?” He points out.

“Yeah I know, but like-“ Leonnius’s eyes dart around. “-What if I want to hear Phainon’s new song?”

Perdikkas groans.

“What? I’m curious!” Leonnius says.

“Then look it up online,” Ptolemy deadpans. “By yourself.”

“What if, uh, what if I want us to make fun of it together?” Leonnius asks.

“Seriously dude, read the room,” Perdikkas says.

“Alright, relax guys,” Hephaestion intervenes, glancing at Mydei. “I’ll switch the radio off. We can use someone’s phone to keep updated with the game in the meantime, deal?”

Hephaestion reaches for the dials before anyone could object. Right as his finger touches down on the stereo, a hand shoots out from the back seat and stops him. Puzzled, Hephaestion turns to look at the perpetuator.

“He should listen to the song,” Peucesta says.

A strange piece of advice, but Hephaestion has always prided himself on listening to his friends. That’s at least two of them that wants to keep the radio on. Hephaestion gives Mydei another once-over and finds plenty to look at, chief among them being Mydei’s waning will.

“I don’t care,” Mydei says, waving him off. “Do what you want.”

Nodding, Hephaestion retracts his hand and lets the radio play. If Peucesta ends up being wrong, he and Leonnius are going to pay it back in ab crunches.

“-isn’t going in a new album either. I think. All I’m saying is that there’s nothing worth expecting yet.”

“Gee, a special song just for us,” Trianne says dreamily. “I’m on the edge of my seat thinking about it!”

“You heard her, Phainon. You better play that song before Trianne falls off her stool,” Tribbie teases.

Phainon laughs again. “Well we can’t have that happen, can we?”

An tentative chord rings from the speakers, at odds with Phainon’s brazen words. The struck strings recoil with a dinky twang, as if Phainon’s fingers are struggling to find purchase on the fretboard. The sound is still there when he tries again, albeit less noticeable beneath his forceful strum.

For once, Mydei’s friends are quiet, allowing for Phainon’s song to play on without interference. There’s a million ways his new song could have sounded like, but never would Mydei have guessed it to sound familiar. Perhaps Krateros was right. Perhaps Mydei should have sold the song when he got the chance.

Instead, he lost it in a wager to Phainon. It’s almost a mercy that the song isn’t quite the same in the singer’s hands. The rhythm has been adjusted to accommodate Phainon’s predilection for down-picking, and although the melody has been left untouched, the chords have clearly been transposed a few keys up. The song strays like a game of telephone, a by-product of being remade whole cloth from memory. It’s kind to Mydei in the same way an axe is kind to a rotting tree.

It’s only once he opens his mouth that Phainon’s creative liberties take flight. Phainon is a shrewd man. He knows that words are where he shines

best, so a song without proper lyrics is a glorious windfall to him. With fanciful metaphors and a mellifluous voice, Phainon transforms an aimless half-cocked love song into a simple ballad about a nameless drifter. He sings about the perils of his fictional journey, as well as the wonderful places and people he comes across.

Despite the dangers and awe-inspiring sights, the drifter never pauses in his stride. His destination is more grand than anything along the way, you see, with golden skies and sweet tangerine trees. He dreams a dream that smells like a freshly cooked meal, sounds like rowdy guitar music, and has a habit of arguing with a doting smile. When he relays this to a kind samaritan, the drifter gets told that he missed his stop a long time ago. What he’s searching is all the way back at the start of his journey.

Phainon sings of remorse and excuses. The drifter refuses to look back, afraid he’ll only see the dangers he escaped. He reasons that as long as he keeps walking, the road will wind back home someday, not seeing how each step takes him further away from his goal. Thus, the foolish drifter continues to roam, his bones creaking as he goes. He imagines a tangerine rolling on the road in front of him, and as the song closes, the drifter carries on chasing after the fruit day after day after day.

“Wowzers! That’s such a good song, Phainon!”

“No it isn’t,” Ptolemy disagrees with Trianne’s pre-recorded comment. “It’s a stupid song.”

“It’s not stupid,” Leonnius protests.

“Please. It’s some hokey nonsense he threw together to sell tickets to teenagers. Noise pollution is more meaningful than this,” Ptolemy says.

“-di. Mydei!”

The hand on Mydei’s shoulder jostles him once again. He looks up at Hephaestion, who looks back not in ridicule, but with patience.

A sharp clap brings Mydei into the present. “That’s it then.” Ptolemy sighs. “Take out your car keys, Leonnius.”

“For the love of- Connect the dots, you dolt,” Ptolemy says. He turns to look at Mydei, who’s still crouched on the ground. “Stand up already. You’ve got questions that need answering, don’t you?”

Despite common sense, despite everything that he has ever known as the truth, Mydei nods his head and gets to his feet.

Leonnius’s Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution X is fitted with a custom aero kit, 16 inch semi slick tires, and a modified 4 cylinder turbocharger. Its engine boasts a decent 1000 horsepower at 9800 revolutions per minute. Given optimal conditions, the car can hit 60 miles per hour in sub 4 seconds, reaching top speed before it could pass the next city block.

Currently, the car can be found hurtling down the backstreets of Marmoreal Lane, making use of the lesser known roads to launch unimpeded at full power. The resulting shock wave disrupts pedestrians and slower vehicles alike, a grievance that goes unseen by the car’s speeding driver.

“I think you can slow down,” Hephaestion suggests, holding onto the grab handles for dear life.

“We can’t,” Leonnius says. “The concert’s already half-way through!”

“That won’t happen,” Leonnius assures Hephaestion. “I learned a trick or two while I was in Edo Star.”

To prove it, Leonnius drifts his way through a sharp corner, his foot barely lifting off of the accelerator. The three bodies in the back slam into one another like a Newton’s cradle, demonstrating the conservation of momentum and energy in a less pacifist manner.

“That cannot be legal,” Ptolemy says from the safety of Peucesta’s phone. He nobly volunteered to stay back to handle the locked door and the groceries, but he had to be kept on call in case the actual tenant needs to be alerted. With all the screaming happening in his ear, it’s like Ptolemy never left them.

“I think we’re fine as long as it’s not on Sunset Road,” says Perdikkas, who is also gripping desperately onto anything bolted into the car. “A single pothole could end us.”

Hephaestion is not listening. His eyes are screwed tight as he prays. “Oh Nikador, righteous in your fury. Deliver us through this battle unharmed and of sound mind-“

As Leonnius’s car continues to terrorize Okhema one quarter-mile at a time, Mydei stays remarkably silent in the passenger seat. Not out of fear, but out of contemplation. If or when they make it to the arena, Mydei will have to say something, and it has to be the best, most incredible set of words to have ever come out of his mouth.

“Oh no,” Leonnius suddenly curses under his breath. “No, no, no, no, no.”

The worst has come to pass. A traffic jam has caught up to them.

Leonnius groans as the car rolls to a stop at the tail-end of traffic. “I swear Luminosa’s usually empty at this time!”

“It’s parents coming to pick their kids up from the concert,” Ptolemy theorizes. “They probably came early because they predicted this.”

“And everyone keeps cutting in,” Leonnius says. “Forget the concert, we’re going to be stuck here until tomorrow!”

“Look for a subway station nearby,” Hephaestion wheezes, slumped over in the back seat. “Or a bike rental or something.”

“The nearest station is ten minutes away,” Perdikkas reads off of his phone. “And you’ll have to walk twenty more minutes once you get down near the arena.”

It beats sitting still. Mydei unclasps his seatbelt.

“Whoa, whoa, wait a second dude,” Leonnius tries to stall. “That’s still a long way to go.”

“I have to try,” Mydei says. “I’ll catch a cab once I pass the worst of it.”

“If you can get a cab,” Leonnius says, sharing the rare pessimistic thought. “We’re three lanes deep on the main road, someone stop him!”

At his request, one of the rear windows slides open before Mydei could unlock the door. Perdikkas pops his head out of the gap and begins to shout at full volume.

“Our friend’s father has gone into sepsis from acute cholangitis!” He screams to the cars ahead. “If we do not reach the hospital in time for the liver transplant, he will not make it past this evening!”

Hephaestion and Peucesta stare at Perdikkas with a scandalized malaise. As if Perdikkas isn’t getting enough of that from the cars around them.

Perdikkas takes a deep breath before opening his big mouth once more. “A father will die tonight-“

By some miracle, the cars in front of Leonnius gradually nudge themselves to the far side of their lanes, opening up enough space for a Mitsubishi Lancer to scoot past. Perdikkas showers everyone involved with thanks as the car shimmies by, like a bizarre parade for one.

“How are you going to explain this to your ethics board?” Ptolemy asks when Perdikkas’s head returns inside the car.

“I don’t know,” Perdikkas answers truthfully. “The hospital’s on the way though. If I clock in and see patients on overtime, do you think it would cancel out?”

“Why are you asking me?” Asks the philosophy professor.

“I think it’s going to be harder to explain to the police,” Hephaestion comments as they reach the front of the line.

“Hey if it all works out, we’ll have Amphoreus’s number one pop star to pay our bail,” Leonnius says.

“I can pay it myself,” Mydei mutters.

No one contests him on that, because Leonnius shifts gears shortly after and subjects everyone to an abrupt hike in G-force. Out of guilt, Perdikkas asks to be dropped off at the hospital first, which is still a preferable detour to an hour of traffic. He makes sure to wish Mydei good luck before he leaves, all while begging everyone else for video proof.

After much trial and tribulation, the car finally arrives at the front gates of the Marmoreal Arena with an ungodly screech. Mydei almost rips the door out of its hinges with how fast he gets out, only to hesitate a couple of steps away.

“What are you doing man?” Leonnius shouts when Mydei looks back. “Keep going!”

“We’ll catch up!” Hephaestion grunts as he sluggishly tries to free himself from the seatbelt.

Only Peucesta manages to get his foot on the ground, but only long enough to toss his phone over to Mydei.

“Look!” Peucesta urges, gesturing to his phone screen. “Look!”

The pianist turns to assist Hephaestion without further explanation. Mydei turns over the phone to see Ptolemy struggling with the locksmith, Figgy,

and the groceries. Underneath that, however, is a screenshot of an email. A VIP ticket to tonight’s show.

Mydei jets off without saying goodbye, mentally promising to make it up to his friends after. Fortunately there aren’t a lot of people still milling around the entrance, making it a breeze for Mydei to burst in and sprint right up to the ticket booth. The lady behind the window gives him a wary once-over when he shows her the ticket, either because of his late arrival, his suspiciously familiar appearance, or because of the tiny Ptolemy fighting in the corner. Either way, she validates his entry and directs him down the correct passage with minimum fuss.

The concert can be heard well enough outside, but it holds no candle inside the actual arena, where Phainon’s voice reverberates from every corner of the venue. Mydei emerges from an entrance near the pit, and is instantly accosted by Phainon’s face projected on a gigantic LED screen. It shows him belting out the first lines of Recurrence, a song that is almost always the penultimate number on Phainon’s set-lists. Mydei made it with time to spare, but seeing Phainon’s resplendent grin as a massive crowd sings his own song back to him is enough to make Mydei falter. It’s not too late for Mydei to change his mind. Can he really bear the cost of his own actions?

As Phainon moves into the chorus, Mydei steps into the crush of people. It’s remarkably packed for a last minute show, but Mydei must press on. Unlike the woman at the ticket booth, Phainon’s fans are much more adept at recognizing Mydei, falling silent once they catch sight of the man. Most of them try to stay out of his way, but they make no attempt to hide their disapproval or shock. Nevertheless Mydei advances, stalking over to the front like a lion carving a path through the reeds.

Mydei is nowhere near the stage when a hand pulls him back.

“End of the line, little lion,” a familiar voice says.

Cipher’s sharp nails dig into his forearm. A warning. Contrary to what the news outlets say, Mydei isn’t stupid enough to start a commotion with so many people clustered together. He relents at once.

The audience breathes a collective sigh of relief as Cipher escorts Mydei out of the crowd. Up on the stage, Phainon continues to sing and prance about, oblivious to the matters of the little people below.

Though quirky and daring in nature, Cipher excels at discretion. She leads Mydei through the less populated routes, forcing him to adopt her hurried pace when witnesses are unavoidable. She’s a whole different woman when she’s actually doing her job, but Mydei refuses to throw in the towel, holding on to the hope that the Cipher he knows is still listening.

“Let me see Phainon,” Mydei says. “I just need a moment.”

“Now who do you think I work for, Goldilocks?” Cipher tuts, pushing him down a long tunnel away from the performance area. “Do you think I’ve got the authority to bring any Joe Schmoe to our precious clientele?”

“I’ve got a premium ticket,” Mydei argues.

“Then you can wait after the concert.”

The sounds of the show fade as they make their way down the bright corridor, with only a faint thump from the bass to let them know the program still going. The further they get, the less there is to hear, and the closer they get to complete silence, the more Mydei worries. If he dislocates his shoulder, he can potentially break free from Cipher’s hold, but there’s no way he’s outrunning her, nor can he fend her off with one arm down.

“I’ll be quick,” Mydei tries again. “I won’t say it was y-oof!”

Cipher shoves Mydei through a door, causing him to careen off balance.

“Do me a favor and stay there,” she says, dusting her hands off.

“Cipher, ple-“

The guard slams the door shut. Mydei rushes towards it, but she engages the locks before he could even try to leave. No matter how much he bangs his fist against the steel and pulls on the handle, the door stays put.

“Cipher! I’ll pay you if you let me back in!”

Why is he even trying to negotiate with someone that’s obviously not there? He should just book it back to the front gates. Mydei frantically turns around to get to the exit, only to find out that he’s trapped. He sees nothing but four walls and a single door, as well as excessively lit dressing tables and low couches and a clothing rack filled with flouncy costumes.

Mydei blinks. It’s a dressing room.

There’s a make-up case left open on one of the vanities, and in it is a collection of pale concealers and even paler mascaras. Hanging at the very end of the clothing rack, buried beneath finely co-ordinated ensembles, is a pair of unevenly dyed puce jeans. The jeans match the crossbody bag slung over one of the couches, though the little orange chimera hanging from the zipper is harder to style around.

This is Phainon’s dressing room, Mydei realizes. He sits down on the couch in a stupor, the adrenaline in his veins taking an abrupt nosedive. The world slows in the relative quiet of the dressing room, and Mydei is left with an opportunity to catch up with his thoughts. In moments like these, the general rule of thumb appears to be to follow your heart, and Mydei’s ratcheting heartbeat apparently doesn’t take kindly to the thoughts of what’s to come.

So Mydei fixates on the factors he can change, starting with what he’ll say when he finally sees Phainon. There’s still the final song and the encore to wait out, which is time that Mydei desperately needs. It’s not going to be easy to sway Phainon while summarizing the last 10 years in the same breath.

The bass gets louder in the distance as a poor sound technician fails to keep the audio from peaking, resulting in the speakers popping incessantly. It might even be a problem in the sound system itself, because the anomaly almost sounds like it’s isolated. Strangely, the way it pans over gives the impression that the sound is physically approaching Mydei. Each blow seems to echo out in the hall, as if it were diegetic rather than a part of the score. As if it were the footsteps of someone running tow-

Something bangs against the door. This something fumbles with the lock before shoving the door wide open with an obnoxious bang. Mydei hasn’t gotten past the apology part of his monologue when Phainon bursts in, limbs splayed.

The two musicians lock eyes on each other as the door slowly swings shut behind Phainon. Neither of them move, twin deers caught in opposing headlights. Despite Mydei’s brashness, it has always been Phainon who was the go-getter between them. It comes as no surprise that he’s the first to attempt contact, opening his mouth to break the silence.

The singer hesitates, unfortunately, and his greeting is lost to history as Mydei lunges at him with a sucker punch.

Phainon lets out a yelp as he catches Mydei’s arm in time, stopping him short of bruising his liver. Before he could question his attacker or ask for praise, another fist comes in to finish what its counterpart had started, forcing Phainon to tug at Mydei’s arm to shake him off his aim.

The punch barely glances off of Phainon’s collarbone, but Phainon has grown wiser in the last few seconds. He tackles Mydei before the man readies his next move, launching them both onto one of the couches. Phainon hits his shin as he knocks the wind out of Mydei, who immediately leverages his long legs to kick Phainon’s actual ass. His flailing is a minor inconvenience, but it’s enough of a distraction to overthrow Phainon, allowing Mydei to finally get a real punch in.

With a groan, Phainon rolls off the couch to avoid any more hits. He tries to trip Mydei with the flare, which is an impressive dance move to pull off but absolutely worthless in this fight. Not that Mydei is any more successful in his attempt to grab Phainon’s spinning ankles. The stalemate ends when Mydei jumps and tries to get him with an elbow drop like the bastard he is. Phainon manages to roll out of the way by the skin of his teeth, but Mydei is never too far behind.

New plan then. Phainon fends Mydei off with tiny wimpy kicks as he inches backward to freedom. Later, when he’s no longer fearing for his life, Phainon will cherish the memory of Mydei crawling towards him

disheveled and panting, with shiny trails of sweat leading down to where his shirt stretches over his cleavage. Until then, Phainon focuses on keeping Mydei at bay, waiting for an opening. As Mydei leaps up to grab his foot, Phainon swings his leg and sends a rack of clothing crashing down on him. Mydei swears up a storm as he tries to untangle himself from a mountain of costumes. He throws off the last piece of tulle once he gets off the floor, only for Phainon to clothesline him from behind with a single pair of pants.

With his arms restrained and Phainon pressed against his back, Mydei is left thrashing about for some leeway. Phainon grits his teeth and pulls with all his might, but fabric is at its weakest when taut. With a firm jerk of his shoulder, Mydei begins ripping through the crotch of Phainon’s favorite jeans, which Phainon couldn’t even mourn before Mydei rushes him.

Mydei wastes no time nailing Phainon with several fast jabs. After being on stage for 2 hours, Phainon isn’t likely to win in a battle of stamina. Dodging and weaving would leave him more vulnerable in the end, so Phainon focuses on a better offense. Mydei’s haymaker may have dealt significant damage to him and his ego, but it also allows for Phainon to slam a fist to Mydei’s exposed flank. He chains it into a quick cross to Mydei’s sternum, which staggers Mydei and leaves Phainon’s knuckles faintly sore. His hand would have hurt more if Mydei’s chest were any less pillowy, and this thought would come to cost Phainon a devastating punch to his stomach.

Phainon keels over with a groan. That cheater definitely wasn’t holding back with that last hit. Before his knees could hit the ground, Mydei hauls the singer up by his glittery collar and glowers at him with the callousness of a lion confronting its prey. Accepting his fate, Phainon closes his eyes in anticipation of the final blow.

Then Mydei kisses him.

It’s as light and sweet as the first rains of autumn. Phainon feels Mydei’s lips purse against his as though to reassure him, purposeful in every way their first kiss was not. There existed no better panacea for Phainon’s ails. He would tank another 30 million bodyslams if it meant Mydei would kiss him like this again, even if Mydei does pull away too soon.

“I love you,” Mydei tells Phainon.

A jolt of lighting runs through Phainon’s spine.

“I said it first,” Mydei continues breathlessly. “I win.”

It only takes a moment for the words to register as reality. Phainon can’t help but smile when it sinks in, the corners of his eyes crinkling in that beautiful way that Mydei has missed. He reaches out to take Mydei’s face in his hands, softly carding his fingers through tresses of gold.

Every win deserves a reward, so Mydei bestows Phainon with another kiss teeming with affection. This time Phainon is there to meet him, sliding their lips together where they fit the best. Admittedly it’s not as passionate as their other kisses, because neither of them could stop smiling long enough to escalate the proceedings. Instead, joy spills out between them in rivulets of laughter, no longer hidden under the cover of sarcasm or skepticism. Phainon proceeds to pamper Mydei’s face with adoring little pecks, and Mydei encourages him by crushing him adoringly in his embrace.

A loud argument outside puts a damper on the occasion. All Mydei wants is to bask in his lover’s undivided attention, yet here comes some scowling miser storming in with a phone in her ear.

“You ungrateful brat,” The woman spits out, pointing the phone at Phainon. “After everything we’ve done for you, you walk out on a show worth millions to play house with this cretin?”

All softness leaves his face at once. His eyes sharpen and his jaw tightens. He places himself between his superior and Mydei, intending to shield Mydei from a middle-aged woman half his size.

It takes more than a temper tantrum to scare her, but Caenis does flinch at the sight of Phainon’s anger. “Is that you, Caenis?” Someone calls out from behind the door. “I thought I smelled something rotten nearby.”

Mydei didn’t think it was possible, but Caenis’s frown deepens at the sound of that voice. Aglaea slips into the room with effortless poise, completely

unfazed by the ridiculous line-up before her.

“This is your doing,” Caenis condemns the new arrival. “You’re behind this charade, aren’t you?”

Aglaea ignores her tirade. “Hello, Mydeimos. It’s nice to see you here.”

“Thank y-“

“Have you gone mad?!” Caenis cuts Mydei off to continue screaming at Aglaea. “Your position is on the line if you don’t get that whelp back on stage this instant!”

Aglaea holds a piece of paper right up in Caenis’s face. “Tell me what this says.”

She points a manicured finger at a word. Phainon.

Caenis stares at the contract in horror, the implications of Aglaea’s words dawning on her. Aghast, she turns to Aglaea, and with a quiver of her lip, bursts out laughing.

“You have to be kidding me,” Caenis says between wheezes. “This is the best you can do? A minor technicality about legal names? Ha!”

“His Okheman records will suffice,” she states in a clipped tone. “No matter if it’s today or ten years ago, everything he signs as Phainon is still legally binding. Stick to posting pictures and playing dress-up, Aglaea. Don’t get arrogant because you had an idea for once in your life.”

Mydei squeezes Phainon’s arm when he feel him jerk forward. As much as he wishes to let go and watch Caenis answer to consequences, the last thing Aglaea needs right now is to be an accessory to murder.

The publicist lets out a weary sigh. “I suppose we’ll lose if we were to take this to trial,” she says.

Caenis smirks. “Don’t waste your breath flattering me now.”

The door opens once more, perhaps answering to Mydei’s call for divine intervention. Anaxa is an alright substitute, Mydei supposes, but he doesn’t like how Caenis maniacally grins when she sees him.

“Perfect timing, Anaxa,” Caenis says. “Get Phainon back out there and call the security to handle the miscreant behind him.”

“Stop insulting Mydei,” Phainon snarls.

Mydei is man enough to admit that Phainon defending him so zealously is making his toes curl, but he’d rather not have everyone’s attention on them at a time like this. The room is so crowded and thick with tension that the 5 foot tall Hyacine can’t find the space to get in. Instead she stands outside keeping the door propped open, eyeing the toppled clothing rack in worry. She’s quick to offer Mydei an encouraging smile from across the room, which she follows with a noncommittal shrug.

“The concert was already nearing its end, so we called it early,” Anaxa informs Caenis. That explains the commotion of busy workers outside. “Naturally there are people who are unhappy with the decision. Callictis wants a word with who’s responsible.”

Caenis dramatically motions to the rest of the room’s occupants. “Take your pick. You won’t believe the preposterous things I’ve heard!”

Anaxa glances at Aglaea. “I can imagine.”

Aglaea crosses her arms, possibly the first sign of vexation she’s shown so far.

“Repeat what you just told me,” Caenis orders Aglaea with a snap of her fingers. “Enlighten Anaxa with the brilliant plan you’ve concocted.”

“We are planning to sue you for using the wrong name on Phainon’s contracts,” Aglaea says curtly.

Caenis lets out another grating titter.

“Yes, it’s very silly of me,” Aglaea concurs. “It’s such an obvious case that the prosecution might investigate a little deeper out of boredom. It’s possible they’ll even discover something about where Grove’s assets are going.”

The laughter fades.

“If we’ve been getting Phainon’s name wrong this whole time, what other things have been slipping through our fingers?” Aglaea says. “What has our manpower been so occupied with that we haven’t been able to factcheck this important detail?”

“These are the ramblings of a desperate woman,” Caenis retorts. Her smug smile is yet to be impacted, though it no longer reaches her eyes. “You would have brought this up sooner if you had real proof.”

“I was waiting for the proof,” Aglaea says. She holds her hand out. “Anaxagoras, if you please.”

At her cue, Hyacine digs in her tote bag and pulls out a manila folder to pass to Anaxa, who places it onto Aglaea’s waiting palm. Caenis gawks at the entire exchange.

“Let’s see what we have here.” Aglaea adjusts her glasses as she peruses the contents. “Balance sheets, market analyses, minutes from a stockholder meeting… Even our customers’ private information? For shame, Caenis.”

Caenis swipes the files from Aglaea’s grip. “You’d bring the company’s sensitive data to a concert just to frame me?!” She yells.

“Of course not, we’re not morons,” Anaxa says. “It’s just the evidence of your collusion.”

In her hands, Caenis finds printouts of e-mails and private text messages, as well as detailed calculations of Grove’s deficits. Each document is so disparate from the last that it should come off as nonsense, and yet it only makes the common denominator all the more conspicuous.

“The problem with having so many advocates is that you get dimwits soliciting your inner circle to anyone, anywhere,” Anaxa lectures. “After the fourth idiot that ‘surreptitiously’ approached me, I decided that I might as well do some research of my own.”

Further in the folder are photos of familiar faces in close quarters with foreign businessmen. They appear innocent enough, taking place in parks or bars that are too public for illicit backdoor transactions, but there are only so many times they can be photographed together before it stops being coincidence.

“I assumed you and your co-conspirators might be peddling information to our competitors,” Anaxa continues. “But your role in Grove is too high to risk for a quick buck. You were already gutting our workforce and recanting your support for acts like Sun and Thunder, so sabotage was my second guess. Without motive however, I was unconvinced.”

“Fortunately it was simple to deduce once I identified your brokers,” Aglaea says. “You’ve been in correspondence with the IPC music group,

haven’t you?”

Mydei frowns. The IPC’s record label is one of the biggest music enterprises in the world. To be affiliated with them suggests power, but Grove Records lack the international market to make any use of it.

“The IPC have been looking to expand their music division towards this side of the Quanta Sea,” Anaxa reveals, solving that riddle. “Acquiring a previously established company would be better than starting from scratch, and you were always pushing Grove to be more than an independent label. Not a popular stance within our company, but that won’t stop you.”

The open door has begun to attract curious passer-by’s, though urgent matters dissuade them to stay. Only a couple of make-up artists have stopped to line up behind Hyacine, appearing happy to wait as Anaxa shares his findings.

“You started with the people you could influence and built up alliances from there,” Anaxa says. “Then you fed the IPC shares and insider information to maintain their interest, and when that wasn’t enough, you tried slashing the buying price in secret. If you curtail Grove’s long term value while leaving the shareholders’ equity intact, you could also shake the executive board’s confidence without implicating yourself. A flawless gambit, had you not panicked when Sun and Thunder started gaining traction.”

It was an overwhelming amount of information to be thrown with at once, and Anaxa’s stringent manner of speaking left no room for questions. Caenis’s oppressive air had shriveled up under its pressure, leaving behind an icy silence.

Caenis calmly raises her head.

“It sounds plausible,” she says, stuffing the documents back in its folder. “For something that can’t be proven. You made loose connections and assumed my thoughts, but nothing I see here is worth calling a crime. You’ll only turn everyone against each other if you turn this in, and we’ve already got plenty of that at work.”

“To be honest I wanted to wait until you’ve progressed further in your plan,” Aglaea admits. “I’d feel safer if I identified all your allies first.”

“Suspect me all you want. My conscience is clear,” Caenis says.

At that, Aglaea smiles. “But we’re not targeting you, remember?”

“I’m targeting Grove,” Phainon says.

Caenis whips her head towards Phainon, already beyond tired of his insolence. Luckily for her, Aglaea speaks first.

“Grove claims Phainon’s contract is valid, but Phainon disagrees,” Aglaea reminds Caenis. “It wouldn’t make for a thrilling trial, but imagine how it would sound, for an accomplished Okheman company to deny a boy from the hinterlands the right to his own name.”

Though her blank expression doesn’t budge, Mydei can see Caenis’s fingers twitch erratically.

“Think of the headlines from that one fact alone,” Aglaea says. “The media loves an underdog, almost as much as Amphoreus loves Phainon. News outlets would scavenge for details until they find everything Anaxagoras told you, and if you’re lucky, your supporters won’t abandon you immediately. The IPC would certainly drop you right away to extricate themselves from your mess.”

More stagehands and members of the crew have gathered by the door, likely wondering where their organizers have gone. What they find probably doesn’t help their confusion, yet it’s satisfying all the same.

Aglaea circles Caenis like a vulture in wait. “The worst will come once they discover your part in Sun and Thunder’s demise,” Aglaea predicts. “That’s the project Phainon personally financed, and his record label culled it just like that. What does it imply for Grove’s reputation as a nurturing environment for artists? If their biggest star can’t determine his own career, then what of the rest? Firing you wouldn’t be enough to fix the blow to their image. Grove might even end up suing you themselves.”

Scorn radiates from Caenis’s entire being. “That’s nowhere near enough to win you the lawsuit,” she says.

Aglaea grins. It’s probably the most emotion she has ever shown. “The underdog loses to a money hungry corporation. Riots take to the streets.”

The folder in Caenis’s hands crumples in her grip.

“We may stand no chance of winning in court,” Aglaea agrees, tucking a perfectly coiffed curl behind her ear. “But can you win against me in the court of public opinion?

“You bitch,” Caenis lashes out. She backs away from Aglaea, as if disgusted by the mere sight of her. “You lying bitch! You’re a hypocrite! Why do you know about being the underdog? You were born in the lap of luxury! You talk like you’re above us, so condescending and ignorant. You’re nothing but a miserable sow, you stupid fucking cu-AGH!“

Caenis goes down with a yelp as she trips backward over the fallen rack of costumes. The crowd outside lets out a collective gasp.

Hyacine winces. “I was worried that was going to happen.”

“You can check on her if you like,” Anaxa says.

Hyacine replies with an unimpressed stare.

“Very well.” Anaxa points to the security guards snooping with the rest of the backstage crew. “You there. Don’t you have any protocols for this kind of scenario?”

The guards sheepishly scratch their heads, but they agree that they can’t leave a woman shrieking on the floor of a performer’s dressing room. They ultimately step in to restrain Caenis, which gets one of them thwacked in the process.

“There’s no more money in Amphoreus!” Caenis shouts as she gets dragged away. “We need to secure foreign cash flow while we still can! We already imported the atrocious drivel they call music, so why stop there?!”

She continues to screech until her voice goes hoarse. It’s anyone’s guess as to where she would be taken to, though another lockable room would be the safest guess. Hyacine wonders if she should still dial the authorities if there are already members of the council present at the scene. Anaxa would much rather pit the incident on the councilmen directly, to watch them squirm if nothing else.

While everyone else attempts to resolve that fiasco in their own way, Aglaea turns to Phainon and Mydei. “I’m sorry you had to see that,” Aglaea says.

“I’m sorry you had to go through whatever that was,” Mydei replies.

Aglaea shrugs. “The price of doing business in Okhema, I’m afraid.”

“Thank you so much for doing this, Aglaea,” Phainon says. “I can’t stress how much I owe you. And Anaxa. And Hyacine.”

“And me,” Cipher says as she pops out of nowhere. “Don’t forget me.”

“And sure, you.” Phainon acknowledges Cipher by happily hooking an arm around her shoulders. His camaraderie is received with a hiss and a scratch.

Mydei regards the people mentioned and their strange preparedness, and though he’s learned a lot over the past hour, he can’t say he understood what any of it means. Phainon is the first to notice Mydei’s daze, his ecstatic grin clouding with worry when Mydei doesn’t snark about Cipher catching him off-guard.

“What’s the matter?” He asks Mydei. “Is it something Caenis said? Tell me while I can still catch up to her, because I think I’ll be okay with hitting an elderly woman.”

“I’m not fragile,” Mydei automatically defends himself. “I was thinking.”

How much of this operation was premeditated, Mydei wonders. It was impressive how everything came together, especially considering that Mydei didn’t know he’d be making a trip to the Marmoreal Arena until a

few hours ago. Did they plan on someone gatecrashing the concert, or is everyone that good at improvising? Phainon presses his thumb over the bridge of Mydei’s nose and smooths down the creases between his brow. “Could I help?” He offers.

A thousand questions clamors for Mydei’s attention.

“What now?” Is the one that he chooses.

Phainon looks at him in the same way Figgy does when Mydei pretends to throw her ball. “Elaborate?”

“Are those accusations real? Wouldn’t it be trouble for Grove?” Mydei says.

Phainon clicks his tongue at Cipher. “You didn’t tell him anything?” He asks her.

“Why? Do I get a bonus if I do?” Cipher shoots back.

“These are real charges,” Aglaea clarifies for Mydei. “You’re correct in that they’ll effect us, but not as much our inaction would.”

If Aglaea and Anaxa hadn’t raised this issue, then Grove would have continued on a downward spiral until it gets acquired by a foreign conglomerate for cheap. It could be a boon for Grove’s employees if the IPC were planning to keep everyone, but they’re more likely to treat the company as an extension of their global distribution rather than a source of music and artists.

Still, it sounds like the issue goes deeper than one woman with an apparent grudge against Aglaea. Putting a target on their backs won’t make for the best working environment, and Phainon’s team was already burdened with office politics before this.

“Grove’s gonna have bigger fish to fry anyway,” Cipher says with a shrug. “They practically got nothing going on without their precious Deliverer.”

Mydei frowns. “Why wouldn’t they have Phainon?”

“Because he’s leaving the label? Duh?”

Contrary to Phainon’s imagination, Mydei does not jump in joy upon hearing the news.

“Are you crazy?” Mydei questions the pop star, eyes wide with consternation.

“I mean it was pretty much implied when I said I was suing them,” Phainon explains in a panic. He turns to scowl at Cipher. “Why’d you say that?”

Cipher throws her arms up. “I don’t say anything, you’re pissed. I say something and you’re still pissed! What’s a girl gotta do, mime?”

“Help Hyacinthia out please,” Aglaea strongly suggests to Cipher. “It appears Anaxagoras is starting his celebrations early.”

“Wh- Oh come on.”

Cipher grumbles, but obediently walks over to where Anaxa is busy provoking 3 different people at the same time. She’s subtle with it, but Aglaea massages her temples when she catches a snippet of Anaxa’s argument. Compared to that, mediating between Phainon and Mydei is a breeze.

“Phainon isn’t planning to sue Grove for money,” Aglaea says, sighing. “He’s suing so he can nullify his contract earlier, hence the need to incite a public outcry.”

“I thought it was only a threat,” Mydei admits.

His last conversation with Phainon is not a pleasant memory. Mydei still stands by what he said, but he’s looked back on it with so much regret that he sometimes wishes he thought differently. It was stupid of Mydei anyway, to criticize Grove’s obsession with control only to turn around and dictate the way Phainon should live his life.

But Phainon apparently exists to oppose Mydei, because he changed his mind too. “I had time to think it over,” Phainon says. “And no matter how I looked at it, you were right. I could do better than sit around and wait for change.”

That’s great, but it didn’t mean Phainon was wrong when he said it was going to cost him. Mydei did some pondering of his own too, and when faced with the options, he’d rather Phainon be secure in his success than left unmoored in the music industry.

“You can’t handle downsizing,” Mydei tells him.

“Says who?” Phainon asks with a smile. “It’s not like I came out with a number one hit right out of the gate.”

“That was a lifetime ago,” Mydei claims. “Look at Sun and Thunder. The only reason it was pitched was to be a money pit.”

Phainon snorts. “Now who said that?”

“Your manager did, about a minute ago.”

“What? He did not!”

“He implied that the reunion was only possible with Caenis’s support,” Mydei says, crossing his arms.

“Hmm, I see the confusion,” Aglaea says. “It’s true that Caenis was one of the people who pushed for the project, but she was not responsible for it nor did she come up with the idea. I’m shocked no one’s told you the full story.”

Mydei shakes his head. “This was the first time I’ve seen her.”

Aglaea chuckles. “Not that. Don’t you know? You’ve worked with a board member’s wife before. Apparently you impressed her, and not long after we received a directive to start planning for Sun and Thunder’s comeback. Short-sighted people tried denying that board member’s orders, but it was futile. Her word was law.”

“And even if Sun and Thunder was engineered to fail,” Phainon cuts in. “We didn’t. The reason Caenis had to back out was because we were too successful.”

“Thanks to Aglaea,” Mydei argues.

“Thank you, Mydeimos,” Aglaea says.

Phainon pouts. “Yeah, well, even if we didn’t have Aglaea and we failed and became Amphoreus’s biggest investment failure, I would still make the same decision. It would just take longer without you to knock some sense to me.”

The way Phainon’s voice pitches low is sickening. Suddenly, Mydei is startlingly aware of his proximity to Phainon, and how difficult it would be to explain to the plethora of stagehands trickling into the room. Mydei tries retreating to a polite distance, but Phainon won’t have it, scuttling along with every step Mydei takes. He has to be kicked to be discouraged from Mydei’s personal space.

“It’s alright, Mydeimos,” Aglaea assures him. “If anyone here has anything to say about you two, they’ll answer to me.”

“I think you’re one that’s making him shy,” Phainon says. That earns him another kick.

“Me?” Aglaea echoes. “But I adore love. I think it’s beautiful that two people can find each other in spite of the chaos in the world. I would never hold it against anyone for indulging in it when they can.”

“You hear that?” Phainon asks. With a firm tug, he pulls Mydei back squarely into his arms. “No more excuses. You’re the one who said I should take what I want with my own hands, so be kind to me and stay right here from now on, okay?”

And of course Mydei makes the mistake of looking into Phainon’s glittering eyes as he speaks. “…Hm.”

“Maybe it wouldn’t hurt to tone it down a bit,” Aglaea deadpans when Phainon buries his head into Mydei’s neck.

“I know, it’s- hehe- Uh, I’m sorry b- ahaha!“ Mydei struggles to go three words without Phainon sending him into a giggling fit.

A loud flash goes off by the door. Phainon at least has the decency to stop and allow Mydei the chance to identify the culprit.

“Fuck,” Leonnius swears, phone pointed straight at the men of the hour. “I meant to take a video.”

“Excuse me.” Anaxa pauses his current quarrel to switch victims. “This area is off limits to reporters.”

“Oh no, we’re not reporters,” Hephaestion quickly intervenes. “We’re Mydei’s friends!”

Leonnius and Peucesta book it before Hephaestion could finish explaining. The two make it a quarter of the way down the hall before Cipher intercepts them with a tackle.

Mydei winces at their screams. “I need to sort that out,” he says.

This time when he pulls away, Mydei makes sure to grab onto Phainon’s hand to keep him from getting the wrong idea. It’s unclear how long Mydei would have to put up with this, but he doesn’t see himself complaining for a long, long while.

“Go save your friends,” Aglaea tells him. “But once you’re done there, I need to have another word with you.”

Mydei looks back at her. A touch of seriousness hardens her features once more, but Phainon’s hand in his lessens the sting of whatever bad news it could be.

“No need to be wary,” Aglaea says, the corner of her mouth raising by a hair. “There’s just an offer that I’d like to make.”
